# Connector & recipe catalog

What ships in the box: **57 connector templates** across **16 categories**, carrying **240 recipes** — pre-authored, runnable workflows you clone instead of starting from a blank page.

A **template** connects a system: base URL, auth flow, endpoint schema, and a vendor-basics Skill. A **recipe** is a complete workflow shipped on that template — say what you want in a conversation and sk clones the closest recipe as your starting draft. Curated, scenario-first picks: [Use cases](use-cases.md).

Grouped by template. **Trigger** is how the workflow starts: `request` (on demand — chat, CLI, MCP, REST), `schedule` (cron), or `webhook` (an external system calls in). **Also uses** lists connectors beyond the template's own.

| `list-indexes` | Return index name, columns, and uniqueness for a target table. | request | — |
| `list-schemas` | Enumerate non-system schemas. | request | — |

| `row-count` | SELECT COUNT(*) for the supplied table. | request | — |

<!-- Source: docs/start-here.md -->

# Start here

sk takes the work your team does the same way every week and runs it for you — reviewed
before it goes live, permission-checked every time, and recorded so you can always show
what happened. This page assumes you know nothing about sk. There is no code on it.

---

## The problem

Every organisation has work that runs the same way every time.

Here is one, told to the end. A new customer pays. Someone notices the payment, copies
the customer into the CRM, and tells the team in chat. Three systems, the same steps,
every time — and when that someone is in a meeting, on holiday, or simply tired, the CRM
is out of date and nobody heard about the sale.

## What sk does

You describe what should happen, in ordinary sentences:

> *"When a new customer pays in Stripe, create the contact in HubSpot and post it to our
> sales channel in Slack."*

sk works out how to do it, shows you what it built, and waits. You look at it. If it is
right, you approve it. From then on, it happens by itself.

That exact process ships in the box as a blueprint (`stripe/new-customer-enrich-notify`),
alongside hundreds of others — and the same shape covers everything from a daily
infrastructure digest to a company knowledge base that answers questions with sources. Real cases, each
traceable to something that ships or something we run ourselves:
[Use cases](use-cases.md).

![Connecting a system in the sk terminal: pick the target, enter credentials, test the connection, save](_tapes/out/operator-onboard.gif)

## Why this is not just automation

A tool that writes an email for you is harmless. A tool that reaches into your real
systems — pays invoices, changes customer records, sends mail in your company's name — is
not.

The useful comparison is a new colleague. They can take a lot of work off your hands. But
you want three questions answered before you hand them the keys:

| The question you'd ask about a new colleague | How sk answers it |
|---|---|
| **What are they even allowed to touch?** | Each process gets exactly the access it needs, and nothing beyond it |
| **Do they check with someone before doing something expensive?** | Before anything is sent, paid, or deleted, the request goes to a person |
| **Can I see afterwards what they did?** | Every run is written down: when, what, with what result, and who approved it |

That last one is the real point. Plenty of tools can automate something. sk automates in a
way you can **account for afterwards** — to your manager, your customer, your auditor.

## The AI builds it. It does not decide while it runs.

This is the part people most often get backwards, so slowly:

**While it is being built**, an assistant helps. It understands your sentence, looks at the
system you are pointing it at, and writes the process down. That is what saves the weeks a
developer used to spend.

**While it runs**, the assistant is out of the loop. A person looked at the finished process
and approved it. From then on, what happens is settled — every Monday, the same thing. The
AI does not reconsider each week what it feels like doing this time.

Why that matters: something that decides freely every time will eventually do something
surprising. For holiday photos, charming. For bank transfers, not.

## Where you do what

sk meets you in several places, and they are not interchangeable. Pick by the job:

| What you want to do | Where |
|---|---|
| Run something and read the result | Your team chat, or a browser AI client |
| Ask how your team normally does something | A coding agent, or a browser AI client |
| Describe a brand-new process for the first time | A conversation — in the terminal or in chat |
| Change one line of a process that already exists | The `sk` command line |
| Go back to an earlier version | The `sk` command line |
| Approve something | The link you were sent, or the command line |
| Connect a new system and enter its credentials | The setup wizard, or the credential page |
| Have something run on a timetable, or when an event fires | A schedule, or a webhook — a URL another system calls when something happens. Nobody has to be present |

The rule underneath all of it: **a chat window runs things; it does not rewrite them.** That
is deliberate. Changing what a process does should pass through something a person can
read. The long version, with worked examples, is
[Choosing your surface](authors/choosing-your-surface.md).

## What you end up with

Three results, not a toolkit:

1. **Your most expensive manual routines run by themselves.** Two to four weeks, and you
   sign off by watching one real run and checking the result.
2. **Your AI experiments become reviewable.** What three people wired together by hand
   becomes one operation your IT leadership will put their name to.
3. **A system stays connected.** When a vendor changes their interface, sk notices and
   suggests the repair, instead of quietly breaking.

## What sk does not do

**It does not move your old data into a new system.** Bulk record migration with
field-by-field reconciliation is a different job and needs different tooling.

**It does not invent work.** If nobody described it and nobody approved it, nothing runs.

## Where to go next

- **You want to try it** → [Self-host quickstart](developers/self-host.md) — from nothing to
  a running engine (the piece of software that does the work) and a first process of your own.
- **Someone already runs sk for you** → [Author quickstart](authors/quickstart.md).
- **You use a coding agent** (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, …) →
  [Use sk from a coding agent](authors/coding-agents.md).
- **You want the whole map** → [Documentation index](README.md).
- **A word did not make sense** → [Glossary](concepts/glossary.md).

<!-- Source: docs/use-cases.md -->

# Use cases

What people actually run on sk — as cases, not features. Every row below is traceable:
**recipe** rows name a blueprint that ships in the box (clone it, bind your credentials,
run — the full list is the [catalog](catalog.md)); **our production** rows name a workflow
from the deployment we run sk's own company operations on. We dogfood sk daily; those are
our workflows, not customer references.

sk shows up in five shapes. Pick yours.

| Shape | In one line |
|---|---|
| [Personal AI assistant](#personal-ai-assistant) | One person, their own tools, running the same day |
| [Corporate LLM](#corporate-llm) | The company answers questions — with sources, or an honest "it's not in there" |
| [Agentic workflows](#agentic-workflows) | An agent builds it, an agent invokes it — the run itself never improvises |
| [Domain-specific AI](#domain-specific-ai) | sk learns a whole field of work, then every workflow in it arrives right |
| [Knowledge-base integration](#knowledge-base-integration) | Documents become searchable knowledge every AI client can ground on |

---

## Personal AI assistant

The smallest useful sk: one person pointing it at the tools they already use. No team
setup, no governance ceremony — that arrives later, when it matters.

| Situation | sk does | Systems | Runs on |
|---|---|---|---|
| A pricing page has no API and the price changes | Renders the page in headless Chrome, reads the price, mails you on change | Browserless + Gmail | our production |
| Receipts from one vendor are scattered across months of inbox | Filters messages with attachments into one list | Gmail | our production |
| "What's on my plate today?" | Pulls your open tickets with full details | Jira | our production |
| A long article, five minutes of time | Renders the page, summarizes it | Browserless + Anthropic | our production |
| Infrastructure cost creeps unnoticed | Mails a daily resource digest, grouped by project | DigitalOcean + Gmail | our production |
| A JS-heavy dashboard should land in your inbox every morning | Scrapes at 07:00, extracts, emails the digest | Browserless + SendGrid | recipe `browserless/scrape-then-email-digest` |

The pattern: **describe it once in a sentence, approve what sk built, and it runs from
then on** — on demand, on a schedule, or when an event fires.
Start: [Author quickstart](authors/quickstart.md).

---

## Corporate LLM

Your team asks questions where they already work — Slack, Teams, Google Chat, a browser AI
client — and the company answers from its own knowledge.

| Situation | sk does | See |
|---|---|---|
| "How do we normally do this here?" | Searches your knowledge sources and answers **with a Sources footer** naming what it read — or says plainly that the answer isn't in there, instead of inventing one | [Answer provenance & honest refusal](concepts/governance-and-audit.md#answer-provenance-and-honest-refusal) |
| The team lives in chat | The sk bot answers questions and runs saved workflows there. Deliberately: **a chat window runs things; it does not rewrite them** — changing a process goes through a surface a person can review | [Chat channels](operators/chat.md) |
| "Who saw what?" | The same RBAC and the same append-only audit trail as every other door — chat is not a side entrance | [Governance & audit](concepts/governance-and-audit.md) |

What makes this a *corporate* LLM rather than a chatbot: the knowledge is curated (a human
approves what gets remembered), the answers carry provenance, and every interaction is
permission-checked and recorded. Details:
[Ask your company's knowledge](authors/asking-your-knowledge.md).

---

## Agentic workflows

The term needs defining, because sk draws the line deliberately:

> **Agentic** here means: *an agent authors the workflow, and an agent can invoke it* —
> every saved workflow is a callable `wf_<slug>` tool on the MCP surface.
> It does **not** mean a model re-decides what to do on each run. Once approved, the
> control flow is fixed — that determinism is what makes the rest safe to leave running.

What the fixed control flow can still express:

| Situation | sk does | Runs on |
|---|---|---|
| A PR must merge only after human sign-off | Opens the PR, waits up to 24 h for an external approval signal, then merges — or abandons on timeout | recipe `github/merge-pr-after-approval` |
| A new customer should be enriched and announced | Stripe customer → HubSpot contact → Slack notification, one workflow across three systems | recipe `stripe/new-customer-enrich-notify` |
| Trial users need day-1/3/7/14 touchpoints | Daily sweep with persistent per-contact state driving the cadence | recipe `intercom/trial-nurture-day-1-3-7-14-via-state` |
| A booking must never half-commit | Debit and credit in one database transaction | recipe `postgres/atomic-debit-credit-double-entry` |
| A failed payment needs eyes now | Signature-verified webhook → redacted Slack alert | recipe `stripe/on-charge-failed-notify-slack` |
| Market signals should become published content | An eight-workflow chain: collect → normalize → analyze → generate → publish → **acceptance check** | our production (`radar-*`) |
| Metrics live in five systems and the report is manual | Daily/weekly/monthly/yearly rollups across analytics, search, repos, and infrastructure — plus retention of old artifacts | our production (`mission-control-*`) |

Which building block carries which shape:

| Building block | Carries |
|---|---|
| `request` — five drivers: HTTP, GraphQL, SQL, S3, MCP | Any system call, uniform retry/backoff/audit |
| `loop` + `transform` | Collect and normalize collections |
| `branch` | Deterministic gates — "if refund, else charge" |
| `parallel` | Fan out independent calls concurrently |
| `call` | Compose workflows into pipelines |
| `wait_for_event` | A human in the loop — the run pauses for a signed signal, with a timeout path |
| `output_schema` + validation expressions | Business invariants that fail the run instead of shipping bad data |
| `response_filters` | PII masking at the tenant boundary, whichever step produced the data |

The model behind the line: [Workflow execution](concepts/workflows.md) ·
[Reversibility & trust domains](concepts/reversibility-and-trust-domains.md).

---

## Domain-specific AI

A single workflow answers one question. A **domain** — your expense policy, your editorial
style, your compliance framework — is the shared context that makes *every* workflow in it
correct. You model one with three primitives: a **Connector** (the system of record),
**Skills** (rules the AI follows), and **Knowledge Sources** (documents the AI searches).

| Domain | Skill prescribes | Knowledge Source informs | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Expense approval | Two-approver rule over €1,000, receipt requirement | The expense policy PDF — thresholds, per-diem rates | worked end to end in [Model a domain](authors/model-a-domain.md) |
| Editorial house style | Punctuation and style conventions the AI must follow | The style corpus it can cite | locked as an eval fixture in the repo (`knowledge-retrieval-blogde-golden`) |
| Vendor quirks | "Stripe returns 200 with an error object for validation failures" — and 44 more `*-basics` Skills like it, shipped per connector template | vendor docs, ingested per connector | shipped in the box |

Honesty note: what ships at boot is **product knowledge** — sk's own reference plus
per-vendor API mechanics. Your business domain is what *you* bring, and the trio above is
how. The worked path: [Model a domain](authors/model-a-domain.md).

---

## Knowledge-base integration

Getting knowledge *in*, keeping it current, and letting every AI client ground on it.

| Situation | sk does | Runs on |
|---|---|---|
| The knowledge lives on a website | Crawls the sitemap, converts every article to clean Markdown for ingestion | recipe `web-scraper/crawl-sitemap-to-markdown` |
| A document exists only as rendered HTML | Converts it to Markdown for downstream extraction | recipe `jina-reader/sec-filing-to-markdown` |
| Every coding-agent session starts from zero | Claude Code / Codex sessions open with a briefing of your approved domain rules, and can look runbooks up instead of inventing them | [Use sk from a coding agent](authors/coding-agents.md) |
| What a session learned evaporates when it ends | Capture an observation → human review → approved, domain-tagged rule the next session carries | our production (`capture-dogfood-observation` → `promote-dogfood-learning`) |
| Nobody knows where the knowledge has gaps | A weekly coverage report over the knowledge base | our production (`wikikit-coverage-weekly`) |
| A model should read these docs itself | The engine serves `/llms.txt`, `/llms-full.txt`, and every page under `/llms/<path>` unauthenticated | [Docs index](README.md#pipe-these-docs-into-an-llm) |

The loop that compounds: knowledge grounds authoring, runs surface patterns, humans
promote what worked — see [Knowledge & skills](concepts/knowledge-and-skills.md).

---

## Where to go next

- **Try one of these today** → [Author quickstart](authors/quickstart.md)
- **Browse everything that ships** → [Connector & recipe catalog](catalog.md)
- **Understand why this holds up in production** → [Architecture overview](concepts/overview.md)

# Concepts

Read this section and you can predict what sk will do before you run it — and say why, in the same words as everyone else on your team. Six pages cover the whole model: how a system gets connected, how a process runs, where the AI helps and where it stops, and what gets written down along the way.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Overview["Architecture Overview<br/>the whole picture"]
    Glossary["Concepts & Domain Model<br/>the vocabulary"]
    Connectors["Connectors & Integration"]
    Workflows["Workflow Execution"]
    Knowledge["Knowledge & Skills"]
    Governance["Governance & Audit"]

    Overview --> Glossary
    Glossary --> Connectors
    Glossary --> Workflows
    Connectors --> Workflows
    Workflows --> Knowledge
    Workflows --> Governance
```

Start with the **Overview** for the big picture, then the **Glossary** to lock the vocabulary. From there, **Connectors** feed **Workflows**, **Knowledge & Skills** shape how the AI authors them, and **Governance & Audit** wraps every run.

| Page | What it covers |
|---|---|
| [Architecture Overview](overview.md) | The first mental model of sk — the major pieces and how they connect. |
| [Concepts & Domain Model](glossary.md) | One vocabulary, defined once: Workflow, Connector, Credential, Audit Log, and the rest. |
| [Connectors & Integration](connectors.md) | Drivers, Connector Templates, and Credentials — authenticate a system once, reuse it everywhere. |
| [Workflow Execution](workflows.md) | The lifecycle, execution model, eight Step kinds, triggers, versioning, scheduling, and self-healing. |
| [Knowledge & Skills](knowledge-and-skills.md) | How Knowledge Sources and Skills shape the AI that authors workflows. |
| [FAQ](faq.md) | Fast answers on workflows, skills, and knowledge sources — each pointing to the page that covers it in full. |
| [Governance & Audit](governance-and-audit.md) | Permission checks, immutable records, and the audit trail behind every run. |
| [Reversibility & Trust Domains](reversibility-and-trust-domains.md) | How much autonomy a piece of work should get — and why authoring and execution are different jobs. |

<!-- Source: docs/concepts/connectors.md -->

# Connectors & Integration

> **Audience:** Engineers wiring sk to external systems, operators curating the catalogue

Connect a system once, then use it from every workflow you ever write — and never let its secret touch a workflow definition, an AI prompt, or a log. That one-time setup replaces the integration glue each project used to rewrite from scratch: it is typed, authenticated, monitored, and audited from the moment you save it. Cloudflare and Firebase/Firestore ship ready to use; anything else you point sk at.

A Connector combines three independently-evolving layers: a **Driver** (protocol), a **Connector Template** (target-specific config + context), and a **Credential** (vault-managed secret).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Driver["Driver<br/>http · graphql · postgres · s3 · mcp"]
    Template["Connector Template<br/>auth + docs + skill"]
    Cred["Credential<br/>AEAD-encrypted in vault"]
    Conn["Connector<br/>tenant-scoped · versioned"]
    Step["Workflow Step<br/>references by id"]

    Driver --> Conn
    Template --> Conn
    Cred --> Conn
    Conn --> Step
```

Each layer evolves independently. A Workflow Step references the Connector by id — the raw credential never enters the workflow definition, the AI context, or any log.

---

## What a Connector Is

A Connector is a configured, authenticated connection to an external integration boundary. It is not a generic HTTP client, and it is not an ad hoc integration configured per-workflow. A Connector is a first-class platform resource: typed, validated, monitored, and reusable across any number of workflows.

The design separates three concerns that are often conflated. The Driver handles the protocol — how requests are formed, sent, and parsed. The Connector Template provides connector-specific configuration and context — what this particular integration target looks like and how to work with it. The Credential provides secure authentication — the secrets needed to connect. Each layer has a distinct responsibility, and each can evolve independently.

This separation has practical consequences. Multiple Connectors can share the same Template — for example, a production Stripe account and a staging Stripe account can each be a separate Connector built from the same Stripe Template, with different Credentials and different Environment tags. The platform can route workflows to the appropriate account based on execution mode without any workflow-level logic.

---

## The Five Drivers

Drivers are the protocol layer. Every Connector in sk uses one of five built-in drivers: `http`, `graphql`, `postgres`, `s3`, and `mcp`. These are the protocols the execution engine dispatches end-to-end at runtime.

The **HTTP driver** handles REST APIs. It manages request construction, response parsing, pagination patterns, and error normalization. When a Step calls an HTTP Connector, the driver handles the protocol details so the workflow step only needs to describe what to call and what to do with the result.

The **GraphQL driver** handles GraphQL APIs. It manages query and mutation construction, variable binding, and schema awareness. Workflows that target GraphQL APIs benefit from the driver's understanding of the schema structure — the AI can propose specific queries rather than generic HTTP calls.

The **PostgreSQL driver** handles direct database connections. It manages query execution, parameterized inputs, and result set handling. This driver enables workflows that read from or write to relational databases directly, without requiring an intermediate API layer.

The **S3 driver** handles object storage. It manages bucket operations, presigned URL generation, and streaming transfers. This covers not just AWS S3 but any S3-compatible object store.

The **MCP driver** handles a remote Model Context Protocol server over streamable HTTP. It negotiates the session, keeps the remote's tool manifest, and exposes each remote tool under the connector's own name. Unlike the four above it holds a live session between calls rather than opening one per request — an MCP handshake is expensive enough that paying for it per step would cost more than the call itself.

An external MCP server is therefore a connector like any other: it is created, listed, patched, enabled, disabled and deleted through the same connector surface, appears in the same catalog and the same tenant snapshot, and carries its credential in the same vault. Two operations are driver-specific because no other driver has them — `POST /v1/connectors/{id}/mcp/inspect` forces one handshake and reports what the remote actually serves, and `POST /v1/connectors/{id}/mcp/authorize` begins the interactive OAuth 2.1 round-trip for a server that publishes its authorization server through protected-resource metadata rather than declaring one in config.

Every Connector in sk uses one of these five drivers. The set is closed — you cannot register a sixth protocol at runtime — but the MCP driver is the extension point that closure used to foreclose. Anything that speaks MCP is reachable by pointing a connector at it: no driver to write, no engine build, no deploy. Where the other four drivers each cover one wire protocol, the MCP driver covers a whole ecosystem of servers, and a vendor shipping an MCP server is a connector you create in a minute rather than an integration you wait for.

The driver is also how the connector catalog is grouped: listings present connectors in blocks by driver, and `category` on each entry (plus a `category` filter) mirrors the workflow catalog so both inventories read the same way on every surface. Unlike workflows — whose blocks are derived from naming — a connector needs nothing derived: it already carries the axis that groups it usefully.

To go the other way and ask *which workflows depend on this connector* — the question that matters before rotating a credential or retiring a system — filter the **workflow** list by connector. See [Finding a Workflow in a Large Catalog](workflows.md#finding-a-workflow-in-a-large-catalog).

### GraphQL vs REST: when to pick which

Several major APIs — GitHub, Linear, Monday, Shopify — offer both REST and GraphQL endpoints. The built-in template catalogue ships both where appropriate (for example `github` and `github-graphql`). Choose by what the workflow actually does:

- **Deep read traversals** (repository → issues → comments → labels): prefer GraphQL. One query replaces many REST roundtrips; the cost-based rate limit is more forgiving than REST's per-request budget.
- **Write operations** (create an issue, merge a PR, commit a file): prefer REST. GraphQL mutations at these providers are incomplete — organisation-admin mutations often don't exist.
- **Simple CRUD on one resource**: REST is usually shorter to author and debug.

The two connectors can coexist in a tenant — one `github` connector for writes, one `github-graphql` connector for reads — sharing the same credential (a PAT with `repo + read:org` works on both endpoints).

---

## The Connector Template Catalog

Templates are what make the AI's proposals accurate. Without templates, the AI cannot propose the correct authentication pattern, suggest the right endpoints, or explain the connector target's specific behaviors and limitations.

sk ships 57 Connector Templates covering the most common enterprise services: Stripe, Salesforce, HubSpot, GitHub, Jira, Slack, Notion, Cloudflare, Firebase/Firestore, Google services, AWS services, databases, and more.

A Template is more than a configuration skeleton. It includes: the appropriate driver, the authentication configuration for that service (OAuth2 scopes, API key placement, basic auth conventions), links to documentation that the platform will index, setup guidance the AI presents when a user configures the Connector, and example Skill content the AI can draw on when proposing integrations.

Templates are the reason the AI can propose accurate integrations rather than generic API calls. The curated knowledge about each connector target is baked into the template, not assembled from general training data at authoring time.

---

## Authentication and Credential Management

Supported patterns, the ones enterprise systems actually use:

- **API key** — header, query, or custom scheme.
- **OAuth2** — authorisation code and client credentials flows.
- **Basic auth** — username + password.
- **AWS SigV4** — signed requests for AWS-compatible surfaces.

**OAuth2 is managed end-to-end by the engine.** An operator configures the Connector once; the platform detects expiry, refreshes, and rotates tokens with no workflow involvement.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Run["Workflow step<br/>runs"] --> Check{Token<br/>expired?}
    Check -- no --> Call["Call vendor API"]
    Check -- yes --> Refresh["Engine uses<br/>refresh_token"]
    Refresh --> Store["Re-encrypt + store<br/>new tokens in vault"]
    Store --> Call
    Call --> Done(["Step result"])
```

![Connecting a system in the sk terminal: pick the target, enter credentials, test the connection, save](../_tapes/out/operator-onboard.gif)

All secrets live in the Credential Vault: encrypted at rest, never logged, never exposed outside the engine. Workflows and Steps reference Credentials by name, not value — sk can propose, configure, and audit integrations without a secret ever surfacing in a workflow definition, a log, or a conversation transcript.

**End-User Credentials** extend this for multi-user scenarios. A user supplies their own credentials for a Connector, and the platform acts as that user when executing on their behalf — proper delegation, not credential sharing.

---

## Schema Versions and Drift

External APIs change. Fields are renamed, endpoints move, new error codes appear, response shapes evolve. A Connector that worked last month may not work the same way today.

sk tracks schema versions per Connector endpoint, Workflow, and Step. Successful responses accumulate observed fields into a contract, so request-dependent or optional fields can appear and disappear without being misclassified as removals. Incompatible type changes remain proactive drift signals; an actual missing path or failed validation is still detected reactively from the affected execution.

Drift is detected from actual execution results, not from periodic polling. The signal comes from real workflow runs encountering real changes in the connected boundary. When drift is detected, it becomes the trigger for the self-healing process described in the execution document.

---

## Health and Validation

Every Connector can be tested independently of any workflow. The engine validates the connection, authenticates with the configured Credentials, and reports the result along with connection latency. Connector tests and workflow request steps share the same underlying request execution path, so a successful connector test reflects the same transport behavior a workflow will use.

Connector validation is available on demand and during authoring. Operators do not need to wait for a full workflow failure before checking whether a Connector is reachable, authenticated, and returning the expected shape.

A draft connector that does not yet have a credential cannot be probed. The probe path returns a structured `credential_required` envelope rather than silently sending an unauthenticated request. `sk` collects the value in its masked terminal form. MCP clients use a single-use URL elicitation for an unsaved static-credential draft; the submission stages the credential in engine memory, resumes the same conversation, and the next green probe persists the connector and encrypted credential atomically. The draft never has to be saved unauthenticated just to obtain a connector id.

Templates may attach bounded, non-secret headers to their health endpoint. The header schema rejects authentication, cookie, transport, and CR/LF-bearing values; a saved credential remains the only source of authentication. This is used for vendor-required protocol headers such as Notion's `Notion-Version`, so a connector probe exercises the same valid request shape as runtime traffic.

---

## Audited DEV to PROD Promotion

An admin can promote a persisted DEV connector without reading or re-entering its credential. The operation is one transaction: connector state, credential state, promotion idempotency record, and immutable audit entries either all commit or all roll back. It requires the dedicated `connector:promote` permission and an `Idempotency-Key`; only the SHA-256 digest of that key is persisted.

Two strategies make retention explicit:

| Strategy | Connector identity | Credential handling | DEV after success |
|---|---|---|---|
| `copy` | Creates a new PROD connector id | Decrypts and re-encrypts supported static credentials under a new credential id and AAD; token-mint caches are cleared | Retained |
| `move` | Keeps the connector id | Keeps credential ids, ciphertext, OAuth refresh state, and end-user bindings; only the environment changes | Removed |

`copy` deliberately rejects OAuth/OAuth-client state and connectors with end-user credential bindings: duplicating either would create ambiguous refresh ownership or silently lose user bindings. Use `move` for those connectors. A conflicting active PROD connector with the same tenant-scoped slug is also rejected. Copy carries the pinned template snapshot, connector configuration, self-description links, circuit/health state, and static credential; ingested document rows and observed schema history stay attached to the DEV connector.

Every successful operation writes `connector.environment_promoted` and one `credential.environment_promoted` event per affected credential. Audit metadata contains ids, environments, strategy, request source, and the idempotency-key digest—never plaintext or ciphertext.

The conversational action is `promote_connector`. The equivalent CLI command is:

```bash
sk connectors promote <dev-connector-id> --to prod --strategy copy
sk connectors promote <dev-connector-id> --to prod --strategy move --yes
```

The REST form is `POST /v1/connectors/{id}/promote` with a required `Idempotency-Key` header and body `{ "target_environment": "prod", "strategy": "copy" | "move" }`. A new copy returns 201; a move or idempotent replay returns 200.

---

## OpenAPI Connector Import

`import_connector_from_spec` creates a connector draft from inline OpenAPI JSON/YAML, Google
REST Discovery JSON, or an HTTP(S) spec URL. The equivalent REST surface is
`POST /v1/connector-templates/import` with `source: "openapi"` or
`source: "google_discovery"`. URL-fetched specification bodies are streamed with a 50 MiB
(52,428,800 byte) hard limit: a declared oversized body is rejected before reading, while an
unknown-length stream is cancelled on the first byte over budget.

The importer reads top-level `servers` and `components.securitySchemes`. Absolute servers are
preferred over the spec-host origin, relative servers resolve against the spec URL, and server
variables use their declared defaults. Supported authentication hints are Bearer, OAuth2,
header/query API keys, and Basic; Bearer wins when the document declares several alternatives.
Google Discovery imports recursively read nested resources and methods, build the service base
URL from `baseUrl` or `rootUrl` + `servicePath`, resolve request/response schema references, and
derive OAuth2 or query-key authentication hints. The public import response shape is unchanged.

Cloudflare now ships as the built-in `cloudflare` template. Create it directly, then add a newly
created least-privilege API token through the credential command's masked/secret input path:

```bash
sk connectors create --template cloudflare --name cloudflare-dev
sk credentials set <CONNECTOR_ID> --mode bearer --token '<NEW_SCOPED_TOKEN>'
sk connectors test <CONNECTOR_ID>
```

The template uses `https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4`, Bearer authentication, the official
[Cloudflare OpenAPI schema](https://github.com/cloudflare/api-schemas), and three read-only
starter recipes: token verification, zone listing, and DNS-record listing. A token that has
appeared in chat, source code, shell history, or logs must be revoked and replaced before use.
The Global API Key is intentionally not the default.

The same official schema can still be imported explicitly when testing or customizing a draft:

```json
{
  "source": "openapi",
  "content": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cloudflare/api-schemas/main/openapi.json",
  "name": "Cloudflare",
  "environment": "dev"
}
```

The resulting draft auto-matches the same built-in template. Never put a token in the spec URL,
public spec-fetch headers, a chat message, connector config, or workflow.

Firebase/Firestore ships as template revision 2 and ingests the official Firestore v1 Google
Discovery document. Configure a Google OAuth client, create the connector, and authorize it:

```bash
sk connector-templates set-oauth --slug firebase \
  --client-id '<GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID>' \
  --client-secret '<GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET>'
sk connectors create --template firebase --name firebase-dev
sk auth --connector-id <CONNECTOR_ID>
```

The built-in OAuth scopes are `cloud-platform` and `datastore`. For end-user requests governed
by Firestore Security Rules, a short-lived Firebase Authentication ID token may instead be stored
as a Bearer credential. A service-account JSON key is not an OAuth client secret and must not be
pasted into the OAuth fields.

This 50 MiB allowance is specific to connector-spec import. Live API Discovery below remains
bounded to 16 MiB and returns a curated, cached endpoint index rather than a connector draft.

---

## Live API Discovery

Connectors that ship with an `ingestion_url` (the OpenAPI or Swagger spec) can be inspected without authoring a single workflow step. The conversational tool `discover_connector_endpoints` and the matching HTTP route fetch and parse the spec server-side, returning a curated index of endpoints with auth schemes, parameters, and pagination hints.

A chain of fallback strategies runs in order — postgres introspection, OpenAPI direct fetch, GraphQL introspection, Swagger UI scrape, llms.txt, HTML/well-known-paths scrape, and a last-resort Playwright crawl. The first strategy that produces a valid spec wins. Each attempt is logged so operators can see where a discovery succeeded or failed.

Discovery results cache for 24 hours per tenant in `knowledge_sources` of kind `connector_endpoint_index`. Pass `force_refresh: true` to bypass the cache. Refreshes write an audit row of kind `knowledge_source.refreshed` with `reason: "discovery_cache_refresh"`.

The conversational agent is expected to call `discover_connector_endpoints` BEFORE proposing endpoints to a workflow. Endpoint guesses against an unfamiliar API are an anti-pattern.

CI scripts and SDK callers can drive the same pipeline directly via `POST /v1/connectors/discover`. The route requires the `connector:read` permission and accepts one of `template_id`, `ingestion_url`, or `base_url` plus an optional `force_refresh: true`.

```bash
curl -X POST "$SK_BASE_URL/v1/connectors/discover" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SK_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "template_id": "stripe" }'
```

The response is `{ source: "cache" | "fresh", cache_key, result: DiscoveryResult }`. Failed discoveries (every strategy bailed) surface as HTTP 503 with `code: "discovery_unavailable"`; bad input (no template_id / base_url / ingestion_url, or an unknown template id) is HTTP 400.

---

## Connector Self-Description

Outcome: the AI grounds a workflow in a connector's *own* published docs instead of guessing from general training data — and it does so without burning the token budget on prose nobody asked for.

Many target systems publish their own machine-readable docs: an `llms.txt` index, a full `llms-full.txt` corpus, an OpenAPI spec, or a GraphQL introspection endpoint. Each Connector remembers where those live in lightweight `self_description.links[]` metadata. Four link kinds are tracked:

| `kind` | What it points at |
|---|---|
| `llms_txt` | The connector target's [llms-txt](https://llmstxt.org) index — a curated map of its docs. |
| `llms_full` | The full single-fetch prose corpus (e.g. `llms-full.txt`). |
| `openapi` | The OpenAPI / Swagger spec. |
| `graphql` | The GraphQL introspection endpoint. |

**Links only — never bodies.** Each entry records the URL, a `source` (`discovery`, `self_healing`, or `manual`), and a `discovered_at` timestamp. The full document bodies are *not* copied into a new store; the connector keeps only the pointer. (The discovery cache, described above, is a separate store that holds richer parsed content; self-description deliberately stays a thin set of links so it never bloats.)

**How links are captured.** A link is recorded whenever discovery runs against a connector — the `discover_connector_endpoints` call forwards the `connector_id`, so a successful spec fetch leaves a remembered pointer behind. A bounded self-healing scheduler pass then broadens and refreshes the set, probing every published surface so the links stay current as the target's docs move.

**How links ground authoring.** When a connector is in scope during workflow authoring, the context-assembler surfaces a single pointer line — *"This connector publishes its own docs — fetch on demand with `fetch_connector_self_description`: …"* — covering the connector's llms / OpenAPI / GraphQL links. Compact endpoint signatures (operation names plus arguments) come inline from the discovery index for OpenAPI and GraphQL connectors. The full prose corpus is **not** eagerly inlined; the authoring LLM fetches it lazily, only when it needs deeper detail, which keeps the prompt budget bounded.

The fetch itself is the conversational / MCP tool `fetch_connector_self_description` — `{ connector_id?, kind?: "llms" | "openapi" | "graphql" | "all" }`. It live-fetches the remembered link transiently (egress-guarded and size-capped) and persists nothing. It is an MCP tool, not an HTTP route, so it does not appear in the engine OpenAPI spec.

---

## Ad-hoc Invocation

Once a connector is persisted, the agent can invoke any endpoint against it for sampling, pagination validation, or response-shape inspection. The conversational tool `call_connector` accepts `{ connector_id, method, path, query?, headers?, body?, timeout_ms? }` and returns the response status, headers, body, latency, and a truncation flag.

`call_connector` is RBAC-checked (`connector:read`), audited (`connector.invoked`), and always confirm-before-execution per the conversational tool policies. Response bodies above ~8 KB are truncated in the tool result with `truncated: true` and `body_byte_count` so the prompt budget stays bounded; the full response is available via the egress telemetry.

Driver coverage differs between the two surfaces. The conversational `call_connector` tool covers HTTP, GraphQL, Postgres, and S3; the REST route below covers HTTP and GraphQL. An unsupported driver returns a structured `driver_not_supported_for_call_connector` envelope and points at `author_workflow` as the path to author a single-step workflow that invokes the driver.

**MCP connectors are not reachable through `call_connector` on either surface.** A remote MCP tool needs a tool name and typed arguments rather than a method and a path, so it is invoked one of two ways: as a `request` step carrying an `mcp` block (see [Workflows → step kinds](./workflows.md#step-kinds)), or from chat, where every tool the connected server publishes already appears in the palette as `mcp_<connector-slug>__<tool>`. To ask what a server serves without calling anything, use `POST /v1/connectors/{id}/mcp/inspect` (`sk connectors mcp-inspect`).

The same surface is reachable as `POST /v1/connectors/{id}/call` for CI scripts and SDK callers. The route applies the saved credential, emits a `connector.invoked` audit row, and returns `{ status, headers, body, latency_ms, body_byte_count, truncated, health, metadata }`.

```bash
curl -X POST "$SK_BASE_URL/v1/connectors/$CONNECTOR_ID/call" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SK_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "method": "GET", "path": "/v2/droplets", "query": { "per_page": 10 } }'
```

Errors are typed: 403 on policy denial, 404 when the connector id is unknown, 422 when the connector exists but is unprocessable (no credential, unsupported driver, GraphQL body shape mismatch). Unsupported drivers carry `details.error_code: "driver_not_supported_for_call_connector"` so SDK callers can disambiguate without parsing the message.

---

## Conversational Creation Contract

Connector creation through the conversational surface follows a single, observable contract. Two persistence paths, one for non-OAuth credentials and one for OAuth2:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Start(["Agent intent:<br/>new connector"])
    Discover["discover_connector_endpoints"]
    Draft["start_connector_from_template<br/>or _from_description"]
    AuthType{Auth type}
    AskForm["secure credential input<br/>(masked in sk · URL-mode over MCP)"]
    AskFormOA["ask_user_form +<br/>commit_intent: save_connector_draft"]
    Probe["probe_connector_draft"]
    OAuth["authenticate_oauth<br/>(browser opens)"]
    ProbeOA["probe_connector_draft<br/>(verify token)"]
    Saved(["Connector + Credential<br/>persisted atomically<br/>auto_saved: true"])
    Call["call_connector<br/>(iterate · paginate · sample)"]

    Start --> Discover --> Draft --> AuthType
    AuthType -- non-OAuth<br/>(bearer/header/query/basic/sigv4) --> AskForm --> Probe --> Saved
    AuthType -- OAuth2 --> AskFormOA --> OAuth --> ProbeOA --> Saved
    Saved --> Call
```

*Both paths end at the same atomic persistence: a green probe (non-OAuth) or a successful OAuth callback (OAuth2) commits the connector and the encrypted credential in one transaction. The diagnostic tools `save_connector_draft` remain available for force-saves and credential rotation.*

**Non-OAuth (bearer / header / query / basic / aws_sigv4):**

1. The agent calls `discover_connector_endpoints` to ground its endpoint choices in real spec data.
2. The agent calls `start_connector_from_template` (or `start_connector_from_description`) to create a draft.
3. The agent requests the credential. `sk` renders a masked terminal form. Over MCP, where protocol form elicitation must not carry secrets, the engine converts the request into a single-use URL-mode elicitation tied to the unsaved draft. In either case the value lands only in the draft credential cache; no connector row or `commit_intent` is needed.
4. The agent calls `probe_connector_draft`. A green probe (`ok: true`) persists the connector + credential atomically inside the same tool call — DB row, encrypted credential, audit entry — and the response envelope carries `auto_saved: true` plus the saved connector shape. The agent does NOT need to call `save_connector_draft` afterward.
5. The agent calls `call_connector` to iterate / paginate / sample.

**OAuth2:**

1–2. As above.
3. `ask_user_form` collects `client_id` + `client_secret` and carries `commit_intent: { kind: "save_connector_draft", payload, description }`. The harness persists the connector + OAuth config on form submit (`authenticate_oauth` needs a persisted connector_id).
4. `authenticate_oauth` opens the authorization URL; tokens land via the OAuth callback.
5. `probe_connector_draft` verifies the access token works.

The diagnostic tools `save_connector_draft` and `save_workflow_draft` remain available for credential rotation, recovery from a partial write, or a force-save after a failed probe (`force_save: true`). They are idempotent — a re-issue against an already-persisted connector returns `{ ok: true, data: { already_persisted: true } }` without a double-write. Audit rows distinguish the three persistence paths via `reason`:

| Reason | Surface | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| `auto_persist_on_green_probe` | `probe_connector_draft` (inline) | A successful probe |
| `auto_persist_on_confirmation` | harness auto-persist | An `ask_user_form` carrying `commit_intent` (OAuth2 happy path, plus delete/revoke confirmations) |
| `manual_re_issue` | `save_connector_draft` / `save_workflow_draft` (direct) | Operator-driven re-save, force-save, credential rotation |

Credentials only flow through a sanctioned secret-input surface: the masked `sk` form or the single-use MCP URL flow. The `update_connector_draft` tool rejects any credential-shaped key in `config` with a structured `credential_must_use_form` envelope. Drivers no longer accept inline credentials from `connector.config` at probe time. There is no chat-text or connector-config shortcut.

---

## Vendor-drift Sweep

Connector templates pin vendor base URLs (`base_url`), probe endpoints, and OAuth issuers. Vendors retire or rename these surfaces over time. The Layer-3 vendor-drift sweep proves the surfaces are still live and stamps `verified_at` per template so operators can spot stale entries before a workflow fails on them.

The catalogue ships three layers of validation:

- **Layer 1 — structural lint.** `apps/engine/src/connectors/templates.test.ts` runs at every PR: every template must parse `ConnectorTemplateSchema`, slugs are globally unique, recipes pass `WorkflowDefSchema`, etc. No network.
- **Layer 2 — cross-reference invariants.** Same test file: every `default_skill` resolves to a known entry in `template-skills.json`, recipe placeholders are bound, no credential-shaped literals leak into recipe workflows. No network.
- **Layer 3 — vendor-drift sweep.** A network sweep HEADs every `base_url`, calls every declared `probe_endpoint`, and fetches `<oauth.issuer_url>/.well-known/openid-configuration` for OAuth templates, stamping `verified_at` per template. It **never runs in CI** — gated by `RUN_TEMPLATE_AUDIT=1` so a careless pipeline can't hammer vendors. The sweep lives in `scripts/template-vendor-sweep.ts` and runs on an operator-chosen cadence against `templates.json`.
- **Layer 4 — conversation journey.** `conversation-native-elicitation.integration.test.ts` drives a real Streamable HTTP MCP client from an unsaved bearer draft through URL elicitation, single-use credential submission, conversation resume, authenticated probe, connector save, and encrypted credential persistence. This composed state-machine test is mandatory because isolated tests of form delivery, probing, and saving cannot detect lifecycle deadlocks between those components.

### Running the sweep

From the repo root (gated by `RUN_TEMPLATE_AUDIT=1`):

```bash
# Full sweep — concurrency=3, 1s/host backoff. Takes a few minutes.
RUN_TEMPLATE_AUDIT=1 bun run scripts/template-vendor-sweep.ts

# Smoke-test a single template; or --update-templates to stamp
# verified_at on every template that came back OK or auth_required.
RUN_TEMPLATE_AUDIT=1 bun run scripts/template-vendor-sweep.ts --only=stripe
RUN_TEMPLATE_AUDIT=1 bun run scripts/template-vendor-sweep.ts --update-templates
```

The sweep classifies every template as one of:

- `ok` — base URL + probe + OAuth discovery all responded with the expected status.
- `auth_required` — vendor answered with 401/403 (the URL is real; we just don't send credentials).
- `drift` — vendor returned 404 / 410 / persistent 5xx. Triage required.
- `error` — network-level failure (DNS, TLS, timeout). May be transient.
- `skipped` — `base_url` is null or carries placeholder segments (`{tenant}`, `{cloudId}`).

Per-vendor backoff escalates exponentially on 429/5xx (cap 30s, 4 attempts). Output is sorted by slug so re-runs produce a byte-stable report when nothing changed.

### What `verified_at` means

`verified_at` is a wall-clock ISO8601 timestamp of the last successful sweep. `null` means the template has never been swept (newly authored, or the script has not been run since the field landed).

The Layer-1 test emits a `console.warn` (it does **not** fail the suite) when a template's `verified_at` is `null` or older than 90 days. Sample output:

```
[connector-templates] vendor-drift sweep stale on 44/57 templates.
Run the Layer-3 vendor-drift sweep (RUN_TEMPLATE_AUDIT=1 bun scripts/template-vendor-sweep.ts) to refresh verified_at.
  - airtable (verified_at=null, never swept)
  - hubspot (verified_at=null, never swept)
  …
```

The deliberate non-fail-on-stale design lets the catalogue ship even when the sweep hasn't run recently — running the sweep is an operator decision (vendor surfaces don't drift on a PR's schedule), and a stale stamp should never block an unrelated change.

---

<!-- Source: docs/concepts/faq.md -->

# FAQ

> **Audience:** Anyone new to sk asking the first questions — what the pieces
> are, how they differ, and where to create them.

Short answers to the questions people ask in their first week, each pointing at
the one page that covers it properly. Nothing here is re-explained twice.

---

## What is a workflow?

A workflow is an ordered list of **steps** the engine runs deterministically —
every run is permission-checked, recorded, and replayable. You author one by
describing the outcome in plain language; the AI proposes the steps and you
approve them. Once committed, a workflow runs the same way every time. See
[Workflow Execution](./workflows.md).

## What is a Skill?

A Skill is dense, operator-authored guidance the AI **follows** while authoring,
discovering, and repairing workflows — your house conventions, integration
patterns, and security policies. Skills load by scope (global, per-connector,
per-workflow) so the right conventions are in context at the right moment. See
[Custom Skills](../authors/custom-skills.md).

## What is a Knowledge Source?

A Knowledge Source is a persistent, indexed document store the AI **searches**
for reference material — runbooks, API specs, compliance frameworks, glossaries.
The engine ingests, chunks, embeds, and searches it, injecting the passages that
match the current question. See [Knowledge Sources](../authors/knowledge-sources.md).

## How do Skills and Knowledge Sources differ?

**Skills prescribe; Knowledge Sources inform.** The AI *obeys* a Skill as a rule
and *consults* a Knowledge Source as reference — never treating the document as a
rule. A quick test: if the sentence starts with "always" or "never", it is a
Skill; if it is a document you would hand a new hire, it is a Knowledge Source.
The full comparison, scoping, and context-assembly order are in
[Knowledge & Skills](./knowledge-and-skills.md).

## How are Knowledge Sources processed?

Four stages: **ingest** (upload, attach, paste, or crawl), **chunk** (split into
searchable passages), **embed + index** (vectors plus tags and a description),
and **search** (hybrid semantic + tag retrieval into the authoring context).
Because retrieval is chunk-level, several focused documents beat one large blob.
See [How grounding works](../authors/knowledge-sources.md#how-grounding-works).

## How do I model a whole domain?

Stand up three primitives around the domain: a **Connector** (its API / system of
record), one or more **Skills** (the conventions the AI must follow), and one or
more **Knowledge Sources** (its reference documents). Together the AI authors
inside your domain — proposing against your conventions and grounding specifics
in your documents. The worked walkthrough is [Model a Domain](../authors/model-a-domain.md).

## Where do I create each?

- **Knowledge Source** — self-serve: in a Conversation, upload or paste a
  document and ask to add it; `sk knowledge-sources create --file …` for one
  file, or `sk knowledge-sources import ./team-wiki` for a whole markdown
  directory (an Obsidian vault, an agent wiki, an OKF bundle).
- **Skill** — operator-owned: author one in a Conversation, `sk skills create
  --file …`, or promote a detected **Skill Candidate**
  (`sk skill-candidates approve <id>`).
- **Workflow / Connector** — start a Conversation and describe the outcome; the
  approve-to-commit loop is covered in the [authoring quickstart](../authors/quickstart.md).

---

## Further reading

- [Knowledge & Skills](./knowledge-and-skills.md) — the conceptual model in full.
- [Model a Domain](../authors/model-a-domain.md) — the connector + skills + knowledge trio, worked end to end.
- [Concepts & Domain Model](./glossary.md) — one-place definitions of every term.

<!-- Source: docs/concepts/glossary.md -->

# Concepts & Domain Model

One vocabulary, defined once. When every team means the same thing by _Workflow_, _Credential_, or _Audit Log_, reviews move faster, handoffs stop leaking, and compliance gaps close before they reach an auditor.

This is the authoritative glossary for sk: each term is defined exactly once, and every other doc uses the meaning given here — not an approximation.

| Group                                              | Covers                         | Key terms                                               |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| [0 — Naming & Acronyms](#group-0-naming--acronyms) | Shared names and expansions    | Contextual learning loop, AEAD, DAG, MCP, RBAC          |
| [1 — Platform Core](#group-1-platform-core)        | Isolation and identity         | Tenant, User, API Key, Portal Token                     |
| [2 — Authoring](#group-2-authoring)                | How workflows get built        | Conversation, Draft, Skill, Knowledge Source, Discovery |
| [3 — Integration](#group-3-integration)            | Reaching external integrations | Connector, Template, Driver, Credential                 |
| [4 — Execution](#group-4-execution)                | What runs, and what it records | Workflow, Step, Execution, Schedule                     |
| [5 — Governance](#group-5-governance)              | Control and proof              | Audit Log, RBAC, Before-Request Hook, Self-Healing      |
| [6 — Surfaces](#group-6-surfaces)                  | How callers reach sk           | sk CLI, MCP Server, Chat Adapter, Notifications         |

Read top to bottom for a full mental model, or jump to a group.

---

## Group 0: Naming & Acronyms

A few names in the codebase differ from the phrasing used in the prose docs, and several acronyms recur across every group. Both are collected here so every reader shares the same vocabulary.

**Contextual learning loop** — the mechanism by which a tenant's authoring context improves over time: every run can surface drift, a drift can produce an operator-reviewed Patch Candidate, a recurring pattern can produce an operator-promoted Skill Candidate, and both feed back into the next authoring run. See [workflows.md](./workflows.md) and the self-healing subsystem.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Run --> Drift --> PC[Patch Candidate] --> SC[Skill Candidate]
  SC --> Author[Better authoring] --> Run
```

**Drift-assisted repair suggestion** — the prose phrasing for the codebase's _self-healing_ subsystem (also called _operator-reviewed remediation_ in governance contexts). Same concept, different audience.

> **Naming note.** The prose docs say "drift-assisted repair"; the codebase keeps stable technical identifiers (`apps/engine/src/self-healing/`, `rbac/`, `credentials/`, etc.). These names must not be renamed for vocabulary alignment — they are referenced by modules, logs, and tests.

### Acronyms

Collected so every reader has the same expansion at hand.

| Acronym   | Expansion                                     | One-line definition                                                                                                           |
| --------- | --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| AEAD      | Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data | Encryption that also detects tampering of the ciphertext and the metadata it is bound to.                                     |
| BPMN      | Business Process Model and Notation           | Classical visual workflow language; cited as a contrast to AI-assisted authoring.                                             |
| DAG       | Directed Acyclic Graph                        | The shape of a Workflow: steps flow forward, never loop back to themselves.                                                   |
| DCR       | Dynamic Client Registration                   | OAuth 2.1 mechanism that lets a new external client self-register with the server (RFC 7591).                                 |
| DLP       | Data Loss Prevention                          | Policy layer that recognises sensitive fields (PII, secrets) and blocks them at the boundary.                                 |
| MCP       | Model Context Protocol                        | The standard by which AI clients (IDE assistants, coding agents, chat clients) connect to external integrations (Connectors). |
| OAuth 2.1 | —                                             | The current consolidated OAuth standard (PKCE-by-default, refresh-token rotation, no implicit grant).                         |
| OIDC      | OpenID Connect                                | Identity layer on top of OAuth 2.x; how sk verifies who a user is.                                                            |
| PII       | Personally Identifiable Information           | Data that identifies a natural person; subject to GDPR / SOC2 controls.                                                       |
| PKCE      | Proof Key for Code Exchange                   | OAuth extension that protects the authorization-code flow on public clients.                                                  |
| RAG       | Retrieval-Augmented Generation                | LLM pattern: ground generation in retrieved tenant-specific context (Lewis et al. 2020).                                      |
| RBAC      | Role-Based Access Control                     | Permission model that grants actions through roles rather than per-user grants.                                               |
| ReAct     | Reasoning + Acting                            | Agent pattern that interleaves model reasoning and tool calls (Yao et al. 2023).                                              |
| RLS       | Row-Level Security                            | PostgreSQL feature that enforces tenant boundaries at the database, not the application.                                      |
| RTO/RPO   | Recovery Time / Point Objective               | Disaster-recovery targets: how fast you recover, and how much data you may lose.                                              |
| SAML      | Security Assertion Markup Language            | Enterprise SSO standard, alternative to OIDC.                                                                                 |
| SCIM      | System for Cross-domain Identity Management   | Standard for automated user provisioning and deprovisioning.                                                                  |
| SSO       | Single Sign-On                                | One login session unlocks multiple applications.                                                                              |

---

## Group 1: Platform Core

**Tenant** — the top-level isolation unit in sk. All resources — workflows, connectors, credentials, users, skills, conversations, and knowledge sources — belong to exactly one Tenant. Multi-tenancy is structural, not configurable; no shared state crosses tenant boundaries, and every platform operation is scoped to the tenant of the authenticated principal.

**User** — a human principal within a Tenant. A User has a role (admin, member, or end-user) that governs which resources they can see and which actions they are permitted to take. Users authenticate through an Auth Provider (OIDC or API Key) and their identity is linked to their chat-platform accounts when chat integrations are enabled.

**API Key** — a bearer token scoped to a Tenant and a set of permissions. Used for programmatic access, service-to-service integration, and CLI authentication. API Keys carry explicit scopes and can be constrained to specific workflows or connectors. They support overlap-window rotation so access is never interrupted during a key change.

**Portal Token** — a short-lived, scoped credential issued to an end user for single-purpose access. Portal Tokens allow external users to interact with specific workflows without becoming full Tenant members. They are a tighter variant of an API Key, with a shorter default lifetime and a narrower permission surface.

---

## Group 2: Authoring

**Conversation** — the primary authoring session in sk. A User and the AI exchange messages; the AI uses structured authoring actions internally to propose, validate, and assemble a workflow. Conversations are persistent and resumable — a session can be paused and continued without losing context. The Conversation is where Drafts are created, refined, and committed.

**Draft** — a workflow under construction within a Conversation. A Draft exists only in the context of the Conversation until it is committed. Committing a Draft creates a versioned, immutable Workflow. A Draft _is_ executable — that is what a dry run does — but only with writes held back, so a Draft run has no side effects outside sk; the unheld path runs committed Workflows.

**Skill** — a reusable, curated piece of context loaded into the AI during Conversations and other AI-assisted authoring flows such as discovery, diagnosis, and bounded repair. Skills encode best practices, integration patterns, domain-specific knowledge, and known failure modes. They are authored or promoted by operators with explicit human approval. Skills are never auto-generated or auto-promoted from execution history, and committed deterministic workflow execution does not load them. See [Model a Domain](../authors/model-a-domain.md) for a Skill and a Knowledge Source configured together for one domain.

**Skill Candidate** — a pattern detected from execution history that might improve AI context quality. The platform proposes Skill Candidates automatically when it detects recurring patterns in successful or failed executions. A Skill Candidate becomes a Skill only through explicit operator approval — the platform never promotes one automatically.

**Knowledge Source** — a persistent document store attached to a Tenant or Workflow. Operators upload documents (PDFs, runbooks, compliance policies, architecture diagrams) which are chunked and indexed for semantic search. On interactive upload the AI auto-analyzes the content to generate a short **description** and a set of topical **tags**, so each source is self-describing and routable — the AI can decide which source covers a topic before searching, and searches can be narrowed by tag. The AI searches Knowledge Sources during Conversations, discovery, and repair-oriented authoring flows to ground its proposals in tenant-specific context. Committed workflow execution does not query Knowledge Sources directly.

**Discovery** — a one-shot analysis where the AI examines uploaded files (API specifications, runbooks, architecture diagrams, OpenAPI docs) and proposes Connectors, Skills, and Knowledge Sources inferred from their content. The result is a set of proposals — called Discovery Artifacts — that operators can approve or reject individually. Discovery does not configure anything automatically.

---

## Group 3: Integration

**Connector** — a configured connection to an external integration boundary. A Connector is built from a template, a driver, and credentials. It represents a specific integration instance — for example, a Stripe production account or a GitHub organisation. Connectors are tenant-scoped and versioned.

**Connector Template** — a pre-built blueprint for a well-known service. Templates include the driver type, authentication configuration, documentation ingestion setup, and guided setup instructions. sk ships 57 Connector Templates covering services across payments, CRM, DevOps, data, communication, and cloud infrastructure. Templates are the starting point for creating a Connector; they are not Connectors themselves.

**Driver** — the protocol layer that executes Connector requests. sk has five built-in drivers: HTTP, GraphQL, PostgreSQL, S3, and MCP. Each driver handles request construction, response parsing, pagination, and error normalisation for its protocol. The driver set itself is closed — you cannot register a sixth protocol at runtime — but the **MCP driver is the extension point**: point a Connector at any Model Context Protocol server and every tool, resource, and prompt that server publishes becomes reachable from workflows and chat, with no new driver to write and no engine change. Unlike the other four, the MCP driver holds a live session between calls rather than opening one per request.

**Credential** — an encrypted secret stored in the platform's credential vault. Credentials include API keys, OAuth2 tokens, connection strings, and similar sensitive values. Connectors reference Credentials by identifier; the raw secret value is never exposed outside the vault. All Credentials are encrypted at rest. OAuth2 Credentials refresh automatically.

---

## Group 4: Execution

**Workflow** — a versioned, directed acyclic graph (DAG) of Steps with a deterministic control flow: which Steps run, in what order, on what condition is fixed at approval time and never re-decided at runtime. Step _results_ can still vary — a Step calls the outside world. Workflows are authored through Conversations, approved by a human, and then committed as immutable versions. Each version is a complete snapshot of the workflow at the time of approval. Workflows are tenant-scoped and support a lifecycle of draft, active, and archived.

**Step** — a single unit of work within a Workflow DAG. Step types are: request (call a Connector), transform (reshape data), branch (conditional routing), loop (iterate over a collection), parallel (run Steps concurrently), wait (introduce a delay), wait_for_event (pause until an inbound signal), and call (invoke another Workflow). Each Step declares retry policy, timeout, error handling behaviour, and optional field masking for sensitive data.

**Execution** — a single run of a Workflow. An Execution carries its own state, step-by-step results, logs, and final status. sk never modifies an Execution record after it completes. Each Execution records its request source (API, CLI, scheduler, webhook, MCP, or chat) and its environment (dev or prod). Executions are queryable and searchable after the fact.

**Execution Fixture** — a recorded snapshot of a past Workflow execution, capturing the request and response at each Step. Fixtures serve as the dry-run corpus for Self-Healing proposals: before a Patch Candidate is presented to an operator for approval, it is validated against relevant Fixtures to confirm the repair does not break known-good behaviour.

**Schedule** — a cron expression or event trigger attached to a Workflow. The scheduler fires the Workflow at the configured time or in response to an inbound event. Schedules are reconciled at engine boot and on configuration changes. Scheduled fires are recorded in the Audit Log with source `scheduler`.

---

## Group 5: Governance

**Audit Log** — the append-only record of every state change in the platform. Every entry carries: what changed, who initiated it, from which surface (API, CLI, MCP, chat, scheduler, webhook), and when. sk exposes no path that modifies or deletes an audit entry — no route, no tool, no job, and `audit:read` is the only audit permission — so nothing reaching the platform through its own surfaces can rewrite history. That is an application-layer guarantee: it does not extend to a party with direct database access, and entries are not hash-chained, so it provides no tamper _evidence_ against one. It is the authoritative record for compliance, debugging, and incident review.

**RBAC** — role-based access control enforced at every platform boundary. Every API route, MCP call, webhook trigger, and execution path checks the caller's role and permissions before proceeding. sk ships five built-in roles: the three user-facing roles (admin, member, enduser) plus the metrics_scraper and portal_token_user system roles. Custom roles and resource-level grants are supported for more granular control. RBAC decisions are recorded in the Audit Log.

**Before-Request Hook** — a sandboxed script that runs before a Connector request executes. Hooks can inspect or modify the outbound request, enforce policy (such as blocking writes during maintenance windows), or abort execution entirely. Hooks run in an isolated sandbox with a strict CPU budget and no access to the host environment. Hook execution is audited. Any error or timeout fails closed and denies the request.

**Self-Healing** — the platform's drift detection and bounded repair system. When a Connector's schema or behaviour changes in a way that causes Step failures, the engine detects the drift, compares the new response against the last known Schema Version, proposes a repair using the AI within a narrow repair loop, and dry-runs the proposed repair against recorded Execution Fixtures. The result is a Patch Candidate presented to an operator for approval. Self-Healing never applies a repair automatically without operator approval.

**Patch Candidate** — a proposed repair generated by the Self-Healing process. Each Patch Candidate carries the proposed change, a classification of safe or unsafe based on the scope and risk of the repair, the Execution Fixtures it was validated against, and a full audit trail. Patch Candidates require explicit operator approval before they are applied to a live Workflow.

---

## Group 6: Surfaces

**sk CLI** — the unified command-line surface and primary human-facing interface for the platform. Built on Ink plus citty commands, it provides a terminal UI that opens a Conversation for end users describing workflow goals, and top-level admin commands for operators managing the platform (`sk connectors`, `sk workflows`, `sk executions`, `sk audit`, and related groups). The sk CLI supports four authentication modes: API Key, OIDC, Portal Token, and headless (stdin pipe for scripted usage). Persona-aware: the surface adapts based on the authenticated user's role.

**MCP Server** — the Model Context Protocol server embedded in the sk engine. It exposes Workflows as callable `wf_<slug>` entries inside the MCP callable surface, Connectors as structured resources, and Skills as curated prompts that can be injected into an AI's context. Any MCP-compatible client — IDE assistants, coding agents, and chat clients alike — can connect to the MCP Server and interact with the platform. All MCP calls are governed by the same RBAC and Audit Log as direct API calls.

**Chat Adapter** — the integration layer for enterprise chat platforms (Slack, Microsoft Teams, Google Chat). Each adapter normalises platform-specific events — mentions, slash commands, interaction callbacks — into sk's Conversation model, and renders responses back as native platform messages. Approval flows surface as interactive cards with approve and reject buttons. Identity linking connects a chat user's platform identity to their Tenant account.

**Notification Rule** — a tenant-scoped row that selects which engine events fan out to which channel. Carries an event-type pattern, an optional workflow pattern, a severity, an optional `request_source_filter`, and the target `(workspace_id, channel_id)` tuple. Backed by the dispatcher in `apps/engine/src/notifications/service.ts` with a leaky-bucket rate limiter and a three-state circuit breaker. See [docs/operators/notifications.md](../operators/notifications.md).

**Notification Delivery** — the per-attempt outcome of dispatching a Notification Rule against an event. Possible statuses: `sent`, `rate_limited`, `breaker_open`, `failed`, `skipped`. Each row is the audit-grade record of what was (or was not) delivered, mirrored in the audit log via `chat.message.sent`, `chat.message.denied`, or `webhook.outbound.failed`.

**Service Metadata** — the identity envelope every engine code path carries: `{ trace_id, tenant_id, actor_id, actor_email, request_source }`. Constructed at every entry point (HTTP middleware, MCP server, scheduler, CLI bin, conversation tool-chain recursion) and threaded through every log line, audit row, and telemetry event. Defined in `apps/engine/src/observability/service-metadata.ts`. The trace_id is what an operator follows across surfaces during incident triage.

**Result Storage URI** — the pointer in `executions.result_storage_uri` (and per-step rows) that resolves a spilled payload back to its full content. Inline payloads up to `STEP_RESULT_DB_BYTES` (10 KB) live in the row; larger payloads spill to the configured S3-compatible private bucket as an immutable `s3://<bucket>/<key>` object with application SHA-256 metadata. A 512-byte text preview always lands inline. `fixture://<uuid>` is a read-only legacy recovery format, never a destination for new writes.

**LLM Judge** — an opt-in scoring layer invoked by the eval runner only when (a) `SUBKIT_EVAL_LLM_JUDGE=1` is set AND (b) the deterministic validator returns `pass=false` with `function_passed=true` (structurally fine, semantically dubious). The judge emits a `passes`/`partial`/`failed` verdict that enriches the report; it never overrides the deterministic gate.

---

## What to Read Next

- [docs/developers/input-surfaces.md](../developers/input-surfaces.md) — How users and systems reach sk: the CLI, REST API, MCP server, chat platforms, webhooks, and scheduled triggers.

<!-- Source: docs/concepts/governance-and-audit.md -->

# Governance & Audit

> **Audience:** Security engineers, compliance reviewers, architects

**Pass the audit on the first pass.** Every interaction in sk is authorised before it runs, recorded in an append-only trail, and stripped of secrets — so "who did what, when, and from where?" is always one query away. Security is the default behaviour by architecture, not by configuration: multi-tenant isolation, a comprehensive audit log, and secret-hygiene defences at the conversational surface. sk produces the evidence a compliance review runs on; it does not make an organisation compliant.

Two adjacent concerns have their own admin homes:

- **Access control (RBAC/ABAC), identity, and Before-Request Hooks.** Every API route, MCP call, and workflow trigger is permission-checked before any resource is touched; a sandboxed, fail-closed Before-Request Hook can add dynamic policy on top of static roles. Full model: [RBAC & Roles](../admins/rbac-and-roles.md).
- **The credential vault.** All integration secrets are stored encrypted with AES-256-GCM, referenced by identifier, decrypted only at the moment of use, and never exposed to the AI or to logs. Full model and rotation: [Credentials & Keys](../admins/credentials-and-keys.md).

---

## How every request is governed

A request from any surface passes the same chain before it touches a resource: it is tagged with its source, checked against RBAC/ABAC, run through any tenant Before-Request Hook, then handed to the driver policy chain — and every decision lands in the tenant-scoped audit log.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R[Request<br/>API · MCP · CLI · webhook · scheduler] --> RS[Tag request source]
    RS --> RBAC{RBAC / ABAC check}
    RBAC -->|deny| D1[403 + audit row]
    RBAC -->|allow| HOOK{Before-Request Hook<br/>sandboxed, fail-closed}
    HOOK -->|deny| D2[Blocked + audit row]
    HOOK -->|allow| DRV[Driver policy chain<br/>tool policy · egress · sandbox]
    DRV --> AUD[(Append-only audit log<br/>tenant-scoped)]
```

Secrets never travel through that chain in the clear. A credential is collected through a masked form, encrypted, and stored by reference; the driver decrypts it only at the moment of use, while the LLM and every log surface see a redacted placeholder instead of the value.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    F[Masked form<br/>ask_user_form sensitive] --> ENC[AES-256-GCM encrypt]
    ENC --> V[(Credential vault<br/>referenced by id)]
    V -->|decrypt at moment of use| DRV[Driver request]
    DRV --> EXT[External connector]
    V -.->|secret never exposed| LLM[LLM tool args · transcript]
    V -.->|scrubbed at write| LOG[Logs · audit · debug.log]
```

---

## Multi-Tenancy as a First-Class Concern

sk is multi-tenant from the ground up. Every resource in the platform — workflows, connectors, credentials, users, skills, conversations, audit log entries — belongs to exactly one Tenant. This is not a deployment mode or a configuration setting. It is the data model.

Tenant isolation is enforced at every layer. Database queries always filter by tenant identity. API responses never include cross-tenant data. The audit log is tenant-scoped. A single engine instance can serve multiple organizations with complete isolation between them.

This design means there is no "global" namespace to accidentally share, no configuration flag to toggle isolation on or off, and no way for one tenant's data to appear in another tenant's context. Isolation is structural.

---

## The Audit Trail
