Every state change in sk produces an audit log entry. This is not selective logging — it is comprehensive.

The audit log captures: workflow creation, modification, approval, and deletion; connector operations; credential creation, rotation, and revocation; user provisioning and role changes; execution triggers and final results; approval events; skill promotions; patch candidate reviews; and more — over 240 distinct action types across all platform surfaces.

Each entry captures the full context of the event: what action was taken, who took it (user or service account identity), from which surface (API, CLI, MCP, chat, webhook, or scheduler), what changed (a structured diff where applicable), and precisely when. The metadata field on every entry is scrubbed for token-shaped values before persistence — bearer tokens, JWTs, AWS access keys, and any value under a key matching a sensitive name (`password`, `token`, `secret`, `credential`, `*_token`, `authorization`) become `***REDACTED:<kind>***` at write time, regardless of how they reached the audit recorder.

The trail is append-only, and that guarantee has a precise shape worth knowing before an auditor asks. sk exposes **no path that modifies or deletes an audit entry** — no route (the audit API is read-only), no tool, no retention job, and `audit:read` is the only audit permission that exists. Nothing reaching the platform through its own surfaces can rewrite history, including a tenant admin, an API key holder, or a connected AI client.

That is an application-layer guarantee, not a storage-layer one. A party with direct database access can still alter rows, and entries are not hash-chained or sequence-numbered, so a deletion leaves no gap to detect — sk provides no tamper *evidence* against that threat model. Operators who need it should pair the audit log with append-only storage or off-box log shipping. It is the compliance and forensics record for the platform, designed to answer the question every audit or incident review requires: "Who did what, when, and from where?"

Audit emissions go through typed recorders under `apps/engine/src/audit/recorders/` — one helper per resource family (connector, workflow, credential, knowledge source, policy). Each recorder requires a non-null `reason` for state-changing rows. Reasons are part of the contract: `auto_persist_on_confirmation` distinguishes harness auto-persist writes from `manual_re_issue` (explicit `save_connector_draft` calls), `force_save_override` marks force-flag overrides of failed probes or previews, `auto_mode_no_prior_approval` marks a commit whose prior-approval gate was skipped because the session ran in `permission_mode=auto` (the row also carries `metadata.bypassed_prior_approval`, so "did anyone approve this commit?" is answerable from the log alone), `credential_must_use_form` records rejected credential attempts at the draft layer, and `confirm_before_execution` records every tool-policy decision that paused for an operator confirmation.

New audit kinds for the conversational surface include `tool_policy.confirmation_required` (every confirmation gate the policy resolver fires), `connector.draft.credential_rejected` (rejections by the `update_connector_draft` contract), `connector.invoked` (each `call_connector` round-trip), `connector.saved_override` (a save persisted with `force_save: true` despite a failed probe), and `knowledge_source.refreshed` (each discovery cache refresh). The conversational context pipeline also emits `conversation.skill_loaded` — a tenant-scoped row written when a Skill is loaded into a conversation working set under the recency-gated `load_skill` path, with reason `skill_loaded` on first load and `skill_re_promoted` when an already-known Skill is re-promoted (see `apps/engine/src/audit/types.ts` `CONVERSATION_SKILL_LOADED` and `apps/engine/src/audit/recorders/conversation.ts`). It records a state-mutating write: `load_skill` updates the persisted `conversations.loaded_skills` palette — tenant-visible state that survives session resumption — so, like every other tenant-state mutation, it goes through the audit chokepoint. Per-turn recency demotions are derived and intentionally not audited.

Operators can query the audit log by actor, action type, resource, time range, and request source. The `sk audit tail` command provides a real-time stream for operational monitoring. The API exposes the same query surface programmatically.

**Asymmetric coverage on `data.exported` from `POST /v1/extract`.** Binary-format extracts (PDF / DOCX / XLSX / XLS / PPTX) emit an `action = "data.exported"` audit row for both success and parse-failure paths — these formats can carry whole tenant documents (CVs, contracts, financial spreadsheets), so the egress trail is explicit. Text-format extracts (JSON / CSV / YAML / XML / plaintext) deliberately skip the audit row because they are shape-only (the caller is sending data the engine already knows about for schema inference). Operators monitoring `data.exported` for *all* extract calls should be aware of this gradient. The 413 body-cap denial path is audited for every format. See [Observability & Resource Limits](../operators/observability.md#resource-limits-and-operational-safety) for the full operator-controlled metadata surface (`audit_log.metadata.filename`, `audit_log.metadata.error`).

---

## The Compliance Posture

The following properties are structural — they hold without being switched on.

**Encryption at rest.** All credentials are encrypted with AES-256-GCM before being written to the database. The encryption key is managed at the engine configuration layer.

**Encryption in transit.** All engine endpoints are served over TLS. The engine does not serve unencrypted HTTP in production configurations.

**API key storage.** Keys are stored as hashes. The comparison during authentication is always against the hash, never against a stored plaintext value. There is no way to recover a key after issuance.

**Webhook signatures.** All inbound webhooks are HMAC-SHA256 signature-verified before any payload is processed; the generic scheme is Standard Webhooks, with vendor adapters for Stripe and GitHub. Requests with missing or invalid signatures are rejected.

**Sandboxing.** Untrusted code — transforms, Before-Request Hooks, and self-healing patch scripts — runs in an isolated QuickJS-WASM sandbox with a strict CPU budget. Sandbox code cannot access the network, the file system, or the database. The sandbox is not a trust boundary that can be configured away; it is where all runtime code execution occurs.

**Egress governance.** Connector requests go through the engine. Clients never call external connector boundaries directly. All egress is logged in the audit log with request source, caller identity, and outcome.

**Request source tracking.** Every platform interaction — API call, MCP invocation, webhook delivery, chat message, CLI command, scheduled trigger — is tagged with its source. "Who initiated this?" is always answerable from the audit log.

---

## Answer Provenance and Honest Refusal

Governance is not only about who may act — it is also about whether an answer can be trusted and whether a refusal is respected. Three properties hold on the conversational surface.

**Provenance you can check.** When an answer is grounded in a knowledge source or connector documentation, sk surfaces a `Sources: <name>` footer naming the sources the answer was built on, and mirrors the same references into the audit log as a `conversation.answer_cited` row. Only citations that resolve to a real, tenant-owned source are ever surfaced or logged — a fabricated or since-deleted provenance handle is dropped before the footer and the audit see it. The footer appears identically on the live surface and on replayed transcripts.

**An answer that quotes must quote faithfully.** Before a grounded chat answer stands, a deterministic anti-drift check confirms that every cited id resolves for the tenant and that every verbatim quoted span appears in a cited excerpt. A failure — an unresolvable citation or a quote grounded in none of the cited sources — is treated like a low-confidence result: the turn surfaces an `ask_user_text` the operator must answer before the conversation continues, rather than letting drifted prose stand as the final answer. The check runs on the citations the model actually cited, so an answer that cited only fabricated sources still fails and abstains.

**A no that is respected.** When an operator declines a concrete action (one that persists or writes externally), sk records the fingerprint of the declined intent. An identical re-proposal in the same conversation is answered with the prior decline instead of re-prompting — and in `auto` mode the decline stays sticky, so a previously-refused action is never silently auto-approved. A bare question is never treated as sticky, and an edited draft is a new proposal that prompts normally; a deliberate later retry in an attended mode reaches a fresh prompt.

**Grounding staleness is visible.** A workflow draft records a fingerprint of the connector schema it was grounded on. At `/context`, sk recomputes it and flags a draft whose connector schema has changed since — a "re-check before saving" advisory. It never blocks, and any ambiguity (a missing or expired discovery index) resolves to silence rather than a false warning.

---

## Secret Hygiene at the Conversational Surface

The conversational surface introduces additional pressure on secret handling: an LLM may attempt to type a credential into a tool argument, an operator may paste a token into the chat input, or a debug log may capture a verbose elicitation payload. sk applies multiple defences so any one of these doesn't propagate into a persistent surface.

The `update_connector_draft` tool rejects any credential-shaped field in `config` with a structured `credential_must_use_form` envelope. The agent is steered, by both the tool contract and the seed skill content, toward the masked-form path: `ask_user_form(type: password, sensitive: true)` collects the value, the harness auto-persists the connector and credential atomically, and the LLM never sees the secret in any tool argument or transcript.

The HTTP / GraphQL / S3 drivers no longer honour inline credentials from `connector.config`. Probing a draft without a saved credential row returns a structured `credential_required` envelope, which the conversational layer turns into the next ask-form turn. The previous shortcut that lifted `config.token` into the Authorization header has been removed — it made the wrong thing look like progress.

Engine logs, audit metadata, conversation event payloads, and the `~/.sk/debug.log` file pass through a centralized scrubber before write. The scrubber matches known token shapes — DigitalOcean, GitHub, GitLab, Slack, Anthropic, Bearer-prefixed bearer tokens, JWTs, AWS access keys — and any value whose key name matches the sensitive-name pattern. Matches become `***REDACTED:<kind>***` at the file-write boundary.

The sk CLI composer detects token-shaped paste in the chat input. When matched, the input is replaced with a one-keystroke confirmation prompt; on confirmation the CLI sends a redirect message that asks the agent to re-prompt through the masked form, instead of forwarding the literal paste to the engine. The detector catches the same regex catalog as the engine scrubber.

**Secret-in-chat guard (MCP).** An AI client reaching the platform over MCP has no masked form to render, so the temptation is to collect a credential as ordinary chat text — exactly the surface where a secret must never travel. sk refuses that path outright. When a turn would elicit a secret-shaped value from a model-only client, the engine does not accept it as plain conversation input; it declines and routes the operator to the secure flow instead — a scoped portal-setup link where the value is typed into a masked field, or the managed OAuth authorization flow. The credential is entered outside the chat transcript, encrypted straight into the vault, and the AI client only ever learns that the connector is now authorized. A secret is never gathered as free-form chat text over MCP, so it cannot land in a transcript, a tool argument, or a client-side history.

Tool policies (`apps/engine/src/conversations/tool-policies.ts`) decide execution mode dynamically per call. Arguments that fill a tool's declared credential slots force the policy resolver to `confirm_before_execution` — whatever the tool's category, and whatever permission mode the client asked for — which inserts an `ask_user_confirm` gate before the tool runs. Every such pause records the resolver rule that produced it: on the chat surface as a `tool_policy.confirmation_required` audit row, and on every surface that mints a durable approval handle as the `resolver_reason` of the `approval.requested` row. Both are read straight off the decision object the gate acts on, so the audit trail can never record a decision that was not enforced.

The resolver does not shape-match arguments against the secret-redaction patterns. That catalog answers "must this string be masked in a log line", not "must a human approve this call": it cannot see what the call does, and it matches high-entropy literals that legitimately appear inside workflow transforms. Secrets are kept out of the conversational surface by the defences above — the masked form, the MCP secret-in-chat guard, and the persist-time scrub — not by pausing every tool that happens to carry a base64 blob.

The `authenticate_oauth` flow surfaces an authorization URL that the sk CLI auto-launches in the operator's browser. That URL is tenant-controlled input: it is derived from the connector's `oauth.issuer_url` config, which a tenant admin can write. The proportionate control is a scheme clamp — `BrowserUrlSchema` accepts only `http`/`https`, closing `file:`, `javascript:`, and `data:` URLs — so the worst a tenant admin can do is cause the CLI to open an arbitrary http(s) page for an operator who has paused on that connector. This is acceptable because connector-config writes are already an audited, RBAC-gated action: the admin who could set a hostile `issuer_url` is the same admin already trusted to configure the connector's real endpoints, and every such write lands in the audit trail.

---

## Further reading

- [Reversibility & Trust Domains](./reversibility-and-trust-domains.md) — how much autonomy a piece of work should get, and why a guardrail is a boundary rather than a request.
- [RBAC & Roles](../admins/rbac-and-roles.md) — identity, authentication, RBAC/ABAC, and Before-Request Hooks.
- [Credentials & Keys](../admins/credentials-and-keys.md) — the credential vault, master-key rotation, and release signing.
- [glossary — governance terms](./glossary.md#group-5-governance) — Audit Log, RBAC, Before-Request Hook, Self-Healing, Patch Candidate.

<!-- Source: docs/concepts/knowledge-and-skills.md -->

# Knowledge & Skills

> **Audience:** Architects and authors who want the model behind the AI's
> organization-specific context.

The AI proposes work the way *your* team does it, not the way a generic API
tutorial does — because your conventions are in front of it while it writes.
That is the difference between a draft you correct three times and one you
approve. This page is the model behind that: what you feed it, how it is
selected, and who decides what gets remembered.

Two primitives carry that context:

| Primitive | What it is | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **Skills** | Dense, operator-authored guidance | Prescriptive rules the AI follows |
| **Knowledge Sources** | Broad organizational documents | Searchable grounding, not rules |

This page covers how the engine assembles them into each authoring turn, how
**Discovery** turns files into proposals, and how the loop compounds. Author
how-tos live in [Custom Skills](../authors/custom-skills.md) and
[Knowledge Sources](../authors/knowledge-sources.md).

---

## Skills: curated context

A Skill is reusable context loaded into the AI during a Conversation and other
AI-assisted flows — discovery, diagnosis, bounded repair. Skills encode your
best practices, integration patterns, security policies, and domain knowledge.
Reference your Stripe connector and the Stripe Skill loads automatically, so
proposals reflect your conventions, not generic API knowledge.

Operators own Skills. Scope each one:

- **Global** — every Conversation.
- **Per-connector** — loaded when that connector is referenced.
- **Per-workflow** — loaded for that workflow.

Skills are never auto-generated or auto-promoted. The engine detects recurring
patterns and surfaces them as Skill Candidates; a candidate becomes an active
Skill only by explicit operator promotion. The engine learns what works; humans
decide what becomes canonical.

---

## Knowledge Sources: enterprise documents

A Knowledge Source is a persistent document store for document-scale context —
runbooks, API specs, compliance frameworks, architecture diagrams. Operators
upload the files; the engine chunks and indexes them for semantic search.
During a Conversation, discovery pass, or repair loop, the AI searches them to
ground its proposals.

Skills prescribe; Knowledge Sources inform. The AI follows Skills as
instructions and searches Knowledge Sources for relevant context without
treating them as rules.

**Committed workflow execution queries neither.** Skills and Knowledge Sources
improve authoring and repair quality; once a workflow is committed, the runtime
path stays deterministic.

---

## Context assembly and trimming

Each authoring turn assembles prompt context in a fixed order. Order matters
twice: it shapes how the model reads context (top is most foundational) and how
the trimmer drops it under budget pressure (top survives longest, bottom goes
first).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph build["Assembly order (top = first written)"]
        direction TB
        B1["1. Base prompt + runtime envelope<br/>(engine · tenant · actor · surface)"]
        B2["2. Auto-loaded Skills<br/>(global → connector → workflow)"]
        B3["3. Explicitly loaded Skills"]
        B4["4. Knowledge Source chunks"]
        B5["5. User memory"]
        B6["6. Connector documentation chunks"]
        B7["7. Prior failures for the current task"]
        B8["8. Authoring-context blocks"]
        B9["9. Current turn history<br/>(user / assistant messages)"]
        B1 --> B2 --> B3 --> B4 --> B5 --> B6 --> B7 --> B8 --> B9
    end
    Trim{{"Trim order (top = dropped first)"}}
    T1["failures → connector docs → knowledge<br/>→ user memory → authoring context<br/>→ explicit Skills → workflow Skills<br/>→ connector Skills → global Skills"]
    Note["User turns are never trimmed"]
    build --> Trim --> T1
    T1 -. preserved .- Note
```

This order is contract, not implementation detail. Under tight budgets,
operator-curated connector and workflow guidance outlives incidental history —
so a tenant's own conventions are the *last* thing dropped, never the first.

Replay stays bounded: tool results are truncated before re-entering later
turns, compaction markers suppress older replay, and oversized histories
collapse into a deterministic summary plus the recent tail.

---

## Discovery: from files to proposals

Discovery cuts onboarding time for a new integration: instead of hand-configuring
every connector and Skill, it starts from documentation that already exists.

An operator uploads files — API specs, data dictionaries, architecture
diagrams, runbooks — and sk produces structured proposals. Each Discovery
Artifact is a proposed connector, Skill, or Knowledge Source, with a confidence
score and links to the supporting evidence.

Nothing is configured automatically. Proposals are starting points; the
operator approves what to keep.

---

## How the loop compounds

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Run["Run"] --> Drift["Drift detected"]
    Drift --> Patch["Patch Candidate<br/>(operator-reviewed)"]
    Run --> Pattern["Recurring pattern"]
    Pattern --> SkillC["Skill Candidate<br/>(operator-promoted)"]
    Session["Coding-agent session"] --> Learning["Session learning<br/>(operator-reviewed)"]
    Learning --> SkillC
    Patch --> Author["Better authoring"]
    SkillC --> Author
    Author --> Run
```

Skill Candidates surface production patterns: when connectors or step sequences
recur together and tend to succeed, the engine proposes a new Skill with
confidence scores and links to the supporting executions. Self-healing drift
detection keeps workflows healthy as connected systems change, proposing the
smallest safe fix as a Patch Candidate.

External coding-agent sessions (Claude Code, Codex) feed the same queue: a
SessionEnd hook posts the transcript to `POST /v1/agent/sessions` for
distillation, and the agent can save an explicitly taught rule mid-session via
the `save_learning` tool. Both paths produce `session_learning` Skill
Candidates reviewed with `sk learnings review`; an approved learning becomes an
active, domain-tagged Skill that the next session briefing carries.

Same shape every time: the engine surfaces proposals, humans decide. The engine
gets smarter over time — but only with human approval at each step.

---

## Further reading

- [Model a Domain](../authors/model-a-domain.md) — the connector + skills + knowledge trio, worked end to end.
- [FAQ](./faq.md) — fast answers on how these pieces differ and where to create each.
- [Custom Skills](../authors/custom-skills.md) — how to author, scope, and promote Skills.
- [Knowledge Sources](../authors/knowledge-sources.md) — how to upload, tag, and refresh documents.
- [Self-healing](../operators/self-healing.md) — the operational side of the repair loop.
- [glossary — authoring terms](./glossary.md#group-2-authoring) — Conversation, Draft, Skill, Skill Candidate, Knowledge Source, Discovery.

<!-- Source: docs/concepts/overview.md -->

# Architecture Overview

> **Audience:** Anyone forming a first mental model of sk — architects, operators, authors, contributors.

This page explains why sk's promise — describe it, approve it, it runs, and you can prove
what it did — survives contact with production. Read it once and you can predict the
system's behaviour instead of discovering it.

The shape is simple. Someone describes an outcome in plain language. sk turns that into a
workflow. A person approves it. From then on the engine runs it against your connectors —
the apps and services your team already uses — along a path that was fixed at approval
time.

One contract holds throughout, and everything else follows from it: **AI assists with
*authoring*; the *control flow* of an approved workflow is fixed and never re-decided at
runtime.** Multi-tenancy, permission checks, encrypted credentials, and an append-only
audit trail apply to every entry point, without exception.

---

## At a glance

![sk architecture at a glance — external AI clients cross the product-local MCP OAuth boundary into the engine; other surfaces enter directly. Tenant Context (Skills · Knowledge · Discovery · Skill/Patch Candidates) is the compounding learning loop.](./overview.png)

*External clients (IDE assistants, employee chat) reach governed workflows only through sk's product-local **MCP OAuth boundary**; other surfaces (Chat adapters, CLI, HTTP REST API, Inbound Webhooks, Scheduler) enter directly. The engine groups into six clusters; the green **Tenant Context** cluster is the compounding loop. Source: [`./overview.drawio`](./overview.drawio).*

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph surfaces["Inbound surfaces"]
        CLI["sk CLI"]
        REST["HTTP REST API"]
        MCP["MCP OAuth boundary<br/>(IDE assistants, employee chat)"]
        Chat["Chat adapters"]
        Hook["Inbound webhooks"]
        Sched["Scheduler"]
    end
    Gate{{"One governance gate<br/>RBAC → Before-Request Hook → audit"}}
    Engine["Engine<br/>(single binary)"]
    PG[("PostgreSQL<br/>queue · scheduler · pub/sub · state")]
    LLM[("LLM provider<br/>(authoring only)")]
    Ctx["Tenant Context<br/>Skills · Knowledge · Discovery<br/>Skill/Patch Candidates"]

    surfaces --> Gate --> Engine
    Engine --> PG
    Engine -. authoring .-> LLM
    Engine <--> Ctx
    Ctx -. improves authoring .-> LLM
```

Every entry point flows through the same governed pipeline. Execution is policy-
and version-bound, auditable, and operator-reviewed for drift-assisted repair.

---

## The governance loop

Authoring and execution are separate trust domains. The model proposes; a human
approves; the engine runs the frozen artefact. Each run can feed the next
authoring — but only through operator promotion, never silently.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Author["Author<br/>(NL → draft)"] --> Review["Review<br/>(human)"]
    Review --> Approve["Approve<br/>(version pinned)"]
    Approve --> Run["Fixed control flow<br/>(engine infers nothing)"]
    Run --> Audit["Immutable audit"]
    Audit --> Drift["Drift detection"]
    Drift --> Candidate["Patch / Skill Candidate"]
    Candidate -. operator promotes .-> Author

    Author -. uses .-> LLM[("LLM provider")]
    Candidate -. enriches .-> Ctx["Tenant Context"]
    Ctx -. grounds .-> Author
```

---

## The three things to internalise

1. **Authoring vs. execution are different trust domains.** The LLM proposes; a human approves; the engine runs the approved artefact deterministically. Committed execution never queries Skills, Knowledge, or the model. See [Authoring workflows](../authors/authoring-workflows.md) and [Workflows](./workflows.md).
2. **One dependency.** The engine compiles to a single binary; PostgreSQL is the only stateful dependency. The job queue, cron scheduler, and pub/sub bus all live in Postgres. See [Self-host](../developers/self-host.md).
3. **The compounding loop.** Run → Drift → Patch Candidate → Skill Candidate → better authoring → better run. Every run can improve the tenant's authoring context — but only through operator promotion. See [Knowledge & Skills](./knowledge-and-skills.md) and [Self-healing](../operators/self-healing.md).

---

## Where to go next

- [Glossary](./glossary.md) — every domain term defined exactly once.
- [Connectors & integration](./connectors.md) — Drivers, Templates, Credentials, the vault, OAuth2.
- [Workflows](./workflows.md) — the execution model, step kinds, triggers, versioning, self-healing.
- [Knowledge & Skills](./knowledge-and-skills.md) — how the authoring context compounds.
- [Governance & Audit](./governance-and-audit.md) — multi-tenancy, RBAC, audit, secret hygiene.
- [`AGENTS.md`](../../AGENTS.md) — the canonical repo-wide contributor contract.

<!-- Source: docs/concepts/reversibility-and-trust-domains.md -->

# Reversibility & Trust Domains

> **Reading time:** ~8 min
> **Audience:** Architects, operators, and authors deciding how much autonomy a piece of automation should get

**Give each piece of work the level of control it actually needs — no ceremony where mistakes are cheap, no blind spots where they are not.** Most automation decisions are made on one question: *is this useful?* That question picks what to automate. It cannot tell you how much freedom the automation should have, or whether a person belongs in front of it. This page adds the two questions that can, and shows where sk fits — and where it deliberately does not.

---

## The question that decides

Before automating anything, ask:

> **What does the worst plausible failure cost, and how long does it take to undo?**

Usefulness picks *what* to automate. Reversibility picks *how much autonomy it gets and which gate it passes.*

The same technology deserves different treatment depending on the answer. A typo in a draft is corrected and forgotten. A sent message is gone. A payment is a phone call and an apology. Automation checklists that ask only about upside green-light all three identically — which is why the one that later hurts is usually the one that passed review most easily.

## Two axes, four quadrants

Reversibility alone is not enough. The second axis is how much judgment the work needs **at the moment it runs**: can the decision be written down as rules, or does someone have to weigh things up?

| | **Formalizable** — rules decide | **Soft judgment** — a call must be made |
|---|---|---|
| **Reversible** | Automate plainly. A gate costs more than it saves. | A briefed, freely iterating agent genuinely fits here. |
| **Irreversible** | **sk's zone.** Versioned artefact, gate, audit trail. | **Danger zone.** |

The danger zone is the honest part of this table: **there is no good answer inside it.** Soft judgment in front of an irreversible effect means an unreviewable decision with a permanent consequence, and no amount of additional guardrail changes that — a guardrail cannot review a decision nobody can inspect.

The correct move is not to secure the quadrant. It is **to leave it**:

- **Pull the judgment forward**, into authoring, where a person reviews an artefact without time pressure.
- **Formalize what remains**, so execution follows rules rather than making calls.
- Where that split genuinely cannot be made, the effect itself needs a person on it — every time, not by exception.

This also names a trade sk makes openly: it exchanges runtime flexibility for authoring effort. For irreversible work that is the right trade — the effort buys a reviewable artefact and a rollback target. For reversible, variance-driven work it is the wrong one, and reaching for a fixed graph there is overkill rather than rigour. Knowing which quadrant you are in is what keeps you from paying either price unnecessarily.

## Authoring and execution are different trust domains

Running an approved workflow is bounded work: the definition already says what may happen, and execution stays inside it. *Changing* that definition is unbounded work: it decides what may happen from then on, for every future run.

Same actor, same intelligence, categorically different blast radius.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Authoring["Authoring — unbounded"]
        A1[Change the definition] --> A2[Human reviews a diff]
        A2 --> A3[Version committed]
    end
    subgraph Execution["Execution — bounded"]
        E1[Run the approved version] --> E2[Effects limited by the definition]
    end
    A3 --> E1
```

Systems that collapse these into one surface end up governing neither: the authoring change slips through the gate built for execution, and the execution gate is too heavy for what it now guards. sk keeps them apart — which is also why the surface you choose to *author* on matters. See [Choosing your surface](../authors/choosing-your-surface.md).

## The readable-artefact test

For any change, one test decides whether review is even possible:

> **Can someone read what will change, before it changes?**

If yes, review is possible and rollback has a target. If no, the only remaining control is trust in the intent — and intent does not survive a paraphrase. Something restated by another party, human or model, is no longer the thing you approved.

This is why a workflow in sk is a **numbered, versioned document** rather than a configured personality. A behaviour change you cannot read is a change with no way back: nothing to compare, no version to name, no target to restore. A document has all three. It is the difference between "the automation behaves differently now" and "this version changed these four lines, and the previous one is a single command away."

The practical consequences run through the whole product: [Workflow Execution](workflows.md) for version binding and replay, [Governance & Audit](governance-and-audit.md) for the trail that records who approved which version.

## A guardrail is a boundary, not a request

"Never do X" written into a prompt is a request. The model may honour it, and usually will — but compliance is the mechanism, and compliance is not a boundary.

These are boundaries:

- a permission check that refuses before the resource is touched
- an execution sandbox with no host globals to reach for
- an approval bound to the exact payload it approves

The distinction has a sharp edge worth stating plainly: **a value the model can place in its own tool call is not an approval.** It is a field with a reassuring name. The same holds for identity — a name and a role description are not an identity subject. What makes attribution possible is identity carried *per action*, on the row, at the moment the action happens.

## Where determinism does and does not reach

sk fixes the **control flow** of an approved workflow. It does not promise that every step returns the same value.

There is no step kind that calls a model: the step kinds are `request`, `transform`, `call`, `wait`, `wait_for_event`, `branch`, `parallel`, and `loop`. A workflow that wants a model's judgment reaches it the way it reaches any other API — a `request` step against a provider. That step is version-bound, recorded, and replayable like every other, and its token cost is accounted for; what it is not is deterministic in its result.

Saying this plainly matters, because the honest boundary is narrower than "deterministic execution" suggests. The guarantee is that the *path* through the workflow is fixed at approval time and never re-decided at runtime — not that every value along it is reproducible. A reader who assumes the stronger version discovers the gap at the worst moment.

It is also why sk prefers a deterministic classifier, or a replay against a recorded real response, over asking a second model for a verdict. Two models built the same way share failure modes: they agree confidently, and agreement between them is not evidence. Where a verdict has to hold, the check should not itself be a judgment call.

## Further reading

- [Choosing your surface](../authors/choosing-your-surface.md) — the practical consequence: which door for which job
- [Workflow Execution](workflows.md) — versioning, replay, and what a fixed control flow buys
- [Governance & Audit](governance-and-audit.md) — the permission chain and the audit trail
- [RBAC & Roles](../admins/rbac-and-roles.md) — how boundaries are actually enforced

<!-- Source: docs/concepts/workflows.md -->

# Workflow Execution

> **Audience:** Engineers integrating the runtime, operators monitoring executions

Once you approve a workflow, it takes the same path every time — no model reconsiders it on the next run. That is what makes it safe to leave month-end reporting, invoice checks, or back-office routine running unattended: each run is permission-checked, recorded, tied to a version, and replayable when someone asks what happened. AI writes the workflow; the engine runs it.

This page covers the workflow lifecycle, the execution model, the eight Step kinds, triggers, versioning and rollback, scheduling, self-healing, and the observability surface operators rely on.

---

## Workflow Lifecycle

A workflow moves through three states. Chat authors a **draft**; approval commits it to **active**; retiring or superseding it moves it to **archived**. Promoting a prior version back to active is the rollback path — no redeploy, instant, audited.

Authoring itself follows a fixed shape: sk builds a grounded draft from the described outcome, tests that draft against real connectors, refines it with targeted patch edits, and only then commits it. Each stage is a discrete, governed step — the draft is never mutated blindly, and the commit is the single gated transition from draft to active. See [AI-assisted authoring](../authors/authoring-workflows.md) for the full loop.

**Playground mode.** Authoring can run in an ephemeral scratch mode that never persists. A playground conversation builds and tests drafts exactly like a normal session, but nothing it produces is written to the tenant's workflow store — the draft evaporates when the conversation ends. This is the safe space to explore a shape, probe a connector, or demonstrate the authoring loop without leaving any committed artifact behind. Playground is a durable, per-conversation flag: it is set when the conversation is opened (an AI client signals it over MCP; an HTTP caller passes it on the start request) and holds for the life of that conversation.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> draft: authored in chat
    draft --> draft: refine / re-preview
    draft --> active: approved + committed
    active --> active: new version (immutable snapshot)
    active --> archived: retired / superseded
    archived --> active: promote a prior version (rollback)
    archived --> [*]
```

_Draft → active → archived. Every transition lands in the Audit Log with the actor, the version, and the timestamp._

### The authoring critic

Static validation catches what a schema can prove: unknown step kinds, malformed placeholders, a scope reference that can't resolve. It cannot catch a draft that is _structurally valid but semantically wrong_ — a workflow that parses cleanly yet quietly drifts from what the author actually asked for (the wrong endpoint, an inverted condition, a dropped field).

The authoring critic closes that gap. It is an LLM gate that runs **after** static validation in the authoring pipeline and reads the draft against the stated intent, flagging semantic drift a parser can't see. When it finds a problem, the finding is fed back into the same bounded-repair loop the engine uses everywhere else, so the fix is proposed and re-validated rather than silently applied.

The critic is **off by default** and enabled through the `llm.critic.*` settings (see the settings reference). It is deliberately **fail-open**: if the critic model is unavailable or errors, authoring proceeds on the static result rather than blocking — the critic sharpens quality when present but is never a hard dependency on the path to a committed workflow.

---

## The Execution Model

The **control flow** of an Execution is deterministic. A Workflow is a DAG of Steps; the execution engine walks that DAG in order, following branching and parallel directives exactly as defined. The engine does not re-interpret, adapt, or infer at runtime: it never calls a model to decide what runs next, and committed execution never queries Skills or Knowledge Sources.

What a Step _returns_ is a different matter — a `request` Step calls the outside world, and the outside world is not deterministic. That includes a Step an author points at a model provider: sk supports this deliberately (see [Calling a model from a Step](#calling-a-model-from-a-step)), and such a Workflow does not produce identical output on every run. The guarantee is that no model decides what the Workflow _does_.

There is a single runtime entry point for manual execution: `POST /v1/executions`. Persisted workflows, inline draft definitions, and single-step previews all flow through this same route and the same execution engine. Inline runs complete synchronously by default. Queued background execution is explicit and reserved for persisted workflows, scheduler fires, webhook fan-out, and other detached cases.

All execution surfaces normalize workflow input through the same boundary before dispatch. Conversation `run_workflow`, MCP callable entries, REST workflow-run routes, webhook-bound executions, queue resumes, and scheduler-triggered runs all end up at the same execution contract with the same effective input payload. Surface adapters may differ in how they collect input, but they do not get to define different runtime semantics.

Provider failures on the authoring side do not leak through as generic internal errors anymore. Usage-limit and rate-limit failures are surfaced as typed provider-limited responses, context-window failures are surfaced as context-too-large responses, and temporary provider outages are surfaced as typed provider-unavailable responses. The execution engine remains deterministic; these envelopes only describe authoring-time model failures.

This is a deliberate architectural decision, not a limitation. AI is for authoring — exploring, proposing, and revising. Once a Workflow is approved and committed, the enterprise needs to know which steps will run, in which order, against which systems. The moment the _engine_ infers that, the audit trail becomes "the AI decided" rather than "the workflow ran as specified."

An Execution is a permanent record. It captures the specific Workflow version that ran, who or what triggered it, the inputs and outputs of every Step, timing at every boundary, and the final status. sk never modifies it after it completes. If something goes wrong, the complete record of what happened is preserved exactly as it occurred.

## Calling a model from a Step

A `request` Step may target a model provider like any other HTTP endpoint, and sk supports this on purpose: it ships a connector template and recipes for it. This is how a Workflow does work that needs judgement — classifying, extracting, summarising — inside an otherwise fixed control flow.

Two things follow, and both are the point rather than a caveat:

- **The run is no longer reproducible.** The same input can yield different output. The control flow is still fixed; the content is not. A Workflow that must produce byte-identical results should not contain such a Step.
- **The spend is bounded, not unbounded.** Declare `max_llm_tokens_per_run` on the Workflow. The engine recognises calls to known provider hosts, meters prompt + completion tokens across the run, and refuses to dispatch a call whose pre-call estimate would exceed the cap — before the provider is charged. Without a cap the tokens are still counted and land on the execution's audit record; they are simply not bounded. The recipe linter marks such Workflows `budgeted-llm` and requires the cap.

---

## Step Kinds

A Workflow is composed of Steps. sk ships eight Step kinds, grouped by what they do. There is no `tool` kind (no docker-based sandbox runner) — this is a data-workflow engine, not a container runtime.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S(["Step (kind)"])
    S --> IO["Data"]
    S --> Logic["Control flow"]
    S --> Time["Time & signals"]

    IO --> request["request<br/>call a connector endpoint"]
    IO --> transform["transform<br/>reshape data (sandboxed JS)"]
    IO --> call["call<br/>invoke another workflow"]

    Logic --> branch["branch<br/>deterministic conditional"]
    Logic --> parallel["parallel<br/>concurrent branches"]
    Logic --> loop["loop<br/>iterate a collection"]

    Time --> wait["wait<br/>fixed delay"]
    Time --> wait_for_event["wait_for_event<br/>HITL signal pause"]
```

| `kind`           | What it carries                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `request`        | Calls a system through a connector — HTTP, GraphQL, SQL, S3, or a remote MCP server. One step kind, five drivers, so retry, backoff, and the audit envelope behave identically whichever system is on the other end.                                                                                 |
| `transform`      | Reshapes data between steps in a sandboxed JavaScript expression — no network access, bounded time and memory.                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `branch`         | Deterministic conditional routing — the engine evaluates the condition and dispatches the matching branch, no inference, no fallthrough.                                                                                                                                                             |
| `loop`           | Iterates a collection, running its body once per item. Expensive or side-effecting loops can set `fail_fast: true` to stop after the first non-tolerated body failure; the default collects every iteration result.                                                                                  |
| `parallel`       | Fans out independent step sequences concurrently and merges their results.                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `wait`           | A deliberate delay (up to 24 h) — polling, rate-limit pacing, human-paced flows.                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `wait_for_event` | Pauses the run for an external signal — the human-in-the-loop gate. The run resumes when the signal arrives, or takes an explicit timeout path the author defines. The shipped `merge-pr-after-approval` recipe is the canonical example: open a PR, wait up to 24 h for approval, merge or abandon. |
| `call`           | Invokes another saved workflow — sub-processes compose into pipelines.                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

Two contracts sit on top and matter to everyone, not just contributors:

**Every request is classified read or write.** The driver classifies at dispatch time (a GET is a read, a mutation is a write; an external MCP tool call is a write until someone inside the tenant says otherwise), and the author can override either way.

**Previews hold writes.** A dry run executes read steps live but fully resolves and _holds_ every write — URL, headers, the materialized body are recorded, nothing is dispatched. You see exactly what would have been sent before anything is sent; executing writes during a preview takes an explicit confirmation.

The exact field contract of every step kind — schemas, sandbox limits, timeout interplay — is the [step-kinds field reference](../developers/step-kinds-reference.md).

---

## Triggers

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Req["request trigger<br/>(default; on-demand)"]
    Hook["webhook trigger<br/>(reverse-bound to<br/>webhooks_inbound row)"]
    Sched["schedule trigger<br/>(cron + tz, reverse-bound<br/>to workflows_schedules row)"]
    Core{{"runExecution()<br/>same contract,<br/>same RBAC, same audit"}}
    Exec[/Execution record/]

    Req --> Core
    Hook --> Core
    Sched --> Core
    Core --> Exec
```

_Three trigger kinds, one execution core. The trigger lands in the immutable Execution and Audit Log alongside the actor identity envelope, so an operator can answer "who/what triggered this and from where" without joining tables._

`WorkflowDef.trigger` is a discriminated union over `kind`. Omitting the block is equivalent to `{ kind: "request" }`, so every workflow authored before this field existed keeps its behaviour. Setting `webhook` or `schedule` reverse-binds an inbound binding or cron schedule keyed on `(tenant_id, workflow_id)` at save time and removes the binding on delete or version rotate. The schema source of truth is [`apps/engine/src/workflows/types.ts`](../../apps/engine/src/workflows/types.ts) (`RequestTriggerSchema`, `WebhookTriggerSchema`, `ScheduleTriggerSchema`).

The trigger is recorded in every Execution and every Audit Log entry alongside the actor identity envelope.

| `kind`     | Fields                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | Behaviour                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `request`  | (none)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | Default. Run is initiated on demand by a caller — chat `run_workflow`, MCP, the CLI, or `POST /v1/executions`. Inline runs complete on the request path; `async: true` is honoured only for `source=saved`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `webhook`  | `source` (string slug per integration — a provider label stored in `native_verifier_config.source`, **not** the ingress URL path), `events[]` (provider event names; empty means "any"), `verify` (`stripe-signature` \| `github-hmac` \| `none`) | Reverse-bound to a `webhooks_inbound` row. Inbound posts are signature-verified before any processing begins; replay-id deduplication suppresses retried deliveries. Executor lives in `apps/engine/src/webhooks/inbound/service.ts`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `schedule` | `cron` (5-field `m h dom mon dow` or `every:N` shorthand), `tz` (IANA, default `UTC`); optional `execution_mode` (`dev` \| `prod`, default `prod`), `business_days_only`, `skip_dates[]` (ISO `YYYY-MM-DD`)                                       | Reverse-bound to a `workflows_schedules` row. The scheduler reconciler validates the cron expression at bind time, persists the connector environment, and uses `tz` so firings land at the operator's local wall-clock time. Unattended runs target production connectors by default; dev schedules are explicit. `business_days_only` skips weekends; `skip_dates` declares holidays / freezes explicitly (no holiday calendar is inferred). Catch-up semantics: a missed firing fires on the next reconciler pass rather than being silently skipped. Executor lives in `apps/engine/src/scheduler/reconciler.ts`. |

All three variants land at the same `runExecution()` core through the same execution contract; only the way the run is initiated differs.

**Schedule resource upserts.** `POST /v1/schedules` is an upsert on `(tenant_id, workflow_id)`. A new row returns 201 with `upsert_status: "created"` and audits `schedule.created`; replacing the existing workflow schedule returns 200 with `upsert_status: "updated"` and audits `schedule.updated`. The persisted JSON `input`—including arrays, scalars, and `null`—is returned by create/update responses and by `GET /v1/schedules`, so the catalog shows the exact payload that unattended runs receive.

**Webhook trigger, exactly.** Two facts trip up authors; both are grounded in `apps/engine/src/webhooks/inbound/service.ts`:

- **`verify` is not the stored verifier.** `stripe-signature` → stored `verifier = "stripe"`; `github-hmac` → `"github"`; `none` → `"standard"` with `native_verifier_config.skip = true`. The stored `verifier` column is always one of `standard` / `github` / `stripe` — never `none`. A row whose `verifier` is set to `none` (or anything unrecognized) is denied at ingress with `unknown_verifier` / 401.
- **The public ingress is `POST /v1/hooks/{slug}`, and `{slug}` is the derived `wf-<workflow-slug>`, not the trigger's `source`.** The default (`standard`) verifier requires the Standard Webhooks headers `webhook-id`, `webhook-timestamp`, `webhook-signature`; the event type is read from the `webhook-type` header and must match one of `events[]` (non-empty) or the delivery is denied with `event_not_subscribed` / 401.

**Reverse-bind is a mirror, not an add.** Saving a workflow _with_ a `webhook` trigger upserts the inbound hook; saving it _without_ one (an edit that drops the `trigger` block, or switches it to `request` / `schedule`) **deletes** the hook and its stored signing secret. Re-adding the trigger recreates the row with a fresh placeholder secret that must be re-provisioned. See [Scheduling & Hooks](../operators/scheduling-and-hooks.md#verify--stored-verifier-mapping-read-this-before-touching-the-crud-api) for the full mapping table, ingress request contract, and end-to-end wiring recipe.

---

## Finding a Workflow in a Large Catalog

A catalog grows into the dozens quickly, and a flat list stops being useful long before it stops being correct. sk therefore presents workflows in **categories** — themed blocks the operator can scan instead of a single undifferentiated list.

A category is **derived, never maintained**. There is no folder to create, no tag to apply, no field to keep current: sk reads the naming your team already uses. Workflows that share a leading slug segment form a block, so `notion-search-pages`, `notion-append-markdown`, and `notion-page-to-markdown` present together as **notion**. A prefix only becomes a block once at least three workflows share it — otherwise every one-off would become a heading of its own, which reads worse than no grouping at all. Everything without a qualifying family collects under **other**.

Because the category comes from the whole catalog rather than from a stored attribute, the blocks _emerge_ as the catalog grows: the third sibling of a would-be family promotes all three out of **other** into a block of their own. Nothing is migrated and nothing is edited.

Two filters follow from this, and they are the same on every surface — CLI, HTTP API, MCP, and chat:

- **by category** — show one block instead of the whole catalog.
- **by connector** — show every workflow that touches a given external system. This answers the operational question directly: _before I rotate these credentials, what depends on them?_ It counts both ways a step can bind a connector, so a workflow referencing it only through a `${connector.<slug>.base_url}` URL is not missed.

Each listed workflow reports its `category` and the `connectors` it uses, so the same answer is available to an operator reading a terminal, a dashboard rendering the API, and an agent calling the tools.

**Moving a workflow between blocks** means renaming its slug — the governed metadata update, which is audited and does not create a new version. Note that the slug is also the workflow's MCP tool name (`wf_<slug>`), so connected clients re-discover it after a rename.

**New workflows land in the right block by construction.** When sk authors a workflow it is shown the families that already exist and asked to reuse one where it fits — so a new Notion reader is named into the `notion` block at the moment of creation, when no tool name exists yet and nothing has to be renamed. The display name stays clean and human; only the slug carries the family. The catalog keeps itself organised as it grows rather than needing a periodic tidy-up.

---

## Versioning

Every change to a Workflow creates a new version. A version is a complete snapshot of the workflow's DAG — not a diff, not a patch, but the full definition as it stood at the moment of change. Versions are immutable once created.

At any given time, exactly one version is designated "active." The active version is what runs when the workflow is triggered. Operators can inspect any prior version and promote it to active in a single action.

This is the rollback story for sk. When a change introduces failures, the response is to promote the previous known-good version to active. No code changes are required, no deployment is needed, and the rollback is immediate. The audit log records the promotion decision — who made it, when, and from which version.

---

## Scheduling and Event Architecture

The scheduler uses a durable job queue so that scheduled runs survive engine restarts. A schedule is a commitment: if the engine was unavailable when a run was due, it will fire when availability is restored. The same queue also backs explicitly asynchronous workflow runs, while synchronous API-initiated runs stay inline on the request path.

Execution state changes — a run starting, a step completing, a run finishing — are published as events through a pub/sub system. Subscribers receive these events in real time: the sk CLI can tail a live execution, chat adapters can show progress in a thread, SSE consumers drive external observers, and outbound webhook Subscriptions can notify external connector boundaries.

The platform uses an outbox pattern to ensure that events are never silently lost. Events are written to the database as part of the same transaction as the state change that produced them. Delivery is attempted after the transaction commits, and any undelivered event is retried. The outbox provides a durable event log that survives restarts and partial failures.

Pub/sub channels are **global, not per-tenant**. The `connector.oauth` channel — over which an out-of-band OAuth callback announces `callback_succeeded` / `callback_failed` — carries events for every tenant. A consumer that subscribes to it (e.g. `waitForOAuthCredential` in [`apps/engine/src/credentials/oauth2/wait.ts`](../../apps/engine/src/credentials/oauth2/wait.ts)) is therefore responsible for tenant isolation itself: it MUST drop any event whose `tenant_id` does not match the wait's own `tenant_id` in-handler, before acting on it. There is no channel-level scoping to fall back on.

---

## Self-Healing

Connected boundaries change. The APIs a workflow depends on today may behave differently in six months. Schema fields are renamed, endpoints are moved, error codes change, pagination patterns evolve. Workflows that are not maintained will eventually fail.

sk's self-healing subsystem is designed to catch these failures early and propose repairs before they cause sustained disruption.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Run["Workflow run"]
    Drift["Schema drift detected<br/>(passive — from real responses)"]
    Repair["Repair loop<br/>(LLM proposes patch)"]
    Classify["Classify safe / unsafe"]
    DryRun["Dry-run against<br/>Execution Fixtures"]
    Patch["Patch Candidate<br/>(operator-reviewed)"]
    Approve["Operator approves"]
    NewVer["New workflow version live"]
    Skill["Skill Candidate<br/>(emerges from recurring patterns)"]

    Run --> Drift --> Repair --> Classify --> DryRun --> Patch --> Approve --> NewVer
    Patch -. recurring pattern .-> Skill
    NewVer -. next run .-> Run
```

_No autonomous repair in production. The loop runs through a human gate. The compounding effect — each run improving the next — comes from operator-reviewed drift repair feeding back into authoring._

The engine monitors active Connectors for schema drift from real execution results. Successful response evidence is accumulated per endpoint, Workflow, and Step; optional field absence is compatible, while incompatible type changes are proactive drift. Missing paths, validation failures, and endpoint removals remain reactive signals from the affected run. Detection is passive: no vendor polling, just observation of what actually executes plus the scheduled comparison of recorded evidence.

When drift is detected, the self-healing loop analyzes the failure, consults the Connector's latest documentation, and proposes the smallest change that would make the Step work again. The proposal is validated by dry-running it against recorded Execution Fixtures — samples of past successful inputs and outputs. This validation step distinguishes a plausible repair from one that would introduce new failures.

The result is a Patch Candidate: a proposed change with a classification of safe or unsafe based on the nature of the repair. Safe Patch Candidates can be applied by an operator with a single approval action. Unsafe ones require manual review of the proposed change.

No Patch Candidate is ever applied automatically. Self-healing is a proposal system, not an autonomous repair system. The platform surfaces the problem and its proposed solution; the human decides whether to apply it.

---

## Synchronous and Queued Execution

`POST /v1/executions` is synchronous by default. The caller receives the full `RunResult` — output, step summaries, connector resolutions, warnings — in the HTTP response body. Draft runs and single-step previews always execute inline regardless of the `async` flag, because they have no persisted workflow context for a queue worker to rehydrate.

Warnings are a first-class runtime state, not a hidden side channel. A run can report
`status: "succeeded"` while still carrying structured `warnings[]`; CLI and MCP clients are
expected to surface that distinction so operators can diagnose partial or suspicious results.

The authoring surfaces are expected to catch the obvious cases before runtime. In particular,
the static verifier rejects the common scope-envelope mistake of writing `$scope.step.field`
instead of `$scope.step.data.field`. Runtime warnings still matter for dynamic cases, but the
baseline contract is to fail fast on structural scope misuse.

Queued (`async: true`) execution is available **only** for `source=saved` runs. In that case the engine inserts the execution row synchronously, enqueues the job on `pg-boss`, and returns `202 Accepted` with `{ execution_id, status: "queued" }`. A worker picks the job up and runs it through the same `runExecution()` core. Scheduler fires, webhook fan-out, and any other detached trigger also land on the queue — but every inline caller gets the run on the request path.

### Following a run live

`GET /v1/executions/:id/stream` is an SSE tail over the execution's outbox events, gated by the resource-scoped `execution:read` permission (following your own run does not require the tenant-wide `audit:read` that `GET /v1/events/stream` carries). The stream replays the run's full event history — `execution.queued` → `execution.started` → per-step `execution.step.started` / `execution.step.finished` frames (with `step_key`, `step_index`, `kind`, `status`, `duration_ms`, and `error_code` on failure) → the terminal `execution.<status>` frame — then tails live and closes right after the terminal frame. `Last-Event-ID` resumes after a dropped connection. `sk workflows run <id> --follow` and `sk executions tail <id>` consume this stream.

Step frames are written transactionally with the `execution_steps` rows, so a follower never observes a step that isn't persisted.

---

## Per-step Request Meta

Every Step in the `RunResult` carries a `request_meta` object with driver-specific fields. For HTTP and GraphQL Request Steps:

- `url` — the final URL actually hit (after path composition and static query merge).
- `method` / `operation` / `operation_name` — HTTP verb or GraphQL operation kind and name.
- `status` — HTTP status code (or HTTP status of the GraphQL endpoint).
- `bytes_in` — response body size in bytes.
- `retry_count` — retries consumed before success or failure (also surfaced at top level).
- `connector` — a sub-object with `connector_id`, `connector_slug`, `driver`, `requested_environment`, `resolved_environment`, `auth_method`, and `base_url`.

`auth_method` is observable at request time, not configured: it distinguishes `oauth2_static` (cached token still fresh) from `oauth2_refreshed` (a stale token was rotated inline before the request went out). Debugging a mysteriously failing credential becomes a lookup in the run result rather than a server-side hunt.

An MCP Request Step carries `driver: "mcp"`, the wire `operation` (`tools/call`, `resources/read`, `prompts/get`), `bytes_in`, the same `connector` sub-object, and `tool_name` when the operation was a tool call. It deliberately carries **no `status`**: a JSON-RPC result has no HTTP status, and inventing one would make the trail claim something the call never produced.

The `RunResult` also rolls the per-step connector info up into `connector_resolutions[]` — one entry per unique connector touched during the run. Operators see at a glance which workflow step landed on which connector, against which environment, with which auth method.

---

## Determinism, Timeouts and Limits

Numeric budgets — step timeouts, recursion limits, payload thresholds,
LLM tool-result truncation, repair attempts — live in
[`apps/engine/src/execution/timeouts.ts`](../../apps/engine/src/execution/timeouts.ts)
so operators have one place to look and reviewers have one place to
gate. The current values:

| Constant                        | Default | What bites first                                             |
| ------------------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `WORKFLOW_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT_MS`   | 6 h     | Workflow status flips to `timed_out`; in-flight steps abort. |
| `STEP_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT_MS`       | 1 h     | Per-step safety net when the step does not declare its own.  |
| `TRANSFORM_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT_MS`  | 60 s    | QuickJS wall-clock and abort signal.                         |
| `MAX_CALL_DEPTH`                | 5       | `call` step refuses to recurse further.                      |
| `MAX_CALL_RETRIES`              | 5       | Transient `request` retries. pg-boss handles backoff.        |
| `MAX_PAGINATION_REQUESTS`       | 1 000   | Safeguard against missing termination conditions.            |
| `MAX_REPAIR_ATTEMPTS`           | 2       | Self-healing LLM revision budget per drift signal.           |
| `STEP_RESULT_DB_BYTES`          | 10 KB   | Payload spillover threshold (see below).                     |
| `STEP_RESULT_PREVIEW_BYTES`     | 512     | Inline operator-facing preview when spilled.                 |
| `LLM_TOOL_RESULT_SUCCESS_BYTES` | 80 KB   | Tool-result truncation budget for successful results.        |
| `LLM_TOOL_RESULT_ERROR_BYTES`   | 50 KB   | Same for error results.                                      |
| `SANDBOX_MEMORY_LIMIT_BYTES`    | 128 MB  | QuickJS heap cap.                                            |
| `SANDBOX_WALL_MS_DEFAULT`       | 30 s    | Default sandbox wall-clock.                                  |

These constants are not env-overridable except where explicitly noted.
The intent is that an operator should be able to read this table once
and know what the engine will and will not do.

### Execution cancellation

Cancellation has a durable control-plane path in addition to the local
`AbortController` fast path. `POST /v1/executions/:id/cancel` first writes
`executions.abort_requested_at` and the matching audit/outbox records in one
transaction. The worker that owns the run polls only its locally registered
execution ids, grouped by tenant, and aborts the in-flight request when it sees
the flag. This remains effective when the cancel request reaches another
replica or the notification stream is interrupted. The worker also refuses the
queued-to-running transition when the flag already exists.

`queue.abort_poll_interval_ms` controls the observation interval. It defaults
to 500 ms, is globally scoped, and is read again after every monitor cycle, so
settings hot-reload changes the next delay without an engine restart. The
durable cross-replica path and queued-start race are exercised in
`apps/engine/src/execution/tests/abort.test.ts` and
`apps/engine/src/execution/execution-state.test.ts`.

### Result Persistence

Step results are written inline when serialized payload size is
≤ `STEP_RESULT_DB_BYTES`. Larger payloads always spill to the configured
S3-compatible object store, and the original row records an immutable
`s3://<bucket>/<key>` pointer plus application SHA-256 metadata. A 512-byte text
preview always lands inline so an operator can see at a glance what the payload
looked like without resolving it. Historical `fixture://` rows remain readable
for recovery, but new writes never use PostgreSQL as a blob fallback.

The `GET /v1/executions/:id` route hydrates from the storage URI when
present; consumers never read the URI directly.

Inside a run, a loop that spills large body payloads keeps its
`iterationResults` array bounded by substituting an `OffloadRef` — a
small in-memory placeholder pointing at the already-spilled
`storage_uri` — in place of each full payload. This is the loop-memory
(OOM) guard: N iterations cost N references, not N resident envelopes.
An `OffloadRef` is an execution-internal, in-memory-only type. It MUST
be fully resolved back to plain JSON before the value crosses any
external surface — the persisted execution result, the REST response,
the MCP `wf_*` tools, or `get_raw_result`. Readers never see the
discriminant; a persisted result that still contains one is a contract
violation. Preview surfaces (loop/parallel step summaries) are exempt
from re-hydration but still carry no discriminant: each `OffloadRef`
collapses to a plain scalar string marker, never a structured object.

### Self-Healing Mode

`RunOptions.self_healing.enabled` lets a caller opt out of the
post-execution drift-detection hook. Default behaviour preserves the
existing path (the tenant policy decides whether to record the
outcome). The eval runner uses the toggle to compare a fixture's
`one_shot` outcome against its `self_healing` outcome — a regression
in either is a gate failure.

## Observability

The execution layer is designed to be fully transparent to operators.

Each Execution emits structured events at every Step boundary. Operators can tail execution logs in real time from the CLI or via SSE streams. Log entries are structured — machine-readable and queryable — not free-form text. Every record carries the same identity envelope (`tenant_id`, `trace_id`, `request_source`, `actor_id`) so an operator can correlate a slow request, an audit row, and a failing step by a single id — see [`apps/engine/src/observability/service-metadata.ts`](../../apps/engine/src/observability/service-metadata.ts).

Prometheus metrics cover the dimensions operators need to monitor platform health: execution duration, Step latency, error rates, retry counts, and queue depth, all scoped per tenant. These metrics are the basis for dashboards, alerts, and capacity planning. Connection pools export their own counters (`pg_pool_*`) so operators can spot saturation before it shows up as step failures. The LLM context-assembly path additionally emits `llm_context_assembled_total{flow,request_source}`, `llm_context_dropped_sections_total{flow,section}`, and a histogram `llm_context_total_tokens` so trimmer pressure surfaces alongside model cost.

The Audit Log records every execution trigger, every Step completion, every error, and every approval decision — with full context for forensic investigation. The trail is append-only: sk exposes no path that modifies or deletes an entry, and it persists independently of execution records. See the [Audit Log](./governance-and-audit.md#the-audit-trail) for what that guarantee does and does not cover.

---

## Further reading

- [Security & governance](../admins/rbac-and-roles.md) — RBAC, API keys, Before-Request Hooks, Audit Log guarantees, and the policy model that governs every surface in sk.
- [glossary — execution terms](./glossary.md#group-4-execution) — Workflow, Step, Execution, Execution Fixture, Schedule.
