# Operators

Keep it running without babysitting it. Connect the systems your team depends on, put work on a schedule or behind a webhook, route the outcome to the people who care — and when a vendor changes their API, get a ready-to-apply repair instead of a 3am page.

![Connecting a system in the sk terminal: pick the target, enter credentials, test the connection, save](../_tapes/out/operator-onboard.gif)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q[quickstart] --> C[connectors-and-credentials]
    C --> S[scheduling-and-hooks]
    S --> N[notifications]
    S --> O[observability]
    O --> H[self-healing]
    N --> O
```

Start at the quickstart, attach a credential, then put workflows on a schedule or behind a webhook. Notifications and observability tell you when and how a run finished; drift-assisted repair turns an upstream break into a change you review and apply.

| Page | What it covers | Link |
|---|---|---|
| Quickstart — Operator | Engine up, admin key minted, first connector registered — three steps to a running engine. | [quickstart.md](quickstart.md) |
| Connectors & Credentials | Register a connector once, attach a credential, and let every workflow reuse it. | [connectors-and-credentials.md](connectors-and-credentials.md) |
| Scheduling & Hooks | Wire scheduled runs that survive restarts and inbound webhooks that trigger workflows. | [scheduling-and-hooks.md](scheduling-and-hooks.md) |
| Notifications | Route run outcomes — succeeded, failed, aborted — to the right people, with per-rule failures logged. | [notifications.md](notifications.md) |
| Chat Channels | Use sk read-only from Google Chat (Slack/Teams to follow): ask, look up, and run workflows from the space your team already lives in. | [chat.md](chat.md) |
| Observability & Resource Limits | Diagnose a run in minutes with metrics, logs, and traces, bounded so no single workflow runs away. | [observability.md](observability.md) |
| Drift-assisted repair | Detect upstream API breaks during real execution and apply a validated repair instead of a 3am page. | [self-healing.md](self-healing.md) |
| Runtime Dependencies | The one host dependency outside the single binary — Chromium + playwright for SPA-docs discovery — and how it is provisioned. | [runtime-dependencies.md](runtime-dependencies.md) |
| Deploy & Upgrade | Replace the single binary and restart — the checksum-verified published-asset scp, `engine --self-update` (and why a private repo needs a token), and rollback. | [deploy.md](deploy.md) |

<!-- Source: docs/operators/chat.md -->

# Chat Channels

**Use sk from the chat your team already lives in.** Link a Google Chat
space (Slack and Microsoft Teams follow the same model) and every
member you approve can ask questions, look up workflows, skills,
knowledge, and executions, and run saved workflows — with the same
RBAC, confirmation gates, and audit trail as every other surface. The
channel is deliberately **read-only**: nobody can build or change
connectors, workflows, skills, or knowledge sources from chat, no
matter which role their linked account holds.

> **Not to be confused with the `google-chat` connector template.** The
> connector catalog also contains a "Google Chat" connector used to
> *post* messages into a space as a workflow step. It shares no
> configuration, credentials, or code with the chat channel described
> here. If you want people to *talk to sk from* Google Chat, you're in
> the right doc; if you want a workflow to *send a message to* a space,
> that's the connector, not this.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    u([Space member message]) --> ev[POST /v1/chat/google/events]
    ev --> ver{JWT verify<br/>aud = project number}
    ver -->|bad| deny([401 + audit])
    ver -->|ok| q[chat.event queue<br/>fast ack]
    q --> id{Identity linked?}
    id -->|no| rej([polite rejection + audit])
    id -->|yes| turn[Conversation turn<br/>read-only palette]
    turn --> reply[Reply into the space]
    turn --> card[Approval card<br/>for workflow runs]
```

## What the channel can and cannot do

| Can | Cannot |
|---|---|
| Answer questions (LLM chat with tenant context) | Create or edit connectors, workflows, skills, knowledge sources |
| List/inspect workflows, executions, skills, knowledge, connector metadata, schedules | Call connectors directly (no `call_connector`, probe, test, discover) |
| Run saved workflows — behind RBAC + a confirmation card | Change roles, keys, schedules, or any tenant resource |
| Ask about files already uploaded to sk (list + preview attachments) | Receive or ingest files posted into the space |

The restriction is **channel-scoped, not role-scoped**: an admin who
asks the bot to "create a stripe connector" gets a one-sentence
redirect to the sk CLI or web portal. Enforcement is structural — the
chat surface assembles a fixed read-only tool palette, harness-side
write dispatch refuses mutating intents on this surface, and per-user
RBAC still applies underneath as the second layer.

### How the bot asks for input

When a turn needs something from you, the bot renders the prompt
natively in Google Chat:

- **Yes/no confirmations, single choices, and multi-selects** arrive
  as interactive cards in the space — click to answer.
- **Free-text questions and multi-field forms** arrive as a card with
  a button that opens a native Google Chat dialog.
- **Typing instead of clicking works for simple prompts**: a plain
  typed reply resolves a pending free-text question (or a one-field
  form) directly. For button prompts and multi-field forms the bot
  points you back to the widget instead of guessing.
- Only the person the bot asked can answer — the same shared-space
  contract as run confirmations.

### Attachments are not ingested

Google Chat delivers only message text and interaction payloads to
the app — files dropped into a space never reach sk, so the bot
cannot read, summarize, or run a workflow over an attachment posted
in chat. To work with a file, upload it to sk first via the sk CLI or
the web portal; the bot can then list and preview the tenant's
attachments and answer questions about them.

## Message formatting

The assistant writes standard Markdown; sk converts it to each
platform's native text dialect before sending, so replies render
cleanly instead of showing literal `**` asterisks or bullet
characters. What renders correctly:

| Construct | Google Chat & Slack |
|---|---|
| Bold, italic, strikethrough | rendered (single-asterisk `*bold*`, `_italic_`, `~strike~`) |
| Inline code and short code blocks | rendered as monospace / fenced blocks |
| Bullet lists (incl. nested) | rendered |
| Links | rendered as tappable links |
| Blockquotes | rendered |

What has **no** clean chat equivalent, even after conversion:

- **Headings** degrade to a bold line (neither platform has heading
  syntax).
- **Numbered lists** display as literal `1.`, `2.` lines — legible, but
  the platform does not auto-renumber them.
- **Tables** have no real chat equivalent and fall back to a fenced
  monospace block. If someone needs tabular data in chat, ask the bot
  for it as a list rather than a table for the cleanest result.

Teams and the sk CLI render full Markdown natively, so no conversion is
applied there.

## Conversation memory: one conversation per space

- **A space (channel) keeps one running conversation.** Every top-level
  message continues it, so the bot remembers the topic across days.
- **A reply inside a thread gets its own focused conversation** —
  threads are sub-topics.
- **A DM with the bot is one continuous personal conversation.**
- Send `/new` (or `/reset`) to drop the binding and start fresh.

Privacy note: all linked members of a space share that space's
conversation history — that is the point of topic memory. Do not
discuss things with the bot in a team space you would not post there
yourself. Each turn still runs under the *sender's* permissions, and
only the person who initiated a workflow-run confirmation can approve
its card.

## Direct messages (DMs)

A 1:1 chat with the bot is its own space (Google marks it
`DIRECT_MESSAGE`) with one continuous personal conversation — no
threads. Registration is mostly automatic on Google Chat:

- **A user already linked in another space of your tenant can just
  DM the bot.** sk recognizes the sender's linked identity,
  auto-registers the DM space under that tenant, and answers the very
  first message — a normal governed read-only turn under the user's
  real role. The install is audited (chat-workspace-installed,
  `dm_autoregister`); no manual registration call is needed.
- **An unlinked sender is politely refused.** The message is dropped
  with a `chat.message.denied` audit row (reason
  `dm_sender_not_linked`, recorded under the platform-system tenant
  since no tenant is known), and the sender gets the generic
  "not connected" reply. Link the user in a team space first (see
  *Link members* below), then the DM works.
- **A user linked in more than one tenant is refused** (reason
  `dm_sender_ambiguous`) — sk never guesses which tenant a DM belongs
  to. Pin it manually: register the DM space with `POST
  /v1/chat/workspaces` under the intended tenant and link the
  identity for that space, exactly like a group space.
- **Slack and Teams DMs will not auto-register.** Their user ids are
  workspace-scoped, so a cross-workspace identity match could bridge
  tenants; DM spaces on those platforms need the manual per-space
  install.

DM users run under their linked account's role like everyone else —
see [Which role should linked chat users
have?](#which-role-should-linked-chat-users-have) for guidance.

## Set up Google Chat

Prerequisites: a Google Workspace domain (consumer `@gmail.com`
accounts cannot install custom Chat apps), a GCP project, and a public
HTTPS route to the engine.

> Worth knowing before you start: Google Chat can always deliver an
> in-chat "this space isn't connected" reply for an unregistered space,
> so a misconfigured Google space tells you so. Slack generally cannot
> (its bot tokens are workspace-scoped), so an unregistered Slack space
> just stays silent — on Slack, check the audit log rather than waiting
> for an error in the channel.

1. **GCP project** — enable the *Google Chat API*.
2. **Service account** — create one, download a JSON key; you need
   `client_email` and `private_key`.
3. **Configure the Chat app** (Chat API → *Configuration*):
   - Leave **"Build this Chat app as a Google Workspace add-on"
     UNCHECKED** — sk speaks the classic HTTP-app contract; the add-on
     style uses a different verifier and payload and will not work.
   - App name, avatar URL, description; enable *Interactive features*;
     check *Join spaces and group conversations*.
   - Connection settings: **HTTP endpoint URL** =
     `https://<engine-host>/v1/chat/google/events`.
   - **Authentication Audience: "Project Number"** (not "HTTP endpoint
     URL") — sk verifies inbound JWTs against this audience.
   - Visibility: your domain users (up to 25 testers without a
     Marketplace listing).
4. **Engine config.** These three leaves are **engine-global** (shared
   by every tenant on this engine — see *Adding a second tenant* below)
   and marked `requiresRestart`. On a production engine
   (`NODE_ENV=production`) each write is rejected unless you pass
   `--force`:

   ```bash
   sk settings set platform.googlechat.client_email "<sa>@<project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com" --force
   sk settings set platform.googlechat.private_key "$(cat key.pem)" --force
   sk settings set platform.googlechat.audience "<project number>" --force
   ```

   **What "restart required" actually means here:** the write takes
   effect in the running process immediately — `sk settings get
   platform.googlechat.client_email` shows the new value right away, and
   a chat event handled by this process picks it up on its next
   workspace-hydration. The restart caveat only matters for (a) *other*
   already-running instances in a multi-instance deploy, and (b) an
   already-hydrated adapter in this process, which rebuilds on the next
   registry install/miss. In a single-instance deployment you almost
   never need to bounce a live engine for this — confirm with `sk
   settings get` and only restart if a workspace still fails to hydrate.

   **`private_key` is the most common copy/paste failure here:** shell
   quoting can silently collapse newlines or trailing whitespace inside
   the PEM, and there is no key-validation step — a mangled key isn't
   caught until an outbound send fails later. Use `$(cat key.pem)`
   verbatim as shown, then run `sk settings get
   platform.googlechat.private_key` to confirm the leaf is recorded (the
   value comes back masked, but a masked-but-present result confirms it
   isn't empty).

5. **Install each space** — add the app to the space in Google Chat,
   then register the space with your tenant (one install per space;
   Google events carry no domain id). Two ways to get the space id
   (`spaces/AAAA...`): copy it from the space URL (always works), or —
   if the space is already messaging the bot and failing — find the
   `chat.message.denied` audit row with `reason: "workspace_not_installed"`
   and read its `metadata.workspace_id_native`. (There is no dedicated
   "app added to space" audit action; don't grep logs for one.)

   ```bash
   curl -X POST https://<engine-host>/v1/chat/workspaces \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $SK_ADMIN_KEY" -H "content-type: application/json" \
     -d '{"platform":"google_chat","workspace_id":"spaces/AAAA...",
          "installer_platform_user_id":"users/1234567890"}'
   ```

   No `bot_token` — Google outbound auth uses the app-level service
   account from engine config.

6. **Link members** — unknown senders get a polite rejection and a
   `chat.message.denied` audit row. Link each user (their Google id is
   in that audit row's metadata):

   ```bash
   curl -X POST https://<engine-host>/v1/chat/identities \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $SK_ADMIN_KEY" -H "content-type: application/json" \
     -d '{"platform":"google_chat","workspace_id":"spaces/AAAA...",
          "platform_user_id":"users/1234567890","user_id":"<subkit-user-uuid>"}'
   ```

### Adding a second tenant on an already-configured engine

`platform.googlechat.*` credentials are **engine-global** — one Google
Chat app / service account serves every tenant on this engine. If
Google Chat already works for tenant A and you're bringing tenant B
onto the same engine, **do not repeat step 4**: re-running it with a
different service account would break tenant A, and re-running it with
the same values is an unnecessary no-op. Attempting to scope these
leaves per-tenant (`--tenant <id>`) is rejected outright — they are not
tenant-overlay settings. What *is* per-tenant is the space↔tenant
binding, so for each new tenant only repeat steps 5–6: install the
app in that tenant's space(s), then link its members.

## Which role should linked chat users have?

The built-in `enduser` role fits the channel: run + read workflows,
read executions, knowledge, and skills, converse — nothing else. Two
reads are deliberately **not** in `enduser`: `connector:read` (the bot
will refuse "which systems are connected?") and `schedule:read`. If
your chat users should see that metadata, create a custom role =
enduser permissions + `connector:read` + `schedule:read` and link
their identities to users holding it. Admin-linked users get admin
*reads and runs* — never authoring; the channel restriction does not
care about roles.

### Finding chat users who need to be linked

There's no dedicated "pending link requests" view. To find everyone who
has tried to message the bot in a workspace but isn't linked yet, pull
the denied-audit rows and filter by reason client-side (the audit API
doesn't filter on `reason` directly):

```bash
sk audit list --action chat.message.denied --json \
  | jq '.items[] | select(.reason=="identity_not_linked") | {ts, metadata}'
```

Each match's `metadata` carries the sender's platform user id
(`users/<id>` for Google Chat) — feed it into `POST /v1/chat/identities`
as in *Link members*. This is a point-in-time snapshot, not a live
queue; re-run it after onboarding a new group.

## Slash commands

| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `/subkit chat <prompt>` (or just mention the bot) | Continue the space conversation |
| `/subkit run <workflow-slug>` | Run a saved workflow — same RBAC + confirmation card as asking in prose |
| `/new` or `/reset` | Start a fresh conversation for this space/thread |

Naming the exact slug (`/subkit run <workflow-slug>`) always works. You
can also just describe what you want in plain prose (in any language) —
when it unambiguously identifies one saved workflow, the bot resolves
it (via the same fuzzy lookup behind `find_workflow`) and runs it
behind the normal confirmation card. If more than one workflow
plausibly matches, the bot asks which one instead of guessing. Naming
the slug is still the fastest, most reliable path.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Look at |
|---|---|
| Bot never answers | Engine log `chat` module; `CHAT_WORKSPACE_HYDRATE_SKIPPED` audit (`google_credentials_unset` = config incomplete) |
| Bot replies "This space isn't connected to sk yet" | The space is not registered. The reply is generic and rate-limited (once per minute per space); the drop is audited as `chat.message.denied` under the platform-system tenant with the space name in metadata. Register it: `POST /v1/chat/workspaces` (see *Install each space*). On Slack this reply usually cannot be delivered (bot tokens are workspace-scoped), so an unregistered Slack space stays silent — check the audit row instead |
| DM gets the "not connected" reply | The sender is not linked in exactly one tenant — the `chat.message.denied` reason is `dm_sender_not_linked` (link them in a team space first) or `dm_sender_ambiguous` (register the DM space manually to pin the tenant); see *Direct messages (DMs)* |
| 401 on every event | Authentication Audience must be "Project Number" and match `platform.googlechat.audience`; app must be classic-style, not add-on |
| "Your chat account isn't linked" | `chat.message.denied` audit (`identity_not_linked`) carries the sender's `users/<id>` for the link call |
| Space stopped answering after the app was removed/re-added | Removal drops the space's session bindings by design; re-adding starts a fresh conversation |
| User clicks a confirmation card, nothing happens | Only the requester can confirm (`actor_not_owner` audit); the clicking user gets an in-channel note |
| Google shows "SubKit Chat Channels reagiert nicht" / "…isn't responding" after every message | Expected Google Chat behavior, not a sk failure. sk acknowledges the webhook immediately and posts the real reply asynchronously (turns can take seconds); Google's client shows this placeholder in the gap. A *real* failure looks different: no reply ever arrives, or a `chat.message.denied`/error audit row exists for that message |
| Google Chat send fails after setup looked clean | The `private_key` PEM likely got mangled by shell quoting during `sk settings set`. Re-run with `$(cat key.pem)` verbatim; there is no server-side key validation, so a bad key only surfaces as a failed outbound send, not a rejected `settings set` |

## Known friction / roadmap

Installing a space and linking members today means hand-rolling the
`curl` calls above against the HTTP API with an admin key — there is no
`sk chat install` / `sk chat link` convenience wrapping those two
routes yet. This is the single biggest rough edge in an otherwise
straightforward setup; a CLI wrapper is a natural follow-up. Until it
lands, keep the two `curl` templates handy — the request bodies are
stable.

## Slack and Microsoft Teams

The same channel contract (read-only palette, space memory, identity
linking, confirmation cards) applies to Slack and Teams; their
activation is tracked separately. Slack's adapter (signing-secret
verification, Block Kit, modals) already ships — setup docs land with
its rollout.

<!-- Source: docs/operators/connectors-and-credentials.md -->

# Connectors & Credentials (operator guide)

**Connect a system once, reuse it everywhere — and the credential is never exposed.**
Operators attach a credential to a connector a single time; every workflow then
references that connector by name. Secrets stay encrypted in the vault, out of
logs, out of LLM context, and out of every response body.

> **Audience:** Operators registering connectors, managing credentials, and
> keeping integrations healthy in production.

This is the operational slice of the connector subsystem: attach and rotate
credentials, test connectivity on demand, invoke an endpoint ad-hoc, and run the
vendor-drift sweep. For the full conceptual model — drivers, templates, the
catalog, schema-version drift — see
[Connectors & Integration](../concepts/connectors.md).

## The onboarding path

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Pick template] --> B[Supply credential]
    B --> V[(Credential Vault<br/>encrypted at rest)]
    B --> C[Probe]
    C -->|ok + latency| D[Reference in a workflow]
    C -->|credential_required| B
    V -.referenced by name.-> D
```

| Step | What you do | What the engine does |
|---|---|---|
| Pick template | Match a vendor or URL to a connector template | Pre-fills driver, auth pattern, endpoints |
| Supply credential | `credentials set` once | Encrypts to vault, returns a reference, never the value |
| Probe | `connectors test` | Authenticates, reports status + latency |
| Reference | Name the connector in a workflow step | Applies the saved credential at run time |

![Connecting a system in the sk terminal: pick the target, enter credentials, test the connection, save](../_tapes/out/operator-onboard.gif)

---

## Authentication and credential management

sk supports the authentication patterns enterprise systems actually use.

| Pattern | Notes |
|---|---|
| API key | `bearer`, `header`, or `query` placement |
| OAuth2 | Authorisation-code and client-credentials flows |
| Basic auth | Username / password |
| AWS SigV4 | Signed requests |
| Custom header | Arbitrary scheme |

**OAuth2 is fully managed.** Configure the connector once; the engine handles
token refresh, expiry detection, and rotation automatically. No workflow ever
manages token lifecycle.

**Secrets live only in the Credential Vault** — encrypted at rest, never logged,
never exposed outside the engine. Workflows and steps reference credentials by
name, not by value. The full vault model and master-key rotation procedure are in
[Credentials & Keys](../admins/credentials-and-keys.md).

**Secrets are never collected in chat.** When onboarding runs through an AI client
over MCP, sk refuses to accept a credential as plain conversation text. A
secret-shaped prompt is declined and the operator is routed to the secure flow
instead — a scoped portal-setup link where the value is typed into a masked field,
or the managed OAuth authorization flow. The credential goes straight into the
encrypted vault outside the chat transcript; the AI client only learns that the
connector is now authorized. This means a token can never leak into a conversation
history, a tool argument, or a log — regardless of which surface drove the
onboarding. Even on a local CLI/web surface, where an operator _may_ type a secret
into a masked form, the answer is redacted (`***redacted***`) before it is persisted
or replayed to the model, and any credential slot in a tool argument is scrubbed at
the same boundary — the raw value only ever exists in memory on its way to the
encrypted vault.

**The portal-setup link needs no sign-in.** The link itself is the authorization:
a single-use grant token minted from your chat session, valid for a few minutes
and burned on submit — so the page never asks you to log in to sk. What the form
does ask for is the credential issued by the external service the connector
targets (its API key, token, or password), because that secret exists only on
the external service's side and cannot be derived from any sk or SSO identity.

**End-User Credentials** extend this for multi-user scenarios: an individual user
supplies their own credentials, and the platform acts as that user when executing
on their behalf — proper delegation, not credential sharing.

Attach a credential from the CLI:

```bash
sk credentials set <CONNECTOR_ID> --mode bearer --token sk_live_…
#   modes: bearer | header | query | basic | aws_sigv4 | none
sk credentials list <CONNECTOR_ID>
```

Cloudflare and Firebase/Firestore are built in:

```bash
# Cloudflare: use a newly created, least-privilege API token.
sk connectors create --template cloudflare --name cloudflare-prod
sk credentials set <CONNECTOR_ID> --mode bearer --token '<NEW_SCOPED_TOKEN>'

# Firebase: store the Google OAuth client once per tenant/template, then authorize the connector.
sk connector-templates set-oauth --slug firebase \
  --client-id '<GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID>' \
  --client-secret '<GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET>'
sk connectors create --template firebase --name firebase-prod
sk auth --connector-id <CONNECTOR_ID>
```

Revoke any Cloudflare token that has appeared in chat, logs, shell history, or source control.
Firebase ID tokens are also accepted as short-lived Bearer credentials for end-user flows; a
service-account JSON key is not an OAuth client secret.

## Connecting a remote MCP server

A remote Model Context Protocol server is a connector like any other — driver
`mcp`. There is no separate MCP-server registry to learn: the same create,
patch, enable, disable, and delete commands apply, the secret goes in the same
vault, and it shows up in the same catalog under the `mcp` driver.

```bash
# driver "mcp", base_url = the server endpoint,
# config: { mcp: { transport: "http", auth: { kind: … } } }
sk connectors create --file server.json
sk credentials set <CONNECTOR_ID> --mode bearer --token '<TOKEN>'

sk connectors mcp-inspect <CONNECTOR_ID>    # one handshake: what does it serve?
sk connectors mcp-authorize <CONNECTOR_ID>  # interactive OAuth 2.1, when the server needs it
```

`mcp-inspect` performs a single handshake and reports the remote's negotiated
capabilities, its instructions, and its tool manifest — the fastest way to
confirm a server is reachable and authorised before anyone authors against it.
`mcp-authorize` is for servers that publish their authorization server through
protected-resource metadata rather than declaring an issuer in config; the
generic connector OAuth flow cannot serve those.

Never put a token in `config`. The `mcp.auth` block is refused at the storage
layer if it carries a secret-shaped key — a database `CHECK`, not a convention.

**The operator off switch works on every driver:**

```bash
sk connectors disable <CONNECTOR_ID>
sk connectors enable  <CONNECTOR_ID>
```

Disabling is immediate and honest: an MCP connector's pooled session is evicted
and a Postgres connector's pool is closed on the way out, so nothing keeps
serving past the switch. A disabled connector is also skipped by the reauth
scan — for MCP that scan is a full handshake, and probing a server an operator
deliberately turned off would park it in backoff for no reason.

Four fields are worth knowing when a remote misbehaves, and every one of them
is written by the engine rather than copied from the upstream — a remote's own
error body can echo the credential it just rejected, so it stays in the
engine's logs and never lands in a field you can export or render.
`last_error` is the engine's account of the most recent failed attempt, in the
form `[<error_code>] <sentence>`. `health_state` is the reconciled verdict
(`ok`, `degraded`, `needs_update`, `needs_reauth`) — whether the engine
considers the connector usable at all, which is a different question from the
`enabled` switch. `health_reason` and `health_error_code` say what the last
change of that verdict was. All four are readable on `GET /v1/connectors` and
on the single-connector GET. Repeated handshake failures count in the database
and arm a backoff that survives an engine restart — so a server that has been
refusing for an hour is not handed a full-rate retry just because the process
bounced.

## Health and validation

Every connector can be tested independently of any workflow. The engine validates
the connection, authenticates with the configured credentials, and reports the
result plus connection latency. Connector tests and workflow request steps share
the same request-execution path, so a passing test reflects the exact transport a
workflow will use.

```bash
sk connectors test <CONNECTOR_ID>   # re-probe connectivity
```

A draft connector with no saved credential cannot be probed: the probe path
returns a structured `credential_required` envelope rather than silently sending
an unauthenticated request.

## Ad-hoc invocation

Once a connector is persisted, invoke any endpoint against it — for sampling,
pagination validation, or response-shape inspection — without authoring a
workflow. The conversational `call_connector` tool and the matching
`POST /v1/connectors/{id}/call` route apply the saved credential, emit a
`connector.invoked` audit row, and return status, headers, body, latency, and a
truncation flag.

```bash
curl -X POST "$SK_BASE_URL/v1/connectors/$CONNECTOR_ID/call" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SK_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "method": "GET", "path": "/v2/droplets", "query": { "per_page": 10 } }'
```

| Driver | `call_connector` (conversational tool) | `POST /v1/connectors/{id}/call` |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP | Supported | Supported |
| GraphQL | Supported | Supported |
| Postgres / S3 | Supported | Returns `driver_not_supported_for_call_connector` |
| MCP | Not applicable — see below | Not applicable — see below |

An unsupported driver returns a structured `driver_not_supported_for_call_connector`
envelope pointing at workflow authoring, rather than failing opaquely.

MCP connectors are outside this surface by shape, not by omission: a remote tool
takes a name and typed arguments, not a method and a path. Invoke one from a
workflow `request` step carrying an `mcp` block, or from chat, where every tool the
server publishes already appears as `mcp_<connector-slug>__<tool>`. To see what a
server offers without calling anything, use `sk connectors mcp-inspect <ID>`.

## Keeping a fleet healthy

Drift is detected from actual execution results, not periodic polling — a
connector that worked last month surfaces drift the moment a real run hits a
changed response shape. That drift feeds the operator-reviewed repair loop in
[Self-healing](./self-healing.md).

To proactively re-verify templates against live vendor APIs, run the vendor-drift
sweep documented in
[Connectors & Integration → Vendor-drift Sweep](../concepts/connectors.md#vendor-drift-sweep).

---

## Further reading

- [Connectors & Integration](../concepts/connectors.md) — the full conceptual model and route surface.
- [Credentials & Keys](../admins/credentials-and-keys.md) — the credential vault and rotation.
- [Self-healing](./self-healing.md) — how connector drift becomes an operator-reviewed Patch Candidate.

# Deploy & upgrade the engine

Upgrading is a two-step operation you can do in the middle of the day: replace one file,
restart one service. Work that was in flight picks up where it left off, because none of it
lives in the process.

That is possible because the engine is a single compiled binary at `/usr/local/bin/engine`,
run by the `subkit-engine` systemd unit, and holds no state of its own — everything durable
is in PostgreSQL.

## Version discipline

- **Never reuse a tag.** Every deploy bumps the semver in `package.json` and
  ships a new `vX.Y.Z` tag. The tag triggers `release.yml`, which builds and
  publishes the signed multi-platform assets (`engine_<os>_<arch>`,
  `SHA256SUMS`, `SHA256SUMS.sig`).
- The running version is reported by `GET /health` (`"version"`).

## Before a major-version upgrade

A major bump means at least one surface was removed rather than deprecated —
this project ships no backwards-compatibility shims, so an old path is gone in
the same release that replaces it. **Read that version's `CHANGELOG.md` entry
before you swap the binary**, and expect one of two failure shapes if you do not:

- **The engine refuses to boot.** Config the engine no longer has is a refusal,
  not a warning — the schema would strip an unknown section silently and the
  next settings write would erase it from disk, so a stale section is data at
  risk, and only stopping is honest. The error names every offending path, how
  many declarations are at stake, and the migration. Fix the config, then start.
- **A caller gets a 404.** A removed route or CLI command is removed. Check the
  CHANGELOG entry for what replaced it.

The pre-flight, run on the staged binary before it replaces the live one:

```bash
# Loads config FIRST, then applies migrations, then exits — without ever
# starting the HTTP listener. A config section the new version dropped
# fails here, on a unit that is still serving the old binary.
ssh root@<engine-host> '/tmp/engine-new --migrate'
```

`--version` is not a substitute: it prints and exits before any config work, by
design, so a version probe never needs a configured environment.

Note what `--migrate` really does — it *applies* the migrations rather than
rehearsing them, and migrations are forward-only. That is the same work the boot
path would do moments later, so it costs nothing extra; it does mean the
database has moved before the binary does. Take the backup before this step, not
after: [Rollback](#rollback) restores the binary, not the schema.

## Standard deploy — published-asset scp (supported path)

This is the reliable path and the one to use when self-update is not configured
(see below). It installs the exact signed release asset.

```bash
# 1. Download + checksum-verify the published Linux binary
gh release download vX.Y.Z --pattern engine_linux_x64 --pattern SHA256SUMS --dir /tmp/rel
cd /tmp/rel
EXP=$(grep 'engine_linux_x64$' SHA256SUMS | grep -oE '^[0-9a-f]{64}')
ACT=$(shasum -a 256 engine_linux_x64 | grep -oE '^[0-9a-f]{64}')
[ "$EXP" = "$ACT" ] && echo CHECKSUM_OK || { echo MISMATCH; exit 1; }

# 2. Back up the running binary, then swap + restart on the host
ssh root@<engine-host> 'cp -a /usr/local/bin/engine /usr/local/bin/engine.bak-$(curl -s localhost:3000/health | grep -o "\"version\":\"[^\"]*\"")'
scp engine_linux_x64 root@<engine-host>:/tmp/engine-new
ssh root@<engine-host> 'chmod +x /tmp/engine-new && mv /tmp/engine-new /usr/local/bin/engine && systemctl restart subkit-engine'

# 3. Verify
ssh root@<engine-host> 'curl -s localhost:3000/health'   # expect the new "version"
ssh root@<engine-host> 'journalctl -u subkit-engine --since "60 seconds ago" | grep -E "ready.*version|migrate.applied|hydrate.completed"'
```

`SHA256SUMS` uses a no-separator format (`<hash>engine_linux_x64`); extract the
hash with `grep -oE '^[0-9a-f]{64}'` on the matching line, not `awk '{print $1}'`.

## Probe endpoints

The engine exposes one canonical path for each probe:

| Path | Probe | Codes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /health` | liveness — if the handler runs, it returns `{status, service, version}` | 200 |
| `GET /ready` | readiness — checks lifecycle and database access | 200 / 503 |

Both are unauthenticated, return JSON with `Cache-Control: no-store`, and are
documented in `openapi.json`. `/health` never checks a dependency. `/ready`
returns `checks.lifecycle` and `checks.database` as `pass` or `fail`; gate
load-balancer routing on `/ready`, never on `/health`. The former legacy paths
`/v1/health` and `/v1/readyz` are intentionally not available.

## Serving the `sk` CLI from the engine (`/install`)

Users install the CLI by running `curl -fsSL https://<engine-hostname>/install | bash`
against the engine they already talk to (chat, MCP, or API), where
`<engine-hostname>` is the DNS name the engine already knows via its
`server.public_base_url` config — always the hostname, never a bare IP (the
install script interpolates it into the profile and OAuth2 redirect URIs). That
script probes `https://<engine-hostname>/install/sk-<os>-<arch>` first and only
falls back to github.com. **While the repo is private, the GitHub fallback
returns 404 for users**, so the engine must serve the binaries itself —
otherwise the install one-liner the chat hands out dead-ends.

Stage all five client-platform binaries into `SUBKIT_BINARIES_DIR` (default
`/usr/local/share/subkit/binaries`), built straight from source with no
github.com dependency:

```bash
# On a build host with the repo checked out at the deploy tag:
bun scripts/stage-cli-binaries.ts --dir /tmp/sk-binaries --version X.Y.Z
# → sk_{darwin,linux,windows}_{arm64,x64}[.exe] + SHA256SUMS

# Ship to the engine host (address it by its DNS hostname, not an IP), then
# (re)start so a cold cache picks them up.
ssh root@<engine-hostname> 'mkdir -p /usr/local/share/subkit/binaries'
scp /tmp/sk-binaries/* root@<engine-hostname>:/usr/local/share/subkit/binaries/
ssh root@<engine-hostname> 'systemctl restart subkit-engine'

# Verify against the public hostname (the same server.public_base_url users
# hit): 200 + x-subkit-sha256 for every client platform.
curl -fsSI https://<engine-hostname>/install/sk-darwin-arm64 | grep -i x-subkit-sha256
```

The staged `SHA256SUMS` uses the two-space `sha256sum` format
(`<hash>  sk_<os>_<arch>`) that both the serving route and the install script's
`grep`/`sha256sum -c` expect — it is intentionally distinct from the
no-separator format of the release `SHA256SUMS` used by self-update. The route
does not cache the empty-directory state, so staging after the engine is already
up is picked up on the next request; the restart above is only needed if you
want it live immediately without waiting for a request to re-probe.

The all-in-one Docker image bakes these binaries in at build time (see the
`stage-cli-binaries` step in the `Dockerfile`), so containerized deploys serve
`/install/{asset}` with no extra step.

## Self-update (`engine --self-update`)

The engine can pull the latest published GitHub release and swap its own binary:

```bash
engine --self-update      # checks the latest release; installs it if NEWER
engine --rollback         # swap back to a previously retained signed binary
```

Two things to know:

- **It only moves FORWARD.** `checkForUpdate` compares versions with `isNewer`
  and never downgrades, so a self-update can never revert you to an older
  release.
- **A PRIVATE repo needs a token.** GitHub returns **404** (not 401) to
  *unauthenticated* reads of a private repo's releases. Without a token,
  self-update cannot see any release and now reports this honestly (previously
  it read as a misleading "already at latest"). To enable self-update on a
  private-repo deployment, put a read-scoped token in the unit's
  `EnvironmentFile` (`/etc/subkit/.env`):

  ```bash
  # /etc/subkit/.env
  GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_...        # or SUBKIT_UPDATE_TOKEN=...
  ```

  then `systemctl restart subkit-engine` so the process picks it up. With the
  token set, `engine --self-update` reads the private repo's releases and
  installs the newest signed asset (Ed25519-verified against `SHA256SUMS.sig`).
  Until a token is set, use the published-asset scp above.

## Rollback

- Fast: `mv /usr/local/bin/engine.bak-<version> /usr/local/bin/engine && systemctl restart subkit-engine`.
- Or `engine --rollback` (swaps to a retained signed binary; keeps the last
  few — see `RETAINED_VERSIONS_KEEP`).
- App-level: every workflow change is an immutable version — roll a workflow
  back independently of the binary.

## Memory / OOM

The unit caps memory (`MemoryHigh=6G`, `MemoryMax=7G`) and steers the OOM killer
toward the engine (not Postgres). A killed engine restarts via `Restart=on-failure`
and resumes queued jobs. See `docs/admins/production-hardening.md` for the full
memory-containment rationale.

<!-- Source: docs/operators/notifications.md -->

# Notifications

**Operators hear about what matters, not noise.** When a workflow run
ends — succeeded, failed, or aborted — the right people learn about it
in the channel they already watch, with rate limits and circuit
breakers keeping a flapping target from drowning out the signal. Less
log-spelunking, faster incident response, a full audit trail of who
was told what.

sk turns engine outbox events into delivered messages, governed by
tenant-scoped rules, with rate limits, circuit breakers, audit, and
RBAC.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    run([Workflow run ends]) --> ev[events row<br/>execution.status]
    ev --> fan[Outbox fanout]
    fan --> rule{Notification rule<br/>match?}
    rule -->|no| drop([No delivery])
    rule -->|yes| brk{Circuit breaker}
    brk -->|open| skip([record breaker_open])
    brk -->|closed / half-open| rl{Rate limiter}
    rl -->|empty bucket| limited([record rate_limited])
    rl -->|token| ch[Channel adapter]
    ch --> slack[Slack]
    ch --> teams[Teams]
    ch --> gchat[Google Chat]
    ch --> hook[Webhook]
    ch --> rec[(notification_deliveries<br/>+ audit row)]
```

## Surface at a glance

| Concept | Where it lives | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Notification rule | `notification_rules` row | Selects which events go where, with severity + filter |
| Notification channel | `notification_channels` row | Concrete delivery target — Slack workspace+channel, Teams team+channel, Google Chat space, or webhook URL |
| Notification delivery | `notification_deliveries` row | Per-attempt result: `sent`, `rate_limited`, `breaker_open`, `failed`, `skipped` |
| Adapter | `chat/{slack,teams,google_chat}/adapter.ts` + `notifications/channels/webhook.ts` | Talks to the platform |
| Dispatcher | `apps/engine/src/notifications/service.ts` | Matches rules → applies rate limit + breaker → invokes adapter → records audit + delivery row |
| Outbox fanout | `apps/engine/src/webhooks/outbound/fanout.ts` | Drains `events` table → calls `dispatchEvent()` |

## End-to-end flow

| Step | Component | Action |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `execution/state.ts` | Workflow finishes → writes an `events` row, channel `execution.status`, type `execution.<status>` (`succeeded`, `failed`, `aborted`, `timed_out`, …). |
| 2 | `webhooks/outbound/fanout.ts` | Outbox listener forwards the row → fanout looks up active subscriptions (outbound webhooks) AND active notification rules (chat / webhook notifications). |
| 3 | `notifications/service.ts#dispatchEvent` | Per matching rule, runs the dispatch pipeline below. |

For each matching rule, `dispatchEvent`:

1. resolves (or auto-creates) the `notification_channels` row,
2. checks the circuit breaker (`closed` → continue, `open` → record
   `breaker_open` and skip, `half-open` → trial-fire),
3. acquires a token from the leaky-bucket rate limiter (records
   `rate_limited` when the bucket is empty),
4. resolves an adapter via the registry,
5. invokes `adapter.send()` with a structured `ChatDelivery`,
6. records a `notification_deliveries` row + an audit row,
7. updates the breaker state from the outcome (`closed → open` after
   `FAILURE_THRESHOLD` consecutive failures; `half-open → closed` on
   first success).

> The dispatcher always resolves. Per-rule failures are logged and
> recorded, never thrown — a misconfigured rule cannot block other
> deliveries.

## Channels

### Chat (Slack, Teams, Google Chat)

The chat adapters under `apps/engine/src/chat/` ship as full peers —
they verify inbound webhooks, normalize platform events, and post
outbound messages. The notification subsystem reuses the same `send()`
surface to deliver completion signals to the operator's chat
workspace.

### Webhook (`notifications/channels/webhook.ts`)

For tenants that prefer a generic HTTP endpoint over a chat platform.

| Behaviour | Detail |
|---|---|
| Payload | POSTs JSON `{ tenant_id, workspace_id, channel_id, kind, text }` |
| Headers | `content-type: application/json`, `x-subkit-notification: 1`, `x-subkit-attempt: <n>`, optional `x-subkit-secret` shared secret |
| Retry | At most `WEBHOOK_MAX_ATTEMPTS` tries (default 3), exponential backoff capped at `WEBHOOK_BACKOFF_CAP_MS` (30 s) |
| Backpressure | Honours `Retry-After` on `429` / `503` responses |
| Terminal errors | Non-`429` `4xx` treated as terminal — retrying a mis-configured receiver wastes budget |

## Rules

A `notification_rules` row carries:

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `event_pattern` | Glob matched against the event type (`execution.*`, `execution.failed`, `*`). |
| `workflow_pattern` | Glob matched against `workflow_id` or `workflow_slug` so a rule can scope to a specific workflow family. |
| `severity` | Drives both the platform-side rendering and the per-rule rate limit. |
| `request_source_filter` | Array of sources the rule should fire for. Default: the dispatcher skips `chat`-sourced runs (the conversation already saw the result) and `mcp` runs (the caller is an LLM, not a human). |
| `target_workspace_id` + `target_channel_id` | Point at the channel row to deliver through. |
| `active` | Soft-disable without deleting. |

## Rate limiting

Per-channel leaky bucket in
`apps/engine/src/notifications/rate-limit.ts`. Tokens regenerate at
`rate_limit_per_minute / 60 000` ms. When the bucket is empty the
dispatcher records `rate_limited` with the resume time and skips
delivery — the rule's downstream consumer is not stalled by the
limiter.

## Circuit breaker

Per-channel three-state breaker in
`apps/engine/src/notifications/circuit-breaker.ts`:

| State | Effect |
|---|---|
| `closed` | Deliveries proceed. Failure count resets on success. |
| `open` | Dispatcher records `breaker_open` and skips. Auto-flips to half-open after `OPEN_DURATION_MS`. |
| `half-open` | One trial delivery is allowed. Success → `closed`; failure → `open`. |

`FAILURE_THRESHOLD` consecutive failures (default 5) opens the breaker.
The breaker is per-channel, not per-rule — a rule that targets a
healthy channel keeps firing even when an unrelated rule's target is
down.

## RBAC

| Permission | Routes / actions |
|---|---|
| `notification:read` | List/get channels, rules, deliveries; `GET` on every notifications endpoint. |
| `notification:write` | Create/update/delete channels and rules; `POST /v1/notifications/rules/:id/test` (because triggering a synthetic event causes a real outbound delivery and a real audit row). |

Every write through the HTTP routes flows through `auditAwait` so the
audit log carries the actor, the resource, and the changed fields.

## HTTP routes

| Method | Path | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/v1/notifications/channels` | |
| `POST` | `/v1/notifications/channels` | |
| `PATCH` | `/v1/notifications/channels/:id` | |
| `DELETE` | `/v1/notifications/channels/:id` | |
| `GET` | `/v1/notifications/rules` | |
| `POST` | `/v1/notifications/rules` | |
| `PATCH` | `/v1/notifications/rules/:id` | |
| `DELETE` | `/v1/notifications/rules/:id` | |
| `POST` | `/v1/notifications/rules/:id/test` | Synthesise a notification event and dispatch it through the rule pipeline. Returns the rule-matching, rate-limit, and channel-dispatch outcome so operators can verify a rule end-to-end without waiting for a real workflow run. Audited as `notification_rule.tested`. |
| `GET` | `/v1/notifications/deliveries?limit=&offset=&status=` | |

All routes are Zod-first (see
`apps/engine/src/http/routes/notifications.ts`) and surface in the
generated OpenAPI document.

## Audit actions

| Action | Trigger |
|---|---|
| `notification_channel.created` / `.updated` / `.deleted` | Channel lifecycle |
| `notification_rule.created` / `.updated` / `.deleted` / `.tested` | Rule lifecycle + test |
| `chat.message.sent` | Delivery `sent` |
| `chat.message.denied` | Delivery `rate_limited` or `breaker_open` |
| `webhook.outbound.failed` | Delivery `failed` |

## Observability

| Signal | Detail |
|---|---|
| Counter `chat_delivery_total{platform,status}` | Partitioned by adapter platform and outcome. |
| Counter `webhook_delivery_total{subscription_id,status}` | For the webhook subscriptions surface (parallel system; see [observability](observability.md)). |
| Structured logs (`notifications/service.ts`) | Carry `tenant_id`, `rule_id`, `channel_id`, `event_type`, `status`. |

## What is intentionally not here

| Not built | Why / where instead |
|---|---|
| Per-user notifications | Recipients are channel-targeted; there is no personal-inbox model. |
| Templating DSL | Message text is built from event metadata. A future template field on rules could land here without changing the dispatch contract. |
| In-app notification surface | No dedicated UI inbox; the deliveries table is the authoritative log. |

## Notification payload pattern — what, why, proposal

Notifications are the first place an operator sees the bounded repair
loop in action. A useful incident message answers four questions in a
single delivery, so the operator can decide without opening logs:

| Question | Carries |
|---|---|
| **What** happened | The failure substance — status, surfaced error, timestamp. |
| **Where** it happened | Workflow slug and version, step id, the external endpoint that drifted. Decisive the moment there is more than one workflow, supplier, or tenant: "the script broke" is not enough. |
| **Why** it happened | The drift the connector or driver actually detected — not just the HTTP status — plus the `patch_candidate` reference when the bounded repair loop has already produced one. |
| **How** to act | The Patch Candidate diff, the deterministic dry-run outcome against recorded fixtures, and the operator actions: **approve**, **reject**, **escalate to human**. |

A concrete delivery body — the same shape across every surface:

```json
{
  "what": {
    "occurred_at": "2026-05-27T14:02:11Z",
    "status": "failed",
    "error": "http_422 — unknown field 'sku_external'"
  },
  "where": {
    "workflow_slug": "sync-suppliers",
    "workflow_version": 4,
    "step_id": "pull-supplier-3",
    "endpoint": "supplier-3/inventory"
  },
  "why": {
    "kind": "schema_drift",
    "diff": { "renamed": [{ "from": "sku_external", "to": "sku" }] },
    "patch_candidate_id": "pc_4711"
  },
  "how": {
    "summary": "Map field 'sku_external' → 'sku' in pull-supplier-3 response shape",
    "dryrun": { "fixtures": 12, "passed": 12, "diverged": 0 },
    "actions": ["approve", "reject", "escalate"]
  }
}
```

One payload contract, every surface:

| Surface | Mode | Renders |
|---|---|---|
| Slack / Teams / Google Chat | Push | Platform-native blocks — four sections as headings, operator actions as buttons. |
| Webhook | Push | The JSON verbatim — the receiving system gets the same four-part answer for its own UI. |
| sk CLI — `sk executions tail` | Pull | Live *what* + *where* + *why* as the run progresses. |
| sk CLI — `sk patch-candidates get <id>` | Pull | The *how*, with `sk patch-candidates approve` / `reject` as the actions. |

The point is not the wire format and not the surface. The point is the
conceptual job: the closed learning loop is only as good as the moment
a human can act on it, and acting requires *what*, *where*, *why*, and
*how* in one place. The alternative — a red workflow plus a "go read
the logs" link — pushes the operator into reconstructing all four
questions from scratch, which is where the compounding loop quietly
stalls into a ticket backlog.

<!-- Source: docs/operators/observability.md -->

# Observability & Resource Limits

> **Audience:** SREs, platform engineers, operators running sk in production

**See every run, understand content-free product usage, and catch drift before it costs
you.** sk runs unattended: observable
enough to diagnose a problem in minutes, bounded enough that no single workflow,
tenant, or external dependency can degrade the platform for everyone else. The payoff
is operational — fewer incidents, faster root-cause, predictable AI spend.

| You want to | Read |
|---|---|
| Scrape process-wide metrics | [`/metrics` (Prometheus)](#observability) |
| Trace one failing run across surfaces | [Telemetry Surface](#telemetry-surface) — correlate by `trace_id` |
| Answer per-tenant questions over time | [`/v1/stats/*`](#tenant-scoped-runtime-stats-v1stats) |
| Optimise HTTP, Chat, Conversation, and MCP product usage | [Privacy-safe usage reports](#privacy-safe-product-usage) |
| Keep a tenant from monopolizing capacity | [Resource Limits](#resource-limits-and-operational-safety) |
| Tune ingestion / knowledge budgets | [Documentation & Knowledge Tunables](#documentation--knowledge-tunables) |

For the leaf-by-leaf tunable reference, see
[`../admins/configuration.md`](../admins/configuration.md) and the generated
[`../admins/settings-reference.md`](../admins/settings-reference.md).

---

## Observability

Four surfaces, one identity envelope. Each answers a different question, and they
chain by `trace_id` so an operator can follow a single request from HTTP edge to
notification.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph emit[Engine emits]
        M[Metrics<br/>/metrics Prometheus]
        L[Structured logs<br/>JSON on stdout]
        T[Execution traces<br/>per-step logs]
        E[SSE event stream<br/>tenant-wide]
    end

    M --> SCRAPE[Prometheus scraper]
    L --> AGG[Datadog / Loki / CloudWatch]
    T --> CLI[sk executions tail]
    E --> DASH[Dashboards / alerting]

    SCRAPE --> STATS[/v1/stats/*<br/>per-tenant, time-bucketed]
    AGG --> STATS
    STATS --> DIGEST[/v1/operator/health-digest<br/>leading-indicator risk]

    M -. trace_id .-> L
    L -. trace_id .-> T
    T -. trace_id .-> E
```

| Surface | Endpoint / command | Scope | Answers |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Metrics** | `/metrics` | Process-wide, resets on redeploy | Latency by route, execution duration + step counts, error/retry rates, queue depth, token usage, pool stats |
| **Structured logging** | JSON on stdout | Per-event | Query/alert on fields directly — `trace_id`, `span_id`, `service.name`, `service.version`, `deployment.environment.name`, `tenant_id`, `request_source`, severity |
| **Execution inspection** | `sk executions tail <id>` + API | Per-execution | Per-step logs; failed steps include full error, inputs, raw connector response |
| **Event streaming** | tenant-wide SSE | Per-tenant | Real-time execution events for external dashboards/alerting |

No external metrics system is required for collection — any Prometheus-compatible
scraper works. Logs ship to any standard aggregator without transformation.

**Product analytics (opt-in).** To forward HTTP-response telemetry to an external
product-analytics platform (PostHog, Mixpanel, a custom ingest endpoint), enable
`observability.analytics`. Off by default — no external calls until the operator
opts in. It reuses the existing `request.telemetry` hook in the metrics middleware;
no parallel hook is added.

```yaml
# sk settings set observability.analytics.enabled true
# sk settings set observability.analytics.endpoint '"https://analytics.example.com/capture"'
# sk settings set observability.analytics.api_key '"…"'
# sk settings set observability.analytics.project '"my-project"'
```

| Field | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `observability.analytics.enabled` | `false` | Master switch. No-op when false. |
| `observability.analytics.endpoint` | `""` | Self-hostable ingest URL. Empty = no-op even if enabled. |
| `observability.analytics.api_key` | `""` | Bearer credential (secret). |
| `observability.analytics.project` | `""` | Project/workspace identifier forwarded in each event body. |

Each event carries `method`, `path` (route template, not raw URL), `status_code`,
`duration_ms`, `request_source`, and `tenant_id`. Errors on the analytics call are
caught and logged at debug level — a slow or unavailable endpoint never stalls a
response.

### Privacy-safe product usage

sk can persist a product-internal usage ledger in its own Postgres. It is disabled by
default and makes no external request. Configure a dedicated product-local key before the
switch so actor and session identities are one-way HMAC pseudonyms:

```bash
sk settings set observability.usage.hmac_secret '"<at-least-32-random-characters>"'
sk settings set observability.usage.retention_days 90
sk settings set observability.usage.enabled true
```

The schema is deliberately payload-free. It stores bounded route/operation classes,
outcomes, traffic class, duration/byte counts, stream result, platform/mode/task phase,
active MCP session counts, and product-local HMACs. It has no columns for HTTP query
strings, unknown raw paths, messages, prompts, MCP arguments/results/resource URIs, Chat
platform IDs, IP addresses, user agents, OAuth material, or credentials. Unknown and
dynamic values collapse to bounded `unmatched`, `other`, or `unknown` classes.

`X-SubKit-Traffic-Class: synthetic` marks content-free canaries; `internal` is reserved for
collectors and reporting. Stats default to `organic`, so health probes and canaries do not
distort product decisions. Google Chat propagates this header only after request
verification; MCP and HTTP apply it at their authenticated transport edge.

Raw rows expire after 90 days by default (configurable from 31–365). The four semantic
reports are exact, never sampled, and return exact full-window unique actors/sessions,
ratio numerator and denominator, duration coverage, `measured|zero|missing` value state,
and retention truncation. Cockpit and ContentKit can therefore distinguish “zero usage”
from “collection disabled” without guessing.

### Telemetry Surface

Every code path an operator may need to debug emits at least one structured event
with a stable `action` field. The full surface:

| Action | Module | When | Key fields |
|---|---|---|---|
| `request.telemetry` | `http` | Every HTTP response (2xx/3xx/4xx) | `method`, `path`, `status_code`, `duration_ms`, `tenant_id`, `trace_id`, `request_source` |
| `request.error` | `http` | 5xx responses | as above + `error` |
| `context.assembled` | `llm` | Every LLM context assembly | `flow`, `model`, `cap_tokens`, `total_tokens`, per-section token counts, `dropped_sections[]` |
| `fallback.triggered` | `llm` | Primary provider error → fallback | `flow`, `primary`, `fallback`, `kind` |
| `tool.loop_detected` | `conversation` | Per-tool loop-breaker fires | `conversation_id`, `tool`, `tool_count` |
| `execution.<status>` | `execution` | Every workflow terminal transition | `execution_id`, `status` |
| `webhook.send_failed` | `notifications` | Webhook adapter exhausted retries | `url`, `last_error` |
| `notification.dispatch_failed` | `notifications` | Per-rule dispatch threw | `rule_id`, `channel_id`, `event_type` |
| `metrics.label_dropped` | `observability` | Metric write used an unknown label | `metric`, `label` (logged once per pair) |
| `metrics.write_failed` | `observability` | Metric write threw | `error` |

**Identity envelope.** Every record above carries `tenant_id` (where applicable),
`trace_id`, `span_id` (HTTP edges), and `request_source`. HTTP requests accept
W3C `traceparent`, retain its 128-bit trace ID and sampled flag, and create a fresh
server span. Operators correlate across surfaces (HTTP → execution → notification)
by `trace_id`.

The full Prometheus metric registry is built in
[`apps/engine/src/observability/metrics.ts`](../../apps/engine/src/observability/metrics.ts).
Context and predictive-maintenance metrics:

| Metric | Labels | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| `llm_context_assembled_total` | `flow`, `request_source` | Assemblies per flow |
| `llm_context_dropped_sections_total` | `flow`, `section` | Which sections the trimmer drops per flow |
| `llm_context_total_tokens` | `flow` | Histogram of total prompt tokens per call |
| `db_pool_{total,idle,waiting}_connections` | — | Pool pressure |
| `db_transient_retries_total` | `label` | Cumulative transient retries |
| `db_transient_retry_rate_per_min` | — | **Windowed** retry rate (leading indicator) |
| `dlq_job_count` | `queue` | Dead-letter depth |
| `connector_call_total` | `slug`, `health` | Connector outcomes |
| `llm_call_duration_ms` | `provider`, `model`, `flow` | LLM latency |
| `llm_fallback_invocations_total` | `from`, `to`, `reason` | Fallback frequency |
| `process_memory_rss_high_water_bytes` | — | Memory high-water mark |

These feed the leading-indicator `risk[]` block of `GET /v1/operator/health-digest`.

> **Why the retry rate is windowed.** The `transient_retry` risk signal reads
> `db_transient_retry_rate_per_min` — a windowed rate the 60s memory sampler computes
> (retries since the previous tick ÷ elapsed minutes) against
> `observability.predictive.transient_retry_rate` — **not** the cumulative
> `db_transient_retries_total` ÷ uptime. The window keeps it a leading indicator: a
> one-off Postgres blip decays to 0 within a tick or two instead of latching the warn
> (short uptime) or being averaged into silence (long uptime).

**Risk-signal audit dedup is per-process.** A risk signal crossing into `critical`
(or recovering) writes a single `operator.risk_signal_raised` /
`operator.risk_signal_cleared` audit row on the transition edge, under the **system**
tenant. The edge tracker is in-process, so in an N-replica deployment a standing
critical can produce up to N rows per edge — one per replica that first reads the
digest. Audit volume is small, but SIEM dedup on `(action, resource_id)` should expect
up to N duplicates per incident. A Postgres-side claim (`INSERT … ON CONFLICT` on a
`(kind, window)` table) is the HA hardening if exactly-once attribution becomes a
requirement.

### Tenant-scoped runtime stats (`/v1/stats/*`)

Where `/metrics` is a process-wide Prometheus snapshot that resets on redeploy and is
**not** tenant-scoped, the `/v1/stats/*` surface answers per-tenant operational
questions over time-bucketed history. Operational routes aggregate at read time from
`executions`, `audit_log`, and `llm_usage`; product usage routes aggregate the bounded
`usage_events` ledger. Every route filters
`tenant_id = principal.tenant_id` as the first predicate and is gated by the single
`stats:read` permission (admins hold it by default; members opt in via a custom role).

| Route | Aggregates over | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /v1/stats/executions` | `executions` | run volume + duration distribution (p50/p95/p99/max) by workflow / status / request_source |
| `GET /v1/stats/connectors` | `audit_log` (`action='connector.invoked'`) | connector-call volume + latency + outcome + status-class (`4xx_auth`/`4xx_rate_limited`/…) |
| `GET /v1/stats/events` | `audit_log` (per `?class=`) | webhook / chat / schedule / self-healing / discovery / policy / external-write event volume |
| `GET /v1/stats/llm` | `llm_usage` | token usage + cache-hit rate + latency by model / flow |
| `GET /v1/stats/http` | `usage_events` | canonical route volume, exact actors/sessions, latency, bytes, outcomes |
| `GET /v1/stats/chat` | `usage_events` | Chat event kind/platform, sync vs async, deduplication, outcomes |
| `GET /v1/stats/mcp` | `usage_events` | JSON-RPC classes, tasks, SSE completion/disconnect, session churn/capacity |
| `GET /v1/stats/conversations` | `usage_events` | cross-surface HTTP/Chat/MCP turns, async task lifecycle, input pauses, completion/disconnect, outcomes |

Connector status classes use the upstream transport status when one exists.
`network_error` means that a connector call failed before receiving such a
status; a successful call without an HTTP-like status is classified as
`no_status`, not as a network error.
The aggregator accepts historical egress aliases while new audit rows carry
the canonical `connector_id`, `method`, `path`, `status_code`, and `latency_ms`
fields.

**Bucket grammar.** `bucket` (`minute|hour|day|month|year`), required `from`, optional
`to` (default now) and `tz` (default UTC). Hard window caps reject scans that would
explode (`minute ≤ 24h`, `hour ≤ 31d`, `day ≤ 366d`, …) with
`400 bucket_window_too_large`. Audit-backed routes clamp `from` to the tenant's
audit-retention horizon and surface `truncated_at` on the envelope. Every response
carries three rollups: per-bucket (`groups[].buckets[]`), per-group totals
(`groups[].totals`), and window totals (top-level `totals`).

Two btree indexes back these routes:
`executions (tenant_id, status, started_at)` and `audit_log (tenant_id, action, ts)`.

Usage routes add `traffic_class` (default `organic`) and controlled filters for
`operation`, `outcome`, `request_source`, `platform`, and `response_mode`. At most two
controlled `group_by` dimensions are accepted. Their response schema is
`subkit.usage-stats.v1`; `quality.sampled=false`, `quality.unique_scope=exact_window`, and
every ratio carries both numerator and denominator.

Operators read this surface from the CLI:
`sk stats executions|connectors|events|llm|http|chat|mcp|conversations`
(human ASCII table + sparkline by default, `--json` for cron/CI/ETL), and it feeds the
`sk` settings Status heatmap + Usage token bar.

---

## Resource Limits and Operational Safety

sk enforces limits at multiple levels so that no single workflow, tenant, or external
connector dependency can degrade the platform for others. All limits have documented
defaults and are operator-tunable.

| Limit | Protects against |
|---|---|
| Per-execution / per-step timeouts | Runaway workflows consuming resources indefinitely |
| Per-tenant token budgets | Unbounded AI usage costs |
| API rate limits | A single caller monopolizing capacity |
| Connector circuit breakers | Cascading failure from a degraded external boundary — after N consecutive failures the circuit opens and requests fail fast until recovery |
| Queue depth caps | Unbounded work accumulation |

When a circuit breaker trips, the audit log records it and the event stream delivers a
notification. Operators see the failure before users do.

### Documentation & Knowledge Tunables

Documentation ingestion and Knowledge Source budgets are env-configurable so operators
can raise them on hardware that warrants larger corpora. Defaults are conservative and
match the docs in [`../authors/knowledge-sources.md`](../authors/knowledge-sources.md).
Each value falls back to the default when the env var is unset, empty, zero, or
unparseable — there is no half-configured state.

| Env var | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `DOCS_INGESTION_MAX_BYTES_PER_CONNECTOR` | `10485760` (10 MB) | Total ingest budget per connector per run. |
| `DOCS_INGESTION_MAX_BYTES_PER_DOC` | `3145728` (3 MB) | Per-page / per-document hard cap. |
| `DOCS_INGESTION_MAX_LINKS` | `20` | Links followed from `llms.txt` / markdown indices. |
| `DOCS_INGESTION_MAX_SPECS` | `100` | OpenAPI / GraphQL specs per ingest run. |
| `DOCS_INGESTION_MAX_CONCURRENT` | `25` | Concurrent fetches per ingest run. |
| `KNOWLEDGE_SOURCE_MAX_BYTES` | `52428800` (50 MB) | Per-source upload cap. |
| `KNOWLEDGE_TENANT_MAX_BYTES` | `524288000` (500 MB) | Per-tenant total knowledge bytes. |
| `KNOWLEDGE_MAX_FILES_PER_MESSAGE` | `10` | Max files attached in a single conversation message. |
| `DOCS_CRAWL_POSITIVE_HIGH` | `api,apis,endpoints,reference,docs` | URL keywords that score `+5` during the playwright fallback crawl. |
| `DOCS_CRAWL_POSITIVE_LOW` | `swagger,openapi` | URL keywords that score `+3`. |
| `DOCS_CRAWL_NEGATIVE` | `pricing,login,signin,signup,/blog/,careers,/locale/,/legal/,/privacy/,/terms/,/contact/` | URL keywords that score `-10`. |

### Binary file parser tunables (compile-time)

The binary office-document parsers (PDF / DOCX / XLSX / PPTX) are guarded by per-format
ceilings that are deliberately **not** env-configurable — the values are
workload-defensive defaults, and an operator who needs to change them should do it in
code with a code review. Their absence from `subkit.config.json` is intentional
(zero-conf principle).

| Constant | Default | Where | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `EXTRACT_BODY_CAP_BYTES` | `104857600` (100 MB) | `http/routes/ai/extract.ts` | Hard request-body cap on `POST /v1/extract` and `POST /v1/ai/extract`. Enforced twice: declared `content-length` and streaming fallback. |
| `TEXT_EXTRACT_PER_FILE_MAX_BYTES` | `1048576` (1 MB) | `llm/core/file-context.ts` | Per-file ceiling on TEXT bytes that reach the LLM context. Applies to the *parsed* output for binary formats. |
| `TEXT_EXTRACT_BINARY_PER_FILE_MAX_BYTES` | `26214400` (25 MB) | `llm/core/file-context.ts` | Per-file ceiling on RAW bytes read for the binary `text_extract` branch. Binaries above this size emit a `[file: <name>] (too large to parse)` placeholder. |
| `TEXT_EXTRACT_PER_TURN_CAP_BYTES` | `4194304` (4 MB) | `llm/core/file-context.ts` | Per-turn cumulative TEXT cap across all files. Subsequent files get a skip placeholder. |
| `PARSER_TIMEOUT_MS.pdf` | `30000` (30 s) | `docs-ingestion/parsers/strategy.ts` | `withParserTimeout` hard kill for PDF. |
| `PARSER_TIMEOUT_MS.docx` | `30000` (30 s) | `docs-ingestion/parsers/strategy.ts` | `withParserTimeout` hard kill for DOCX. |
| `PARSER_TIMEOUT_MS.pptx` | `30000` (30 s) | `docs-ingestion/parsers/strategy.ts` | `withParserTimeout` hard kill for PPTX. |
| `PARSER_TIMEOUT_MS.xlsx` / `.xls` | `60000` (60 s) | `docs-ingestion/parsers/strategy.ts` | Longer budget; SheetJS can hit O(n²) layouts on pathological workbooks. |
| `XLSX_ROW_CAP_PER_SHEET` | `200` | `docs-ingestion/parsers/xlsx.ts` | Per-sheet row cap (mirrors the CSV row cap). |
| `PPTX_SLIDE_CAP` | `2000` | `docs-ingestion/parsers/pptx.ts` | Per-archive slide cap; short-circuits ZIP walk when exceeded. |

When a parser trips its timeout, the request fails with a typed `BinaryParseError`
mapped to HTTP 400 and the structured logger records a
`docs_ingestion.binary_parsers.parse_failed` row. The
`subkit_docs_binary_parse_total{format,result="error"}` counter increments so operators
can chart per-format failure rates.

**Audit-log surface for binary extracts.** Successful and failed binary
`POST /v1/extract` calls emit `audit_log` rows under `action = "data.exported"`. Each
row carries up to ~455 bytes of operator-controlled input inside `metadata`:

- `metadata.filename` — the validated `x-filename` header (≤ 255 chars, no path
  separators or NULs; rejected at the Zod boundary before parse).
- `metadata.error` — the parser's diagnostic (≤ 200 chars, ASCII control characters
  stripped via `audit/sanitize.ts`).

SIEM consumers should expect both fields to be free-form text from the caller's side.
Both pass through `sanitizeForAudit` in `apps/engine/src/audit/sanitize.ts` so a
malformed PDF whose parser message embeds a few bytes of the input can't smuggle
TAB / NUL / CR into the audit row.

**Metric vs audit denominator gradient.** The
`subkit_docs_binary_parse_total{format,result}` counter increments on *every* binary
parse dispatch path — the `/v1/extract` HTTP route, the docs-ingestion file-upload
source, **and** the LLM `text_extract` context-assembly branch. The `audit_log`
`data.exported` rows, by contrast, are written only by the `/v1/extract` route and the
docs-ingestion service (not the LLM context path, which is read-only assembly with no
egress). An operator charting parse errors should therefore expect
`subkit_docs_binary_parse_total{result="error"}` to be a strict superset of `audit_log`
`data.exported` rows with `result="error"` — the metric is the broader denominator.
Reconcile by parsing surface, not 1:1.

---
