<!-- Source: docs/authors/asking-your-knowledge.md -->

# Ask your company's knowledge

> **Audience:** Anyone who wants to ask questions in chat, a browser AI client, or a
> coding agent — and trust what comes back.

**Ask a question where you already work, and the company answers from its own documents —
naming what it read, or saying plainly that the answer isn't in there.** That second half
is the point: an assistant that cannot say "I don't know" is a liability with good
grammar.

## What a grounded answer looks like

You ask, in Slack or in an MCP client:

> *"What's the per-diem cap for international travel?"*

sk searches the knowledge sources your operators uploaded, answers from the matching
passages, and closes with a footer:

```
Sources: expense-policy-2026, travel-approval-runbook
```

Every name in that footer is a real, tenant-owned source — the same references land in
the audit log, so "where did that answer come from?" stays answerable later.

## The four guarantees

| Guarantee | What it means for you |
|---|---|
| **Provenance you can check** | Grounded answers carry a `Sources:` footer. A citation that doesn't resolve to a real source of yours is dropped before you ever see it — and the footer is identical on live answers and replayed transcripts. |
| **Quotes are faithful** | Before a grounded answer stands, a deterministic check confirms every quoted span actually appears in a cited source. An answer that fails is not allowed to stand as final — you get asked instead. |
| **Honest refusal** | If the knowledge base has no answer, sk says so instead of improvising one. The same discipline applies to its own abilities: it doesn't describe tools it cannot reach from your surface. |
| **A no is respected** | Decline a proposed action and the decline sticks for identical re-proposals in that conversation — including in auto mode. |

The mechanics behind these live in
[Governance & audit → Answer provenance and honest refusal](../concepts/governance-and-audit.md#answer-provenance-and-honest-refusal).

## Where you can ask

| Door | What it feels like | Setup |
|---|---|---|
| **Slack / Teams / Google Chat** | `@sk …` in a channel or DM. Ask questions, run saved workflows. Deliberately read-and-run only — chat never rewrites a process | [Chat channels](../operators/chat.md) |
| **A browser AI client or MCP client** | Claude, ChatGPT, Claude Desktop, Cursor, … connected to your engine — the client searches your knowledge as a tool | [Author quickstart, path D](./quickstart.md#path-d--mcp-client-claude-desktop-cursor-etc) |
| **A coding agent** | Claude Code / Codex sessions open already briefed on your approved domain rules, and look your runbooks up instead of inventing them | [Use sk from a coding agent](./coding-agents.md) |
| **The `sk` CLI** | Same conversations, plus authoring — the one door where processes get *changed* | [REPL tour](./repl-tour.md) |

## What the answers are built from

Two primitives, one distinction:

- **Skills prescribe.** Dense, operator-approved rules the AI follows — your conventions,
  not a generic tutorial's.
- **Knowledge Sources inform.** Your documents — runbooks, policies, specs — chunked and
  searchable; the AI cites them, it doesn't obey them.

What ships at boot is product knowledge: sk's own reference, plus per-vendor API mechanics
for the shipped connectors. **Your business domain is what you bring** — uploading it
takes minutes ([Knowledge sources](./knowledge-sources.md)), and teaching sk a whole field
of work is one page further ([Model a domain](./model-a-domain.md)).

## Keeping it honest over time

Curation is human: the engine may *propose* new knowledge and skills from what it observes,
but nothing becomes part of the answering corpus without a person approving it. And when
grounding goes stale — a connector's schema changed under a draft — sk flags it as a
re-check advisory rather than silently answering from yesterday's world.

## Further reading

- [Knowledge & skills](../concepts/knowledge-and-skills.md) — the model behind the context: assembly order, trimming, the compounding loop.
- [Use cases → Corporate LLM](../use-cases.md#corporate-llm) — this capability in the company-wide frame.
- [Governance & audit](../concepts/governance-and-audit.md) — audit trail, secret hygiene, and the provenance mechanics.

<!-- Source: docs/authors/authoring-workflows.md -->

# AI-Assisted Authoring

Describe what should happen and have a reviewed, versioned workflow the same afternoon — instead of a build project that runs for weeks.

The usual bottleneck is that whoever wants the automation cannot build it, and whoever can build it has a queue. So you ship what the queue allows, not what the work needs. sk removes that handoff: you state the intent in plain language, the AI does the structural work, and a person signs off before anything goes live.

| Business outcome | How sk delivers it |
|---|---|
| **Time** — first workflow in minutes | One `author_workflow` pass generates the complete definition, grounded in real endpoint evidence |
| **Compliance** — every change reviewable and attributable | A commit lands on a human review and an audit row that names the actor; every step is reviewable |
| **Risk** — no raw secrets in the loop | Credentials are referenced by name through the Credential Vault, never seen during authoring |
| **Predictability** — the engine never improvises | Once committed, the control flow is fixed: the engine infers nothing and loads no Skills or Knowledge at runtime |

![Describing a workflow in plain language, previewing it, approving it, and running it](../_tapes/out/repl-author.gif)

> **Reading time:** ~18 min · **Audience:** engineers integrating with sk's authoring, operators curating Skills & Knowledge

> **Before you start — pick the right door.** This page describes authoring by
> conversation, which is how you get from an idea to a first working workflow.
> Editing an *existing* definition is a different job and belongs in the `sk`
> CLI, where you write the definition yourself instead of describing the change.
> A browser client over MCP cannot write definitions at all. Two minutes on
> [Choosing your surface](choosing-your-surface.md) saves an afternoon of
> restating the same edit.

---

## The Conversation Model

A Conversation is the primary authoring interface. The user describes a goal; the AI replies with a structured proposal — a Draft workflow that can be inspected, modified, and approved — never free-form code or autonomous decisions.

| Property | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Persistent** | Survives reloads, reconnects, multi-day sessions |
| **Resumable** | Start Monday, return Wednesday, pick up exactly where you left off — context, draft state, pending questions recalled |
| **Structured** | The AI operates over a fixed palette of authoring actions; its reasoning is a visible sequence of explicit moves, not opaque text |

The primary entry is `author_workflow` — one call that takes the user's goal verbatim, grounds generation in recorded endpoint samples and ingested docs, emits the complete evaluated draft, and returns structured `recorded_eval` findings. Around it sit grounding actions (probe a connector, search docs), the hold-writes preview, and repair actions that each apply one specific finding.

Operators and scripted clients that already know the target definition use the same model through the direct workflow and execution surface — skipping the conversational loop and working directly with definitions plus `POST /v1/executions` for preview and execution.

### One turn, end to end

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    actor U as User
    participant C as Conversation (sk)
    participant G as Grounding tools
    participant E as Engine
    participant J as Judge
    U->>C: Describe the outcome (plain language)
    C->>G: probe_connector / search_docs / search_knowledge
    G-->>C: recorded endpoint samples + docs
    C->>E: author_workflow (one pass)
    E-->>C: complete draft + recorded_eval findings
    C->>E: dry_run_workflow (writes held)
    E-->>C: reads run live, writes resolved but not dispatched
    C->>J: evaluate artifacts vs stashed goal
    J-->>C: verdict (pass / findings)
    C->>U: preview draft for approval
    U->>C: approve
    C->>E: save_workflow_draft (commit versioned workflow)
    E-->>U: runnable, governed workflow
```

---

## The Authoring State Machine

The engine maintains an explicit state machine per conversation and uses it to decide which actions are visible, which moves are blocked, and what the next valid move is. The model does not infer progress from transcript history.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ConnectorDraft
    ConnectorDraft --> ConnectorInspected: inspect
    ConnectorInspected --> ConnectorValidated: validate
    ConnectorValidated --> ConnectorProbed: probe
    ConnectorProbed --> ConnectorPersisted: green probe (auto)
    ConnectorPersisted --> WorkflowDraft: author_workflow (one-shot generate + evaluate)
    WorkflowDraft --> WorkflowPreviewed: dry_run_workflow (writes held)
    WorkflowPreviewed --> WorkflowJudged: instruction-grounded judge reads artifacts incl. held payloads
    WorkflowJudged --> WorkflowPersisted: auto mode or approved save_workflow_draft
    WorkflowJudged --> WorkflowRepair: judge / recorded_eval findings
    WorkflowPreviewed --> WorkflowRepair: preview failure
    WorkflowRepair --> WorkflowPreviewed: edit_workflow_patch (RFC-6902), then preview again
    WorkflowPersisted --> WorkflowExecuted: run
    WorkflowExecuted --> Diagnosis: warnings / failure
    Diagnosis --> WorkflowRepair: repair draft
    WorkflowExecuted --> [*]: success
```

**Verification precedes persistence.** Probe persists the connector inline. A green, judged workflow dry-run proves the preview; in permission mode `auto` it may commit inline, while `ask` and `plan` return `save_required` and use the normal human save gate. Dry-runs hold writes — read steps execute live, write steps are fully resolved (URL, headers, materialized body) but never dispatched, and the held request is recorded as the artifact the judge evaluates. Any draft mutation invalidates downstream checkpoints automatically.

**The authoring triad.** Workflow authoring is four verbs, in order: `author_workflow` (generate the complete grounded draft), `dry_run_workflow` (test it with writes held), `edit_workflow_patch` (revise it with an RFC-6902 JSON-Patch), and `save_workflow_draft` (commit the version). Generation is ONE `author_workflow` call, not a micro-iterated step-by-step build.

**Stage gate.** `edit_workflow_patch` is the repair-stage verb. While the draft is in its initial stage — no recorded preview, no recorded-eval/judge findings — it refuses with `authoring_stage_violation` and names the exact next valid actions (`author_workflow`, `dry_run_workflow`, `save_workflow_draft`), none of which is ever gated. The moment a preview or findings exist, it unlocks unconditionally — that is when a patch edit has real artifacts to reason against.

The state is persisted in the conversation draft summary:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `mode` | `connector`, `workflow`, `execution`, or `diagnosis` |
| `stage` | concrete state, e.g. `connector_probed`, `workflow_previewed` |
| `lifecycle_state` | active target is `draft_only` or `persisted` |
| `blocked_by` | exact missing checkpoints/fields blocking the next durable action |
| `next_required_action` | next state-advancing action to take or have the user approve |
| `checkpoints[]` | freshness for `inspect`, `validate`, `probe`, `preview`, `persist`, `execute`, `diagnose` |

The current stage, active target, and checkpoint freshness are part of the runtime contract, not prompt advice. The same grounding rule applies to explanatory follow-ups: when a user asks why something was named or configured a certain way, the assistant answers from recorded state, audit history, ingested docs, or a fresh grounding call — or says plainly that the reason is not recorded. It does not speculate.

When an answer is grounded in a knowledge source or connector documentation, `sk` shows a dim `Sources: …` footer beneath it — the source names the answer was built on, so a reader can verify the claim rather than trust the prose. The footer appears only when the turn actually cited a source that resolves for the tenant (the same refs written to the audit log); a source-less answer shows nothing. It carries no new interaction — it is a display of the grounding that already happened.

### New draft versus saved workflow

A conversation can stay bound to a saved workflow after rename, commit, and execution so follow-up runs and repairs stay grounded. That binding is intentional but not sticky against explicit new-workflow intent.

When the user says they want to create a new workflow after inspecting or running an existing one, the engine clears the saved-workflow binding before the next authoring move. The next `author_workflow` call targets a fresh draft, not an in-place update. Updating a saved workflow remains an explicit path: keep the bound target and commit back into it.

---

## The Human-in-the-Loop Approval Gate

The most important architectural decision in sk: **the author sees what a workflow will do before it can do it.** In `ask` and `plan`, a commit lands only after the structured human save gate. In explicitly selected `auto` mode, a clean judged dry-run may commit inline. Starting an unattended trigger takes a further, separate decision.

When the AI finishes a Draft, it pauses the authoring loop and presents it for review. The operator sees every step, connector reference, parameter, and branching condition — and can push back, ask for changes, iterate. On approval, the Draft is committed as a new versioned Workflow; the Conversation transitions to active and the workflow is ready to run.

This is the governance model, not a UX convenience. It is the structural answer to "How do we know the AI did the right thing?" — because a human read what it would do, on a preview whose writes were held, before it ran for real.

The gate sits on top of hard quality gates:

| Gate | Rule |
|---|---|
| Connector save | Blocked until `inspect`, `validate`, `probe` checkpoints are fresh |
| Workflow commit | Blocked until `inspect`, `validate`, `preview` checkpoints are fresh |
| Workflow run | Always targets a persisted version, never an ambiguous draft |
| Connector persistence | A green `probe_connector_draft` calls `saveConnectorAtomic` inline (audit reason `auto_persist_on_green_probe`), returns `auto_saved: true` |
| Workflow persistence | In `auto`, a green judged dry-run may call `commitWorkflowAtomic` inline. In `ask`/`plan`, it returns `save_required` and `save_workflow_draft` uses the human gate. |
| Force overrides | `force_save: true` (after a failed probe) and `force_commit: true` (after a failed dry-run) go through the explicit `ask_user_confirm` carrier so the deviation is auditable |

Approval is the final human sign-off after the state machine has already established that the draft is internally coherent — not a substitute for missing technical checks.

---

## Probe Before Save, Preview Before Commit

The clean authoring experience treats intermediate verification as first-class product steps, not optional debugging.

**Connectors:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | Start or update the connector draft |
| 2 | Inspect the current draft |
| 3 | Validate required fields and config shape |
| 4 | Collect static credentials through the masked `sk` form or MCP single-use URL elicitation; never through chat text |
| 5 | Probe the real upstream boundary — a green probe persists inline; envelope carries `auto_saved: true` |

**Workflows:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | **Ground** — `list_connectors`, `probe_connector` for any never-called connector (records the real response shape), `search_docs` / `search_knowledge` when the endpoint surface is unclear |
| 2 | **`author_workflow`** (one call) — generates the COMPLETE definition (steps, transforms, input/output schema, trigger), evaluates it against recorded evidence with bounded auto-repair, stashes it as the draft; read the `recorded_eval` findings |
| 3 | **`dry_run_workflow`** — hold-writes preview: reads run live; writes resolved (URL, headers, materialized body) but never dispatched, recorded as held request artifacts |
| 4 | **Judge** — instruction-grounded judge evaluates the artifacts (held payloads included) against the stashed goal |
| 5 | **Repair on findings** — apply specific findings via `edit_workflow_patch` (an RFC-6902 JSON-Patch over the draft; accept all, decline all, or accept a partial subset of its operations), iterate a transform with `dry_run_transform`, then preview again |
| 6 | **Persist** — `auto` may commit inline; `ask`/`plan` call `save_workflow_draft` and wait for its structured human decision |
| 7 | **Run** the persisted workflow |

In `ask` and `plan`, preview and persistence are deliberately separate. Backgrounded MCP clients receive the durable save approval URL through conversation polling; being headless does not grant write permission. Executing write steps for real during a preview is the rare exception, behind explicit user confirmation (`execute_writes: true`); externally visible destinations (recipient addresses, channels, webhook URLs) must always come from the user, never fabricated placeholders.

The engine tracks checkpoints as fresh or stale. Any draft mutation invalidates later checkpoints — editing after a successful preview makes the preview stale, so the workflow must be previewed again before commit. The assistant does not "think" a connector is ready; it reads that from checkpoint state. The draft summary carries the concrete next suggested tool, so prompt assembly, confirmations, and surface-specific evaluations all reason from the same contract.

### CLI parity

The `sk` CLI mirrors the conversational gates, so operators get the same guarantees from a script or pipeline:

| Conversation tool | sk CLI subcommand |
|---|---|
| `validate_draft` | `sk workflows validate <file.json>` |
| `dry_run_workflow` / `dry_run_step` | `sk workflows preview <file.json>` (alias: `dry-run`) |
| `save_workflow_draft` | `sk workflows create <file.json>` |
| `validate_connector_draft` (shape check) | — (use the conversational loop for structural checks) |
| `probe_connector_draft` / `test` | `sk connectors probe <id>` (alias of `test`) |
| `inspect_connector_draft` | `sk connectors inspect <id>` (alias of `get`) |

`sk workflows create` runs `validate` + `preview` as a pre-flight by default. `sk connectors create` runs a driver probe after the create returns. Both accept `--skip-checks` as an explicit escape hatch — it surfaces a stderr warning and is reserved for callers that already validated elsewhere. The same `inspect → validate → preview/probe → commit/save` state machine gates the persisted write on both surfaces.

### Warnings feed the next turn

When a dry-run (`dry_run_workflow`, `dry_run_step`) produces structured warnings — unresolved identifiers, rate-limit signals, pagination edges — they attach to the draft's `latest_preview` and feed automatically into the next turn's `prior_failures` block. The assistant sees them as structured context without the user quoting them back. `sk workflows run` mirrors this by printing a `WARN step=<key> code=<code> msg=<text>` line per warning on stderr while keeping the JSON payload on stdout unchanged.

### Submit/abort retry loop

Every structured LLM flow — `generate`, `extract`, `repair`, `discover` — goes through the same tool loop in `AiSdkModel.generateObject`. The model must call `submit` (return the final structured object) or `abort` (give up with a reason). Unknown tool calls trigger another iteration with the result appended so the model can self-correct. The loop is hard-capped at `MAX_TOOL_LOOP_ATTEMPTS = 8`; callers can tighten it per-flow via `maxAttempts`.

### Prompt caching

Stable context (skills, ingested docs, knowledge chunks) is marked with an Anthropic ephemeral `cache_control: { type: "ephemeral", ttl: "1h" }` breakpoint. Volatile context (user memory, prior failures, the current turn's messages) refreshes every call. The `llm.cache.hit_rate` metric (`llm_cache_hit_tokens_total` / `llm_prompt_tokens_total`) tracks reuse of stable blocks within the 1-hour window; the mock provider simulates the same accounting so tests can assert on cache behaviour.

### Tools for context

The assembler pre-loads Skills + docs + Knowledge chunks before every turn. On-demand retrieval uses four conversation tools, in precedence order:

| Order | Tool | Use |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `search_knowledge` | semantic search over tenant Knowledge Sources |
| 2 | `search_docs` | ranked search over a connector's ingested docs (OpenAPI/GraphQL/HTML/Markdown); hits carry a `match_type` (endpoint / auth / schema / text). Use when `search_knowledge` is empty and the answer is connector-specific |
| 3 | `fetch_connector_docs` | full doc overview for a connector |
| 4 | `fetch_connector_self_description` | live-fetch the connector's *own* published docs — its `llms.txt` / `llms-full.txt`, OpenAPI spec, or GraphQL introspection (`kind: "llms" \| "openapi" \| "graphql" \| "all"`). Use to pull deeper detail the inline endpoint signatures don't carry |
| 5 | `web_search` | Anthropic-native server-side web search (billed per search; Claude models only). On by default; advisory escalation in `policies/web-search-escalation.ts`; gated per tenant by `llm.web_search` (toggle via /settings) |

When a connector is in scope, the assembler doesn't inline its full doc corpus — that would blow the token budget. Instead it surfaces a one-line pointer (*"this connector publishes its own docs — fetch on demand with `fetch_connector_self_description`"*) alongside compact endpoint signatures pulled from the discovery index. sk fetches the connector's own published docs lazily, only when the model needs more than the signatures, so the workflow is grounded in the target's real documentation without paying for prose it never reads. The remembered links are described in [Connectors → Connector Self-Description](../concepts/connectors.md#connector-self-description).

### Self-healing retry

When drift is detected, the repair flow proposes a patch, classifies it, and dry-runs it against the most recent `execution_fixtures` row. If either gate rejects, the loop re-prompts the LLM with the structured rejection folded into `prior_failures`, up to `MAX_REPAIR_ATTEMPTS = 2` total. The final patch candidate carries a `metadata.rejection_chain` array recording every prior rejection, so reviewers see what was tried. Rate-limit-class drift (HTTP 429 / 503 with a template `rate_limits` hint) produces a distinct `kind: "rate_limited"` candidate — same retry loop, but the patch only adjusts backoff metadata.

---

## Playground Mode — Scratch Authoring That Never Persists

Sometimes you want to explore — try a connector shape, sketch a workflow, see what a dry-run returns — without leaving anything behind. Playground mode is an ephemeral authoring space: the full triad works exactly as it does normally (author, dry-run, edit, even the judge), but nothing is ever written to the tenant. No draft is persisted, no connector is saved, no workflow is committed. When the conversation ends, the scratch work is gone.

It is a durable per-conversation flag — set it once when you start, and every turn in that conversation stays ephemeral. There is nothing to remember to clean up afterward.

| Surface | How to start a playground conversation |
|---|---|
| MCP client | Set `_meta.sk_playground` on the conversation-start call |
| HTTP API | Pass a `playground` field in the conversation-start body |

Use it for a throwaway exploration, a live demo, or a "what would this even look like?" question where committing anything would be noise. When you want the real thing, start an ordinary conversation and the same steps persist as usual.

---

## Partial-Accept Of Edits

When you ask for a change to a draft, `edit_workflow_patch` expresses it as an RFC-6902 JSON-Patch — a precise, ordered list of operations against the workflow definition (add this header, replace that URL, remove this step). Before any operation is applied, the patch is presented for confirmation, and you have three responses, not two:

| Response | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Accept all** | Every operation in the patch is applied. |
| **Decline all** | The draft is untouched; nothing changes. |
| **Accept a partial subset** | You choose which operations to apply; the rest are dropped. |

Partial-accept matters when a single edit bundles a change you want with one you don't — take the corrected pagination cursor, leave the header rename you didn't ask for. The accepted subset is applied atomically and, as with any draft mutation, invalidates downstream checkpoints so the draft is previewed again before it can commit. Nothing is silently applied: every operation you see is either accepted by you or dropped.

---

## Payload-First: A Sample Payload Drives The Input Contract

Authoring is easier when you can hand the AI a concrete example of the data the workflow will receive. That is `input_schema_sample` — a sample TEST payload that grounds the resolved input contract and seeds the first dry-run.

The input contract resolves by a fixed precedence:

| Priority | Source | When it applies |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Declared** | An explicit `input_schema` on the workflow always wins |
| 2 | **Sample** | With no declared schema, the shape is inferred from `input_schema_sample` |
| 3 | **Synthesized** | With neither, the engine synthesizes a minimal contract from how the steps reference their inputs |

The sample is scaffolding, not content. **The test payload is never persisted into the workflow definition.** It drives dry-runs and shapes the contract during authoring, then is discarded — what gets committed is the resolved `input_schema`, never the example values you tested with. A committed workflow stays free of throwaway test data while you still author against realistic inputs.

---

## Testing A Draft With `includeStepResults`

A dry-run tells you whether the draft is green. When you need to know *why* a step behaved the way it did, pass `includeStepResults` on `dry_run_workflow` (or on `run_workflow` for a committed workflow). The response then carries the raw per-step inputs and outputs — exactly what each step received and exactly what it produced.

This is the self-diagnosis lever. Instead of guessing which step mangled a field, read the actual value that flowed into it and the value it emitted:

- A transform returns something unexpected → read its input scope and its return value side by side.
- A downstream step can't resolve a scope path → see the real shape the upstream step actually produced.
- You are calibrating a new draft against an `input_schema_sample` → confirm each step consumes the sample the way you intended.

It is opt-in because the per-step payloads are verbose — omit it for a quick green/red check, include it the moment you are actually debugging.

---

## Diagnosis Is Part of Authoring

Execution is not the end of the loop. When a persisted workflow runs and produces warnings or a suspicious result, the conversation enters diagnosis mode instead of generic retry.

Diagnosis keeps the latest execution and its causal context attached to the draft summary:

| Field | Captures |
|---|---|
| `latest_execution` | exact persisted workflow id and version that ran |
| `diagnosis_available` | the latest run should be inspected before editing |
| `latest_diagnosis` | structured reason, warning sources, step-level summaries from the diagnosis pass |

This matters most for expression-heavy workflows. A run can technically succeed while carrying warnings such as unresolved identifiers in scope paths. The static verifier checks the step-id segment of a reference: a reference to a non-existent step — writing `$scope.wrong_step.data` when no `wrong_step` exists — is blocked before commit. It does not catch field-path mistakes on an existing step: writing `$scope.step.field` instead of `$scope.step.data.field` passes the static check and surfaces only as a runtime unresolved-identifier warning. For those, the right recovery is not "run it again" but "diagnose, repair the draft, preview again, commit again, then run again." Diagnosis is a first-class authoring phase, not an operator-only debugging escape hatch.

---

## Stage-Aware Prompting And Tool Narrowing

The loop constrains both prompt guidance and the visible authoring surface by mode and stage:

| Mode | Prompt focus | Visible surface |
|---|---|---|
| connector | Stay inside connector work until the connector is persisted | Connector actions |
| workflow | Inspection, validation, preview, commit | Workflow actions; commit only when checkpoints permit |
| execution / diagnosis | The latest persisted run and its repair path | Run + diagnosis actions |

Premature actions — connector save, workflow commit, diagnosis — only become visible when the relevant stage and checkpoint state permit them, rather than always-visible with runtime rejection. Prompt guidance, action visibility, and runtime gates all read from the same state model, which is why the flow stays consistent across turns.

---

## Multi-AI Provider

sk is not tied to a single AI model. It supports Claude (Anthropic), OpenAI GPT models, and Google Gemini. Providers are interchangeable — swapping models requires no changes to connectors, workflows, or skills.

| Property | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Routing | Best available provider by operator config and task type |
| Budgets | Token budgets enforced per tenant and per Conversation; operators set a monthly ceiling, consumption surfaces in the audit log |
| Runtime | The provider is an authoring-layer detail; the engine calls no model to run a committed workflow, regardless of which model authored it |

### OpenAI-compatible endpoints

The `openai` provider also drives any **OpenAI-compatible** endpoint — a self-hosted open-weight model, an internal gateway, or a third-party API speaking the OpenAI wire format. Point the slot at the endpoint:

```
llm.provider                  = openai
llm.providers.openai.base_url = https://llm.internal.example/v1   # your endpoint
llm.providers.openai.api_key  = <key>                             # sent as a Bearer token
llm.providers.openai.model    = <model-id>
llm.summarize_provider        = openai                            # optional
llm.summarize_model           = <fast-model-id>                   # optional
```

Two behaviours switch on automatically whenever `base_url` is non-empty, because a custom host typically implements only a subset of the OpenAI surface:

- **Transport.** Requests use `POST <base_url>/chat/completions` (Chat Completions), not the OpenAI Responses API.
- **Attachments.** The Files API upload path and audio/video inputs are disabled; files fall back to inline content or extracted text. Inline images and small documents still work.

Leaving `base_url` empty keeps the slot on real OpenAI with full Responses API and Files API behaviour. Structured-output authoring works on any tool-calling endpoint — it runs through a provider-agnostic tool loop rather than OpenAI-specific JSON-schema response formats.

> **Known limitation.** The attachment downgrade is a conservative default: it assumes an arbitrary custom endpoint serves text and inline images only. Some OpenAI-compatible servers (e.g. vLLM, SGLang) do serve vision/audio and a real Files API — there is currently no per-endpoint opt-back-in, so those richer capabilities aren't used on a custom `base_url`. A per-endpoint capability override is a tracked follow-up.

---

## Skills: Curated Context

The AI is only as useful as its context. Without organization-specific context it proposes generic workflows — not one that follows your GDPR handling policy, uses your Salesforce field mappings, or respects your API versioning conventions.

A Skill is a curated, reusable piece of context loaded into the AI's window during a Conversation and other AI-assisted flows (discovery, diagnosis, bounded repair). Skills encode best practices, integration patterns, security policies, and domain knowledge specific to your organization. When the AI proposes a workflow involving your Stripe connector, the Stripe Skill loads automatically — and the proposals reflect your conventions, not just generic Stripe API knowledge.

| Aspect | Rule |
|---|---|
| Ownership | Operators create and manage Skills |
| Scope | Global (all Conversations), per-Connector (loaded when referenced), or per-Workflow |
| Promotion | Not auto-generated, not auto-promoted; the platform surfaces Skill Candidates from execution history, a human promotes |

The platform learns from what works; humans decide what becomes canonical guidance.

---

## Knowledge Sources: Enterprise Documents

Skills are concise and curated. For document-scale context — runbooks, API specifications, compliance frameworks, architecture diagrams — sk provides Knowledge Sources.

A Knowledge Source is a persistent document store. Operators upload PDFs, runbooks, API specs, compliance documents, and diagrams; the platform chunks and indexes them for semantic search. During a Conversation, discovery pass, or diagnosis/repair loop, the AI searches them to ground its proposals. A workflow that correctly follows your GDPR compliance runbook is possible because the runbook is a searchable Knowledge Source.

When a document is uploaded interactively — from chat, an attached file, or `sk knowledge-sources create` — the AI auto-analyzes it to generate a short description and topical tags, making each source self-describing: the AI can list sources and decide which covers a topic before searching, and a search can be narrowed to a tag. The description is generated only when none was supplied; tags are a deduped set that re-analysis replaces wholesale. Auto-analysis is best-effort — if it fails (e.g. the model budget is exhausted) the upload still succeeds without enrichment. Re-run it anytime (`sk knowledge-sources analyze <id>`, or the `analyze_knowledge_source` tool in chat). Bulk paths — crawled pages, scheduled refreshes — stay mechanical and are not auto-analyzed.

Knowledge Sources have configurable refresh strategies — manual, scheduled, or webhook-triggered — and can be scoped to a tenant (global) or to specific workflows.

| | Skills | Knowledge Sources |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | Dense, operator-authored guidance | Broader organizational artifacts |
| Treatment | Specific instructions the AI should follow | Searched for context, not prescriptive rules |

Committed workflow execution does not query Skills or Knowledge Sources. Those systems improve authoring and repair quality; the runtime path stays deterministic once a workflow is committed.

## Context Assembly And Trimming

For each AI-assisted turn, the engine assembles prompt context in a fixed order. Order matters twice — it shapes how the model sees context (top is most foundational) and how the trimmer drops it under pressure (top survives longest, bottom goes first):

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph build["Assembly order (top = first written)"]
        direction TB
        B1["1. Base prompt + runtime envelope<br/>(engine · tenant · actor · surface)"]
        B2["2. Auto-loaded Skills<br/>(global → connector → workflow)"]
        B3["3. Explicitly loaded Skills"]
        B4["4. Knowledge Source chunks"]
        B5["5. Connector documentation chunks"]
        B6["6. Prior failures for the current task"]
        B7["7. User memory + authoring-context blocks"]
        B8["8. Current turn history<br/>(user / assistant messages)"]
        B1 --> B2 --> B3 --> B4 --> B5 --> B6 --> B7 --> B8
    end
    Trim{{"Trim order (top = dropped first)"}}
    T1["failures → connector docs → knowledge<br/>→ user memory → authoring context<br/>→ explicit Skills → workflow Skills<br/>→ connector Skills → global Skills"]
    Note["User turns are never trimmed"]
    build --> Trim --> T1
    T1 -. preserved .- Note
```

This order is part of the contract. Operator-curated connector and workflow guidance survives longer than incidental historical context under tight budgets — so the AI's deep grounding in a tenant's own conventions is the *last* thing dropped, not the first.

Conversation replay is bounded: tool results are truncated before re-feeding into later turns, explicit compaction markers suppress older replay, and oversized histories collapse into a deterministic summary plus the recent tail. The model keeps the current task context without dragging every historical tool payload back through the window.

---

## The Connector Catalog

When a user names an external boundary — "pull from our Salesforce instance" or "post to Slack" — the AI needs connector-specific knowledge. Generic HTTP knowledge is not enough.

| Source | What it gives the AI |
|---|---|
| Connector Templates | A catalog covering common enterprise services — driver type, auth config, doc references, setup guidance. The AI understands the target API, not just the idea of it |
| Documentation Ingestion | OpenAPI specs, GraphQL schemas, and HTML docs are indexed and become context for that connector — specific endpoints, parameters, error codes |
| Credential Vault | Users never handle raw secrets; the AI proposes "use your Stripe connector" without seeing the key. Credentials are referenced by name, never by value |

Cloudflare and Firebase/Firestore are catalog templates (`cloudflare` and `firebase`). When no
catalog template exists, `import_connector_from_spec` can start from OpenAPI JSON/YAML or Google
REST Discovery JSON, inline or at a URL. URL imports are streamed up to 50 MiB and use server,
service-root, and security metadata to seed the draft. Cloudflare's official OpenAPI document
auto-matches the Cloudflare template; Firestore's official Discovery document auto-matches
Firebase revision 2. Credentials are collected only after import through the masked or managed
OAuth flow and must never appear in the public spec fetch or conversation transcript.

---

## Discovery: From Files to Proposals

Discovery accelerates onboarding new systems. Rather than manually configuring every connector and skill, it starts from documentation that already exists.

An operator uploads files — API specs, data dictionaries, architecture diagrams, runbooks — and sk analyzes them into structured proposals. Each Discovery Artifact is a proposed Connector, Skill, or Knowledge Source, with a confidence score and links to the specific evidence in the uploaded files. The operator reviews each proposal and decides what to approve.

Nothing is automatically configured — the proposals are starting points, not decisions. Discovery is built for the scenarios enterprises actually hit: a new vendor relationship, an acquired company's systems, a newly discovered internal API. The goal is documentation into a working starting point in minutes rather than weeks, while keeping every configuration decision in human hands.

---

## How Authoring Improves Over Time

sk's authoring layer is not static — it improves as the platform accumulates execution history and operator feedback.

| Mechanism | Trigger | Output | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Skill Candidates** | Connectors / step sequences used together frequently and succeeding | A proposed Skill with confidence scores and links to supporting executions | Operator promotes or rejects |
| **Self-healing drift detection** | A connector's behavior diverges from what the workflow expects (endpoints move, fields shift, new error codes) | A Patch Candidate — the smallest safe change the AI can propose | Operator reviews before anything is applied |

The pattern is identical: the platform surfaces improvement proposals, humans make the decisions. The platform gets smarter over time, but only with human approval at each step.

---

## The sk-Stdlib In The Sandbox

Operator-authored JavaScript — transform steps with `language: "javascript"`, before-request hooks — runs inside a QuickJS-WASM sandbox with zero host globals. To keep that code concise, uniform, and reviewable, every context ships a curated `sk` global: a frozen, versioned, deterministic standard library.

The surface is intentionally small — the patterns that showed up repeatedly in real tenant code: HTTP-method classification, null-safe property access, allow/deny builders, common array reshapers, type guards.

| Instead of | Authors write |
|---|---|
| Maintaining a POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE list by hand | `sk.http.isMutating(method)` |
| Hand-coding `{ allow: false, reason }` | `sk.deny("reason")` |
| Chained null checks | `sk.get(input, "request.method", "")` |

Nothing in the stdlib touches the host — no `Date.now`, no `Math.random`, no I/O — so dry-runs stay reproducible and self-healing stays deterministic. The stdlib is versioned with semantic versioning: additive changes are minor bumps; signature or semantic changes are major bumps paired with a migration proposal. When the engine's stdlib version drifts past the major recorded on a persisted workflow, self-healing surfaces a Patch Candidate so operators can review the migration before anything runs.

The conversational layer is aware of the stdlib and proposes `sk.*` forms by default. Operators can still write raw comparisons in edge cases, but the stdlib form is the norm — it shortens review and keeps policy uniform across tenants.

---

## Further reading

- [Connectors & integration](../concepts/connectors.md) — how Connectors, Drivers, and Credentials form the integration fabric authoring draws on.
- [Workflow execution](../concepts/workflows.md) — how approved workflows run deterministically, what governance looks like at execution time, and how self-healing keeps them healthy.
- [glossary — authoring terms](../concepts/glossary.md#group-2-authoring) — Conversation, Draft, Skill, Skill Candidate, Knowledge Source, Discovery.
</content>
</invoke>

<!-- Source: docs/authors/choosing-your-surface.md -->

# Choosing your surface

> **Reading time:** ~9 min
> **Audience:** Anyone building or running workflows with an AI assistant

**Do the work where it actually goes faster.** sk meets you in a browser chat, in your terminal, and in your coding agent — but those doors are not interchangeable. Pick the wrong one and a five-minute edit becomes an afternoon of describing the same change over and over. This page tells you which door fits which job, and how to notice mid-task that you are standing at the wrong one.

---

## Look it up by what you want to do

| What you want to do | Where | Why there |
|---|---|---|
| Run something and read the result | Slack / Teams / Google Chat, or a browser AI client | No setup, follow-up questions work, built for exactly this |
| Ask how your team normally does something | A coding agent, or a browser AI client | Answers from your own knowledge, not from general knowledge |
| Describe a new process for the first time | The `sk` REPL or chat — an authoring conversation | Exploring, discarding, retrying is what a conversation is good at |
| Change one line of a process that already exists | The `sk` CLI | You write the change yourself; nothing paraphrases it |
| Go back to an earlier version | The `sk` CLI (`sk workflows history` → `restore`) | A browser client does not carry the command at all |
| Approve something | The portal link, or the CLI | Deliberately outside the chat — a decision should be visible and recorded, not expire in a dialog |
| Connect a new system, enter credentials | The REPL's `/install` wizard, or the credential portal | Secrets never travel through a conversation |
| Run on a schedule, or when an event fires | A schedule or an inbound webhook | Runs with nobody present |
| Wire sk into another system | The REST API | Machine to machine |
| Find out why a run failed | `sk diagnostics` in the CLI; read-only also from chat | The trace id joins the two |

The rest of this page is why that table looks the way it does — and what it costs you to
ignore it.

---

## One question

> **Am I changing a definition, or running one?**

Everything else follows from the answer.

| | **Change a definition** | **Run one** |
|---|---|---|
| Use | a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, …) + the `sk` CLI | claude.ai / ChatGPT over MCP |
| Why | you write the exact definition; nothing paraphrases it | built for this, low friction, no setup |

A browser client is not a weaker tool. It is a tool for a different job. It runs workflows, reads results, and reasons about what came back — and it does all of that well. What it cannot do is write a workflow definition directly. Ask it to, and your sentence has to travel through a second model that interprets it.

## Seven examples

### 1. "In `normalize`, take the timestamp from the collection metadata, not the clock."

**Wrong door — browser chat.** Your sentence becomes an instruction to an authoring model, which turns it into an edit. The edit may land somewhere else than you meant, and you often find out only after it is live.

**Right door — your terminal:**

```bash
sk workflows get <id> > normalize.json
# edit the one line
sk workflows validate normalize.json
sk workflows preview  normalize.json
sk workflows update   <id> --file=normalize.json
```

You see the diff. The change is the change you wrote.

`update` runs `validate` and `preview` itself before writing, so the two explicit
steps above are for reading the result yourself — the point of the whole exercise.
An unchanged definition does not rotate a version.

### 2. "Roll back to the previous version."

**Wrong door — browser chat.** Version restore is a tenant write, and the authoring surface publishes none of those except running a workflow. The tool is not in the client's catalogue at all, so the assistant cannot see it — and tends to propose detours rather than say "I cannot reach that."

**Right door — your terminal**, where restoring safely also means reading the history first:

```bash
sk workflows history <id>
sk workflows restore <id> <version>
```

Never guess the version number. Restoring is not a repair: if you do not know which version was good, find out before you replace what is live.

### 3. "Prove that two runs produce identical output."

**Wrong door — browser chat.** The client sees only what a tool hands back. It cannot compare two artefacts byte for byte, so it will answer the question by reasoning about it — which sounds like a proof and is not one.

**Right door — run it twice and compare the checksums yourself.** Determinism claims need a diff, not an argument.

### 4. "Run the weekly report and tell me what stands out."

**Right door — browser chat.** This is exactly what it is for: call the workflow, read the result, notice the outlier, ask a follow-up. No setup, no files, no CLI.

### 5. "Keep these five related workflows consistent."

**Wrong door — browser chat.** Each conversation carries its own context. The convention you established in the first workflow has quietly drifted by the fifth, and nothing shows you that it did.

**Right door — the repo.** Five files, one commit, one review. Consistency becomes something you can see rather than something you hope for.

### 6. "Approve this proposal."

**Wrong door — an in-band confirmation.** Some clients render their own approval dialog; when a client does not, the request degrades to a link that has to be opened in time. Often it is not, and the decision quietly expires.

**Right door — approve in the portal or the CLI**, deliberately, where the decision is visible and recorded.

### 7. "Sketch me something in this direction."

**Right door — browser chat**, for the *first draft*. Exploring, shaping, throwing away, trying again: this is where a conversational surface is strongest.

Then export it and continue in the repo. The handover belongs exactly where an idea turns into a definition — not later.

## Warning signs you are at the wrong door

Any one of these means stop and switch, not try again:

- You have described the same change three times.
- The assistant **runs** the thing instead of changing it.
- A dry run reported green and nobody actually read the result.
- You are waiting on a confirmation that never arrives.
- You cannot say which version is currently live.

The last one is the most expensive, because it is the one you notice last.

## What a browser client cannot do — and why that is deliberate

A browser client connects in **authoring mode**, which publishes the conversation tools, tenant reads, and exactly one write: running a workflow. Concretely:

- **No tenant writes reach the catalogue.** `restore_workflow_version` and `update_workflow` are not listed, so the assistant cannot call them — asking returns "no tool named that is available on this surface." `run_workflow` is the deliberate exception: it runs a workflow rather than mutating a definition.
- **The step-level editors are not in the catalogue either** — in any mode, including admin. `edit_workflow_patch`, `save_workflow_draft`, `dry_run_workflow`, and `validate_draft` are omitted from the tool list, and calling one directly is refused rather than silently failing. They are driven by sk's own authoring loop inside a conversation, never by the external client.
- **No tool accepts a full workflow definition.** There is no MCP equivalent of `PUT /v1/workflows/{id}`.
- **A broader credential does not widen this.** Even a wildcard scope resolves to authoring, and authoring withholds tenant writes unconditionally — no key changes that. The admin surface is a separate, explicitly requested scope.

So every definition edit over MCP routes through the authoring conversation, where a model turns your sentence into the patch. That is a deliberate boundary, not an oversight: a definition edit should pass through something a person can read. Mechanics in [Input Surfaces → MCP Integration](../developers/input-surfaces.md#mcp-integration); the reasoning in [Reversibility & Trust Domains](../concepts/reversibility-and-trust-domains.md).

## Green is not the same as correct

A dry run checks that the workflow **executes**. It does not check that the result is **right**.

A workflow can read the wrong field, produce empty values for every record, and finish without a single error — green, and wrong. If you did not read the preview, you have confirmation that nothing crashed and nothing more.

This matters most on an **unattended turn** — a background client with no way to surface a prompt. A deferral there would strand the work mid-flight, so sk commits instead. What it commits, and what it holds back, is worth knowing exactly:

| Unattended turn, dry run green | Outcome |
|---|---|
| the preview judge returned a verdict | commits |
| judge skipped, and the workflow is **new** | commits — there is nothing to lose |
| judge skipped, and it would **replace** an existing workflow | **held back** |

That last row exists because the alternative went wrong in production: an unjudged green preview once landed a generic normaliser on top of a purpose-built one, and "green" there meant only "no exception". Replacing verified work now needs more than an absent objection.

The first two rows still commit without anyone agreeing to it. An auto-commit is not evidence a person reviewed anything — it tells you the run was clean, not that it was right.

Read the preview. Especially when it is green.

## Further reading

- [Reversibility & Trust Domains](../concepts/reversibility-and-trust-domains.md) — why authoring and execution are different jobs
- [Use sk from a coding agent](coding-agents.md) — connecting Claude Code, Codex, and other clients
- [AI-Assisted Authoring](authoring-workflows.md) — the full authoring loop
- [Input Surfaces](../developers/input-surfaces.md) — every door and what it carries

<!-- Source: docs/authors/coding-agents.md -->

# Use sk from a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, …)

> **Audience:** You use Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Claude Desktop, claude.ai,
> or ChatGPT, and want it grounded in your team's knowledge instead of guessing.

Every new session starts already knowing your domain's rules, looks your
runbooks up instead of inventing them, and remembers what you taught it last
time — once you have reviewed and approved that lesson.

This page is the whole path: install → connect your client → import your
knowledge → ask a grounded question. About 10 minutes.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Wiki["Your wiki<br/>(markdown directory)"] -->|"sk knowledge-sources import<br/>--tags domain:&lt;slug&gt;"| Engine[("sk engine")]
    Engine -->|"session briefing<br/>(hook)"| Session["Coding-agent session"]
    Session -->|"search_knowledge_v2 / read_knowledge<br/>(over MCP)"| Engine
    Session -->|"capture hook / save_learning"| Queue["Review queue"]
    Queue -->|"sk learnings review"| Engine
```

## What your client can do

Two channels do different jobs. **MCP** lets a session search and read your
knowledge; the **briefing hook** tells it your rules and what knowledge exists
before it starts. Not every client supports both:

| Client | MCP (lookup) | Briefing hook | Writes workflow definitions | Setup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | yes | yes | yes — via the `sk` CLI | [below](#claude-code) |
| **Codex** | yes | yes (feature-gated) | yes — via the `sk` CLI | [below](#codex) |
| **Cursor**, **Claude Desktop** | yes | no | yes, if it can run `sk` | [below](#cursor-claude-desktop-and-other-mcp-clients) |
| **claude.ai**, **ChatGPT** | yes (OAuth) | no | **no** — MCP carries no definition writes | [below](#claudeai-and-chatgpt-oauth) |

A client without hooks still gets every tool — it just is not *told* about your
domain up front, so ask it to search, or put the instruction in the client's own
rules file (`CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, Cursor rules …).

The last column is the one that surprises people. MCP is a lookup and run
surface: it carries reads and `run_workflow`, not definition writes. A client
that can run `sk` in a shell edits definitions directly and byte-exactly; a
browser client has to route every edit through an authoring conversation
instead. Pick accordingly — see [Choosing your surface](choosing-your-surface.md).

## Before you start

You need the `sk` CLI installed and logged in:

```bash
curl -fsSL <engine-url>/install | bash      # the CLI is served by your engine
sk login --engine-url <engine-url> --api-key <wf_live_…>
sk status                                   # engine + key confirmed
```

Your operator gives you the engine URL and the API key. If you run the engine
yourself, start at the [self-host guide](../developers/self-host.md).

## 1. Declare the domain in your repo

A **domain** is a business area you curate knowledge for — `blog-de`,
`payments`, `platform`. It is nothing but the tag `domain:<slug>` on Skills and
Knowledge Sources; there is no table and no config object to create.

```bash
cd <your-repo>
sk agent init --domains <domain-slug>
```

This writes `.sk/agent.json` (commit it — it is how a session in this repo knows
which domains to pull), wires the Claude Code hooks, and prints the Codex
snippets plus the MCP command for both. Re-running it never duplicates anything.

Worth running even on a client without hooks: `.sk/agent.json` is what
`sk agent briefing` reads, so you can always fetch the briefing by hand.

## 2. Connect your client

The registration commands below need the API key in your shell. It is the same
key you logged in with; if you no longer have it at hand:

```bash
export SK_API_KEY="$(jq -r '.profiles.default.api_key' ~/.sk/config.json)"
```

### Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http --scope user sk <engine-url>/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${SK_API_KEY}"
```

Your shell expands `${SK_API_KEY}` as you run the line, so the key is stored in
Claude Code's own config — the export is only needed once, at registration time.
Confirm with `claude mcp list`; `sk` should show as connected.

`sk agent init` already wired the hooks in `~/.claude/settings.json`:
`SessionStart` (matcher `startup|resume|compact`, so it survives context
compaction) injects the briefing, and `SessionEnd` posts the transcript for
learning capture.

> **Already connected?** If your Claude account carries the sk connector, your
> sessions can already call `search_knowledge_v2`, `read_knowledge`,
> `find_skill`, and `save_learning`. Do not add a second registration for the
> same engine — it duplicates the whole tool catalog.

### Codex

```bash
codex mcp add sk --url <engine-url>/mcp --bearer-token-env-var SK_API_KEY
```

Codex reads `SK_API_KEY` at call time, not just at registration — so export it
in your shell profile, not just the current shell.

Hooks are feature-gated. `sk agent init` prints, but cannot apply, two manual
steps:

1. Enable them in `~/.codex/config.toml`:
   ```toml
   [features]
   hooks = true
   ```
2. Add the printed `~/.codex/hooks.json`. Codex has no `SessionEnd` event, so
   capture runs on the `Stop` hook — which fires per turn. That is cheap: the
   engine dedups repeated captures by learning fingerprint.

Hooks additionally need a one-time trust confirmation via `/hooks` in the Codex
TUI.

### Cursor, Claude Desktop, and other MCP clients

Add the engine as a streamable-HTTP MCP server in the client's config:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sk": {
      "url": "https://<engine-host>/mcp",
      "transport": "streamable-http",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer wf_live_…" }
    }
  }
}
```

These clients have no session hook, so nothing injects the briefing. Paste the
grounding rule into the client's own rules file so sessions know to look up:

```text
For facts about <domain-slug>, call search_knowledge_v2 with
tags: ["domain:<domain-slug>"] instead of guessing. If it returns
nothing, say so.
```

### claude.ai and ChatGPT (OAuth)

These clients cannot hold a static key. The engine is a full OAuth 2.1
authorization server for `/mcp`, so they authenticate interactively instead:
point the connector at `https://<engine-host>/mcp` and the client discovers
OAuth via `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`, registers itself, and opens
the sk login + consent flow. No header, no key. The ChatGPT connector steps and
the full flow: [input surfaces](../developers/input-surfaces.md).

> **`sk mcp` is a different thing.** It is a stdio proxy exposing
> `sk_conversation_*` tools for driving conversations from an IDE plugin. It
> does **not** carry the knowledge tools, so it is not the path for this page.

## 3. Import your knowledge — tagged with the domain

This is the step that connects the two halves. Knowledge only reaches a session
if it carries that session's `domain:` tag.

```bash
sk knowledge-sources import ./team-wiki --tags "domain:<domain-slug>"
```

`import` takes a whole markdown directory — an Obsidian vault, an
agent-maintained wiki, an [OKF](https://okf.md/) bundle, a Notion export — and
makes one searchable source with a passage per file. Re-running it is a no-op
when nothing changed, so a nightly CI job keeps sk in sync with a git wiki
without churn. Details and the frontmatter rules:
[Knowledge Sources](./knowledge-sources.md).

For a single file, `sk knowledge-sources create --file ./runbook.md --tags
"domain:<domain-slug>"` does the same job.

> **The tag is not optional.** An import without `--tags "domain:<slug>"`
> succeeds and is searchable — but the briefing never indexes it and sessions
> in that domain will not know it exists.

## 4. Verify before you trust it

```bash
sk agent briefing        # what a fresh session will be told
```

You should see your source under **Knowledge index** and a grounding rule
naming your domain:

```text
# sk session briefing — domains: payments

Grounding rule: for facts of these domains, look up instead of guessing —
call `search_knowledge_v2` with `tags: ["domain:payments"]`.
If the search returns nothing, say so; do not invent domain internals.

## Knowledge index (search, don't preload)
- **Team Wiki** (`team-wiki`)
```

Full documents are never preloaded — the session gets an index and fetches
details on demand, which is what keeps the context small.

Now start your agent in the repo and ask something only your wiki knows. It
searches instead of guessing, and cites the source it used.

## 5. Teach it once, keep it

When you correct the agent, that correction can outlive the session:

- **Automatic** — the capture hook posts the transcript; the engine distills
  only durable rules a human actually taught. A routine session correctly
  produces nothing. (Claude Code and Codex only — it is the hook that posts it.)
- **Explicit** — say "remember this" and the agent calls `save_learning`. This
  works on every MCP client, hooks or not.

Both create *proposals*, never live knowledge. You decide:

```bash
sk learnings list        # what is waiting
sk learnings review      # approve / edit / reject
```

An approved learning becomes an active skill carrying the domain tag — the very
next briefing in that domain includes it. You can also approve without leaving
the session: ask the agent to approve the candidate and confirm your client's
native dialog.

Optionally materialise the domain's skills as `SKILL.md` files, so the
conventions work even with no engine connection. Both Claude Code and Codex
hot-reload them:

```bash
sk skills sync
```

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| `sk agent briefing` says "no domains" | The directory (or a parent) has no `.sk/agent.json` — run `sk agent init`, or pass `--domains`. |
| Briefing shows no knowledge index | The source is missing the `domain:<slug>` tag. Check `sk knowledge-sources list`; fix with `sk knowledge-sources patch <id> --tags "domain:<slug>,…"` (tags are replaced wholesale). |
| The session ignores your knowledge | The hook fires but MCP is not registered — the agent knows what exists but cannot fetch it. Check `claude mcp list` / `codex mcp list`. |
| No briefing at all, but tools work | Expected on a client without hooks (Cursor, Claude Desktop, claude.ai, ChatGPT) — put the grounding rule in the client's rules file. |
| The briefing misses a skill | Only **active** skills with the domain tag are included. Check `sk skills list`. |
| Codex: hooks never fire | `[features] hooks = true` missing in `~/.codex/config.toml`, or the one-time `/hooks` trust confirmation is pending. |
| Nothing happens at all | Hooks never break a session: on any error they print nothing and exit 0. The swallowed error is in `~/.sk/debug.log` (`agent.briefing_hook_failed`, `agent.capture_hook_failed`). |

## Related

- [Coding-agent integration](../developers/coding-agent-integration.md) — the
  loop's mechanics: briefing assembly, capture, dedup, review.
- [Knowledge Sources](./knowledge-sources.md) — import, tags, refresh, and
  reading knowledge back.
- [Input surfaces](../developers/input-surfaces.md) — MCP transport, OAuth 2.1,
  and every other door into the engine.
- [Knowledge & Skills](../concepts/knowledge-and-skills.md) — the concepts and
  why the loop compounds.
- [Model a Domain](./model-a-domain.md) — connector + skills + knowledge for a
  whole domain.

<!-- Source: docs/authors/custom-skills.md -->

# Custom Skills

> **Audience:** Authors and operators encoding organization-specific guidance for
> the AI.

Write down a convention once and stop repeating it. From then on sk applies it
on every conversation, every discovery, every repair — so drafts arrive already
in your house style and reviews get shorter. When a pattern shows up often
enough, sk proposes it as a new Skill, and you decide whether it becomes one.

A Skill is a curated, reusable piece of context loaded into the AI's context
window during a Conversation and other AI-assisted authoring flows (discovery,
diagnosis, bounded repair). Skills encode best practices, integration patterns,
security policies, and the domain knowledge that makes the AI propose *your*
conventions, not generic ones. For how Skills sit alongside Knowledge Sources and
how the engine assembles them into each turn, see
[Knowledge & Skills](../concepts/knowledge-and-skills.md).

## How a Skill reaches the AI

Three sources feed Skills; activation rules decide which load; the engine then
assembles the active set into the turn.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Sources
        M[Manual<br/>create_skill / CLI]
        T[Template<br/>seeded conventions]
        C[Skill Candidate<br/>promoted by operator]
    end

    subgraph Activation
        G[Global scope]
        CN[Connector scope]
        WF[Workflow scope]
    end

    M --> G
    T --> CN
    C --> WF
    M --> CN
    M --> WF

    G --> A[Active skill set]
    CN -->|Connector referenced| A
    WF -->|Authoring / repairing workflow| A

    A --> L[Context load<br/>into the turn]
    L --> AI([AI proposes your conventions])
```

| Source | Origin | Becomes active when |
|---|---|---|
| **Manual** | `create_skill` / `update_skill` in chat, or `sk skills create` | Its scope matches the turn |
| **Template** | Seeded conventions shipped with the platform | Its scope matches the turn |
| **Candidate** | Detected from execution history, **promoted by an operator** | Its scope matches the turn |

---

## Authoring and scoping a Skill

Operators create and manage Skills. They can be scoped:

| Scope | Loads when |
|---|---|
| **globally** | Available in all Conversations |
| **per-Connector** | That Connector is referenced (the Stripe Skill loads when the AI touches your Stripe connector) |
| **per-Workflow** | Authoring or repairing that workflow |

In chat you can author a Skill conversationally (`create_skill` / `update_skill`),
or manage them from the CLI:

```bash
sk skills list
sk skills create --file ./stripe-skill.json
```

The `--file` argument is a SkillDef JSON, not markdown. The SkillDef body carries
the `scope`, `connector_id`, and `title` — there are no separate `--title` or
`--scope` flags.

A Skill is dense, prescriptive guidance the AI should follow — keep each one tight and single-purpose. Broader, document-scale context belongs in a [Knowledge Source](./knowledge-sources.md) instead.

| Use a Skill when | Use a [Knowledge Source](./knowledge-sources.md) when |
|---|---|
| Guidance is prescriptive — "always do X" | Context is reference material to draw from |
| It fits in a tight, single-purpose page | It is document-scale |
| You want it followed, not just consulted | You want it available for lookup |

## Skill Candidates: learning from what works

Skills are not auto-generated and not auto-promoted. The platform detects recurring patterns from execution history — Connectors or step sequences that are used together frequently and tend to succeed — and surfaces them as **Skill Candidates** for operator review. Each candidate carries a confidence tier (low / medium / high) and links to the executions that support it.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    E[Execution history] --> D{Recurring,<br/>successful pattern?}
    D -->|no| E
    D -->|yes| SC[Skill Candidate<br/>confidence tier + supporting executions]
    SC --> R{Operator review}
    R -->|reject| X[Discarded]
    R -->|promote| AS[Active Skill]
    AS --> CTX[Loaded into future turns]
    CTX --> E
```

A candidate becomes an active Skill only through explicit operator promotion:

```bash
sk skill-candidates list
sk skill-candidates approve <id>
```

sk learns from what works, but humans decide what becomes canonical guidance.

## The sk-Stdlib the AI proposes

JavaScript that authors write — transform steps with `language: "javascript"`, before-request hooks — runs inside a QuickJS-WASM sandbox with zero host globals. Every sandbox context ships a frozen, versioned, deterministic `sk` standard library (HTTP-method classification, null-safe access, allow/deny builders, array reshapers, type guards). The conversational authoring layer is aware of the stdlib and proposes `sk.*` forms by default — `sk.http.isMutating(method)`, `sk.deny("reason")`, `sk.get(input, "request.method", "")` — which shortens code review and keeps policy uniform across tenants. Nothing in the stdlib touches the host, so dry-runs and self-healing stay reproducible.

---

- [Knowledge & Skills](../concepts/knowledge-and-skills.md) — the conceptual model, context-assembly order, and the compounding loop.
- [Model a Domain](./model-a-domain.md) — a Skill and a Knowledge Source configured side by side for one domain, worked end to end.
- [Knowledge Sources](./knowledge-sources.md) — the broad-context counterpart.
