binding on save: when Stripe posts `charge.failed` to the workflow's
inbound URL, the engine verifies the Stripe signature, extracts the
failed-charge fields, and posts a redacted alert into the operator's
Slack channel.

```json
{
  "slug": "on-charge-failed-notify-slack",
  "title": "On Stripe charge.failed, post a Slack alert",
  "description": "Webhook-triggered: when Stripe fires `charge.failed` against the workflow's inbound URL, this recipe verifies the Stripe signature, extracts the failed-charge fields (id, amount, currency, decline reason, customer email), and posts a redacted alert into the operator's chosen Slack channel. Demonstrates the workflow `trigger: { kind: 'webhook' }` block end-to-end.",
  "intent_keywords": [
    "charge failed slack",
    "stripe failure alert",
    "notify slack on failed charge",
    "stripe webhook alert"
  ],
  "derived_from_skill": "stripe-basics",
  "category": "payments",
  "tags": ["webhook", "trigger", "alerting", "demonstration"],
  "difficulty": "advanced",
  "estimated_setup_minutes": 12,
  "prerequisites": [
    "Stripe webhook endpoint signing secret (whsec_...) configured on the bound webhook row",
    "Slack bot token connector with chat:write scope",
    "Slack channel id where the alert should land"
  ],
  "required_connectors": [
    { "placeholder": "7d046f2e-9c40-4b8a-aa14-ff3eb87b5046", "template": "slack" }
  ],
  "workflow": {
    "name": "stripe-on-charge-failed-notify-slack",
    "description": "Triggered by an inbound Stripe `charge.failed` webhook; posts a redacted alert into the operator's Slack channel.",
    "trigger": {
      "kind": "webhook",
      "source": "stripe",
      "events": ["charge.failed"],
      "verify": "stripe-signature"
    },
    "input_schema": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": ["body", "alert_channel"],
      "properties": {
        "body": { "type": "object", "required": ["data", "type"] },
        "alert_channel": {
          "type": "string",
          "description": "Slack channel id (e.g. C0123ALERT) where the alert should be posted."
        }
      }
    },
    "steps": [
      {
        "kind": "transform",
        "id": "extract",
        "language": "javascript",
        "expression": "const o = input.input.body.data.object; return { charge_id: o.id, amount: o.amount, currency: o.currency, failure_code: o.failure_code, failure_message: o.failure_message, email: o.billing_details.email };"
      },
      {
        "kind": "request",
        "id": "post",
        "method": "POST",
        "connector_id": "7d046f2e-9c40-4b8a-aa14-ff3eb87b5046",
        "url": "${connector.slack.base_url}/chat.postMessage",
        "headers": { "Content-Type": "application/json; charset=utf-8" },
        "body": {
          "channel": "${input.alert_channel}",
          "text": "[stripe] charge.failed — ${scope.extract.data.currency} ${scope.extract.data.amount} — ${scope.extract.data.failure_code} — ${scope.extract.data.email} — ${scope.extract.data.charge_id}"
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Notes for authors:

- `verify: "stripe-signature"` requires the inbound binding to carry the
  `whsec_...` signing secret. The driver rejects unsigned or
  signature-mismatched posts before any step runs.
- `events: ["charge.failed"]` filters at the inbound driver, so noisy
  events never reach `runExecution()`. Use `[]` only when the workflow
  legitimately needs every event from `source`.
- The `input_schema` documents what the engine guarantees the workflow
  scope holds at step time — `body` is the verified Stripe payload and
  `alert_channel` is the per-tenant Slack channel id supplied at bind
  time.

## Walkthrough — schedule-triggered recipe (daily charges digest)

This is the shipped `stripe.daily-charges-digest` recipe. Saving it
upserts a `workflows_schedules` row keyed on `(tenant_id, workflow_id)`;
the scheduler reconciler wakes the workflow up at 08:00 Europe/Berlin on
business days and skips the listed German bank holidays for 2026. No
external cron, no `sk run` loop.

```json
{
  "slug": "daily-charges-digest",
  "title": "Daily charges digest (08:00 Europe/Berlin, business days only)",
  "description": "Pull yesterday's charges every business day at 08:00 Europe/Berlin and summarise total volume + count by currency. Skips weekends and the dates listed in `skip_dates` (German bank holidays seeded for 2026). Wired through the schedule trigger so the workflow wakes itself up — no external cron, no `sk run` loop.",
  "intent_keywords": [
    "daily charges digest",
    "scheduled charges report",
    "yesterday charges",
    "daily revenue summary"
  ],
  "derived_from_skill": "stripe-basics",
  "category": "payments",
  "tags": ["scheduled", "trigger:schedule", "digest"],
  "difficulty": "intermediate",
  "estimated_setup_minutes": 8,
  "prerequisites": [
    "Stripe connector with read access to /v1/charges",
    "Schedule trigger requires the engine's scheduler reconciler to be running"
  ],
  "required_connectors": [],
  "workflow": {
    "name": "stripe-daily-charges-digest",
    "description": "Pull yesterday's charges and summarise by currency. Wakes itself up at 08:00 Europe/Berlin every business day.",
    "trigger": {
      "kind": "schedule",
      "cron": "0 8 * * *",
      "tz": "Europe/Berlin",
      "business_days_only": true,
      "skip_dates": [
        "2026-01-01",
        "2026-04-03",
        "2026-04-06",
        "2026-05-01",
        "2026-05-14",
        "2026-05-25",
        "2026-10-03",
        "2026-12-25",
        "2026-12-26"
      ]
    },
    "steps": [
      {
        "kind": "request",
        "id": "list",
        "method": "GET",
        "url": "${connector.stripe.base_url}/charges",
        "query": { "limit": 100 },
        "pagination": {
          "strategy": "cursor",
          "cursor_request_param": "starting_after",
          "cursor_response_path": "data[last].id",
          "page_size": 100
        }
      },
      {
        "kind": "transform",
        "id": "summary",
        "language": "javascript",
        "expression": "const charges = input.scope.list.data.body.data; const byCurrency = {}; for (const c of charges) { const g = (byCurrency[c.currency] ??= { count: 0, amount_total: 0 }); g.count += 1; g.amount_total += c.amount; } return { count: charges.length, by_currency: byCurrency };"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Notes for authors:

- `cron` is the standard 5-field expression (`m h dom mon dow`); the
  reconciler also accepts the engine's `every:N` shorthand for sub-minute
  cadences.
- `tz` must be a valid IANA timezone — the reconciler hands it to
  pg-boss so the firing lands at the operator's local wall-clock time
  instead of UTC.
- `business_days_only` skips weekends. Holiday calendars are NOT
  inferred — declare every freeze date explicitly via `skip_dates`. The
  reconciler compares each entry against the trigger's `tz` so a date
  here means "this calendar day in the workflow's timezone".
- A schedule recipe typically has `sample_input: null` because the
  scheduler itself supplies no payload — the workflow reads its inputs
  from the connectors it queries.

## Walkthrough — auth-chain recipe (mint then use)

This is the shipped `firebase.signin-email-password-then-firestore-read`
recipe. It demonstrates the canonical *mint then use* shape for any
non-OAuth2 username/password JWT flow — Firebase Auth REST, Cognito
InitiateAuth (when not handled by the connector's OAuth2 grant),
generic POST `/login` endpoints, etc. Two patterns are load-bearing:
**redacted secret outputs** and **dot-path scope substitution** in
downstream headers.

```json
{
  "slug": "signin-email-password-then-firestore-read",
  "workflow": {
    "name": "firebase-signin-email-password-then-firestore-read",
    "steps": [
      {
        "kind": "request",
        "id": "signin",
        "method": "POST",
        "url": "https://identitytoolkit.googleapis.com/v1/accounts:signInWithPassword",
        "query": { "key": "${input.api_key}" },
        "body": {
          "email": "${input.email}",
          "password": "${input.password}",
          "returnSecureToken": true
        },
        "outputs": {
          "idToken": { "secret": true },
          "refreshToken": { "secret": true }
        }
      },
      {
        "kind": "request",
        "id": "read_document",
        "method": "GET",
        "url": "https://firestore.googleapis.com/v1/projects/${input.project_id}/databases/(default)/documents/${input.collection}/${input.document_id}",
        "headers": {
          "Authorization": "Bearer ${scope.signin.idToken}"
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Notes for authors:

- **`outputs.<path>.secret = true`** marks the field for redaction in
  audit log, step preview, and offload — but the raw value stays in the
  in-memory scope so downstream steps can still substitute it. Reach for
  this on every minted token (`idToken`, `access_token`,
  `AuthenticationResult.IdToken`, `AssumeRoleResult.Credentials.SessionToken`).
- **`${scope.<step_id>.<dot.path>}`** is dot-notation, NOT JSON-pointer.
  Nested paths work transparently:
  `${scope.signin.idToken}` (top-level) and
  `${scope.assume.AssumeRoleResult.Credentials.AccessKeyId}` (nested) both
  resolve via repeated property lookup.
- The first step has no `connector_id` substitution because the auth API
  lives at a fixed URL distinct from the protected resource. Use the
  hard-coded URL in step 1 and `${connector.<slug>.base_url}` (or another
  hard-coded URL) in step 2.
- When the protected resource API is reachable via a connector with an
  existing auth mode (`oauth2` Authorization Code, `oauth2` Password
  Grant, `aws_sigv4`, `bearer`, etc.), prefer that mode over a hand-wired
  two-step chain — the connector's `refreshIfStale()` handles minting
  transparently and the workflow stays single-step. Use this two-step
  pattern only when no built-in auth mode fits the provider's flow.

## Quality gate

Every recipe-touching PR runs:

```sh
bun run lint:recipes        # recipe lint
bun run test:unit           # includes apps/engine/src/connectors/recipes.test.ts
bun run verify:ai           # includes recipe-discovery validator
```

`lint-recipes` enforces:

- `category` is set and a member of `RecipeCategoryEnum`.
- `intent_keywords` is 3-7, lowercase, no title-word duplicates.
- `sample_input` covers `input_schema.required` when both are set.
- `required_connectors` placeholders all appear in `workflow.steps`.
- Per-primitive coverage of `WorkflowDefSchema` step kinds (catches
  regressions when a previously-demonstrated primitive drops to zero
  recipes).

## Promotion checklist

Before opening a PR:

1. Recipe loads through `loadBuiltinTemplates()` without throwing.
2. `bun run lint:recipes` is green.
3. `intent_keywords` reflects how the operator would phrase the
   request, not the workflow's mechanics.
4. `sample_input` is realistic (no `"foo"` / `"bar"` placeholders).
5. If the recipe was dry-run against a vendor sandbox, set
   `last_validated_at` to today's ISO date.
6. If you are deprecating an existing recipe, set `deprecated` rather
   than deleting the slug — operators may have cloned drafts that
   reference it.
7. PR description names the operator pain the recipe solves. The
   recipe must beat any industry equivalent on validation,
   prerequisites clarity, or step efficiency — not just match.

## Related

- `docs/concepts/connectors.md` — connector templates (parent surface).
- `apps/engine/src/connectors/AGENTS.md` — connector subsystem rules.
- `scripts/lint-recipes.ts` — quality lint source.

<!-- Source: docs/developers/self-host.md -->

# Self-Host sk — Zero to Running

sk runs inside your own infrastructure, so your data stays where it already is. One
container, PostgreSQL, a private S3-compatible bucket, and nothing leaves your network except the
outbound calls to your LLM provider. Start from nothing and finish this page with a running
engine, an authenticated `sk` CLI, a working connector, a workflow you can run, and an
indexed knowledge article — all from the released Docker image.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Op["docker compose"] --> Engine["engine container<br/>(engine + sk + Cockpit + Chromium)"]
    Op --> PG
    Op --> S3
    Engine --> PG[("PostgreSQL<br/>your data, your volume")]
    Engine --> S3[("Private object storage<br/>files + large results")]
    Engine -. outbound only .-> LLM[("LLM provider")]
```

| What         | Detail                                                               |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Time**     | ~15 minutes                                                          |
| **You need** | Docker + one free [Anthropic API key](https://console.anthropic.com) |
| **Cost**     | The weather API used here (open-meteo) is free and keyless           |
| **Outcome**  | A governed engine you own, end-to-end                                |

> **The primary interface is the conversational `sk` REPL.** You describe what you
> want in plain language; the AI proposes a connector or workflow, you review and
> approve. Declarative JSON and one-shot commands exist too — for scripting and CI —
> see [Scripting & CI](#scripting--ci-non-interactive). Every command and output
> below is real, run end-to-end against the released image.

## In one command, from a checkout

If you have this repository, everything in Steps 1 and 2 below happens for you:

```bash
bun run start:local
```

It starts the stack, waits for readiness, completes first-run setup without asking
anything, runs one of the starter workflows that ship with a fresh tenant, and prints
the Cockpit URL. No API key, no account: the LLM provider is set to `mock`, so nothing
leaves your machine. Re-running it is safe.

The trade is real and worth naming. With the `mock` provider the conversational
authoring loop in Step 3 does not do any authoring — it is inert. You get a running
engine, a tenant, and workflows you can execute and inspect. To describe new work in
plain language you need a real provider, which the command prints instructions for at
the end.

Prefer to make each choice yourself, or not running from a checkout? Continue with
Step 1.

---

## Concepts in 60 seconds

| Term                 | One line                                                                           |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Tenant**           | Your isolated workspace — every connector, workflow, and user lives in one tenant. |
| **Connector**        | An authenticated link to an external API (here: open-meteo).                       |
| **Workflow**         | A versioned sequence of steps (call an API, transform the result).                 |
| **Execution**        | One immutable run of a workflow.                                                   |
| **Knowledge source** | A document (runbook, PDF) indexed for semantic search.                             |

Full glossary: [`docs/concepts/glossary.md`](../concepts/glossary.md).

---

## Step 1 — Run the engine

The application-complete image bundles the engine, Cockpit, migrations,
Chromium, **and** the `sk` CLI plus every supported client-platform artifact.
PostgreSQL and S3-compatible object storage remain separate, mandatory services.
The repository Compose file starts the pinned application, PostgreSQL, MinIO,
and a one-shot private-bucket initializer together.

```bash
docker compose up -d
```

Wait a few seconds, then confirm it is healthy:

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:3000/health
# {"status":"ok","service":"subkit","version":"<version>"}

curl -s http://localhost:3000/ready
# {"status":"ready","service":"subkit","version":"<version>","checks":{"lifecycle":"pass","database":"pass"}}
```

The engine container has no application-state volume. PostgreSQL stores runtime
configuration, encrypted secret versions, metadata, and object pointers; MinIO
stores file bodies and oversized results. The only engine filesystem writes are
disposable scratch files under `/tmp`.

---

## Step 2 — First-run bootstrap (tenant + admin key + LLM)

A fresh engine has no tenants. Read the one-time bootstrap key from the engine
log (or inject `SUBKIT_BOOTSTRAP_KEY`) and complete setup with `sk init`:

```bash
docker compose exec engine sk init \
  --token <one-time-bootstrap-key> \
  --admin-email you@example.com \
  --tenant-name "My Org" \
  --llm-provider anthropic \
  --llm-api-key sk-ant-YOUR-KEY
# sk init: bootstrap complete — tenant 6c82c719-…
```

> **No API key handy?** Use `--llm-provider mock` to walk the mechanics with zero
> external accounts.
>
> **Manual token (non-bundled deploys):** copy it from the logs and pass
> `--token` (valid 15 min; the engine reprints a fresh one on the next attempt):
>
> ```bash
> docker compose logs engine 2>&1 | grep -oE 'sk init --token [a-f0-9]{64}' | tail -1
> ```

> **Authentication defaults to the `api_key` adapter** — people are added by
> admin invite and authenticate with engine-issued API keys. Configure direct
> OIDC in Cockpit's Authentication settings, through HTTP/MCP settings, or with
> `sk settings set auth.providers`. No provider-specific setting or route is
> required. Provider-registry changes are stored as an immutable,
> restart-required PostgreSQL revision so the authentication middleware
> switches the complete registry atomically on the coordinated restart.

For example, an sk-owned direct OIDC client is one configuration record:

```json
{
  "auth": {
    "providers": [
      { "protocol": "api_key", "id": "api-key", "label": "SubKit API key" },
      {
        "protocol": "oidc",
        "id": "workforce-oidc",
        "label": "Workforce OIDC",
        "issuer_url": "https://identity.example.com",
        "client_id": "<subkit-client-id>",
        "scopes": "openid profile email",
        "tenant_slug": "default"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Direct OIDC adapters are public clients using Authorization Code with PKCE.
Register the callback below and configure the issuer for
`token_endpoint_auth_method=none`. SubKit deliberately does not store a client
secret in `auth.providers`; confidential-only issuers are not supported by this
runtime setting.

The only browser endpoints remain `/v1/identity/login/start`,
`/v1/identity/login/callback`, and `/v1/identity/logout` regardless of adapter
id or vendor.

The chooser is deliberately not vendor-configurable: `mcp-auth` always
shows **Continue with SSO** first and **Continue with API key** second. Provider
ids remain opaque deployment configuration, discovery returns canonical
labels (`SSO`, `API key`), and assertion exchange uses only
`POST /v1/identity/sessions` with the shared
`{provider_id,identity_token}` → `{api_key,principal_id,context_id,email}`
contract. The immutable OIDC `sub` is required; `email` is nullable and
contains only a provider-verified address.

Verify:

```bash
docker compose exec engine sk doctor
# ✔ profile / reachability / authn / setup / version_match … (exit 0)
docker compose exec engine sk -p "Say only the word: pong" --output text
# pong            ← confirms the LLM is wired correctly
```

---

## Step 3 — Build by talking to it (the `sk` REPL) ★

This is the main way to use sk. Open the interactive REPL (it needs a terminal,
so add `-it`):

```bash
docker compose exec engine sk
```

Now just say what you want. The AI proposes; **nothing is saved or run until you
`/approve`.** A real session — connector, then workflow, then a run — looks like:

```text
you ▸ create a keyless HTTP connector for the open-meteo forecast API
      (https://api.open-meteo.com, endpoint GET /v1/forecast), then probe it
 sk ▸ Created connector "open-meteo" (http, dev). Probe: GET /v1/forecast… → HTTP 200. ✓

you ▸ now a workflow that returns the current temperature in Berlin using it
 sk ▸ Proposed workflow "berlin-current-temperature":
        1. request   GET /v1/forecast?latitude=52.52&longitude=13.41&current=temperature_2m
        2. transform extract { city, time, temperature_c }
      Dry-run preview → { city: "Berlin", temperature_c: 23.7 }. Approve to save?
you ▸ /approve
 sk ▸ Saved "berlin-current-temperature" (v1).
you ▸ run it
 sk ▸ execution succeeded → { city: "Berlin", time: "…", temperature_c: 23.7 }
```

That's the whole loop: **describe → review the proposal + dry-run → `/approve` →
run.** You never hand-write JSON or look up an API shape.

### Slash commands (type `/` for the menu)

The ones you'll reach for, grouped by what they do (verified against the shipped
build):

| Command                                     | Does                                                           |
| ------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/approve` · `/reject`                      | commit the AI's current proposal, or reject it (with a reason) |
| `/preview` · `/probe`                       | dry-run the workflow draft / test the connector draft now      |
| `/draft` · `/connector` · `/workflow`       | inspect the current authoring state                            |
| `/templates`                                | browse connector templates suggested for the draft             |
| `/onboard`                                  | guided wizard: pick a template, enter credentials, probe, save |
| `/versions` · `/restore <n>`                | list committed workflow versions / roll back                   |
| `/skills` · `/knowledge`                    | list reusable context / knowledge sources in scope             |
| `/clear` (`/new`) · `/compact` · `/resume`  | new conversation · shrink history · reattach                   |
| `/setup` · `/status` · `/cost` · `/usage`   | readiness · session+persona · token budget                     |
| `/config` · `/settings`                     | open the searchable settings UI (every engine setting)         |
| `/model` · `/tenant` · `/login` · `/logout` | switch model · switch/list tenants · auth                      |
| `/attach` · `/upload` · `/files`            | attach a file to the message · upload · list files             |
| `/help` · `/exit` (`/quit`)                 | cheat sheet · leave                                            |

Mentions: `@file:<id>` attaches an uploaded file; `@skill:<name>` pulls a Skill
into context. Full walkthrough: [`repl-tour.md`](../authors/repl-tour.md).

> **One-shot / scripted?** The exact same authoring loop runs non-interactively
> with `sk -p "<request>"` — see [Scripting & CI](#scripting--ci-non-interactive).

---

## Step 4 — Inspect what you built

Whether you authored in the REPL or via a script, the artifacts are normal,
versioned resources you can list and run:

```bash
docker compose exec engine sk connectors list                 # name + slug + status
docker compose exec engine sk connectors test <CONNECTOR_ID>  # re-probe connectivity
docker compose exec engine sk workflows run berlin-current-temperature --follow
docker compose exec engine sk executions list --limit 5
docker compose exec engine sk executions result <EXECUTION_ID>  # the value it produced
```

---

## Step 5 — Add a knowledge article

In the REPL you can just say _“add this file as a knowledge source tagged
weather, runbook”_. The scriptable form:

```bash
docker compose cp note.md engine:/tmp/note.md
docker compose exec engine sk knowledge-sources create --file /tmp/note.md \
  --title "Weather Runbook" --tags "weather,runbook,open-meteo"
# ✓ Created knowledge source "Weather Runbook" · 4 chunks
docker compose exec engine sk knowledge-sources list
docker compose exec engine sk knowledge-sources search "open-meteo"   # semantic search; ranks by relevance
```

`--tags` you supply are authoritative (no AI auto-tagging); omit both `--tags`
and `--description` to let the engine generate them.

---

## Step 6 — Use it from Codex / any MCP client

The engine is an **MCP server**, so AI coding tools (Codex, Claude Desktop,
Cursor, …) can drive your governed workflows directly. Mint a Bearer key first
(see [from your own machine](#use-sk-from-your-own-machine-instead-of-docker-exec)).

**A. Streamable HTTP (recommended).** For **Codex** (`~/.codex/config.toml`, or
Settings → MCP Servers) — Codex auto-detects the transport from `url`, and
`bearer_token_env_var` names an env var so the key stays out of the file:

```toml
[mcp_servers.sk]
url = "http://localhost:3000/mcp"
bearer_token_env_var = "SK_API_KEY"
```

```bash
export SK_API_KEY=wf_live_…   # the key from `engine --issue-admin-key`
```

Inline-header JSON shape (Claude Desktop / Cursor):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sk": {
      "url": "http://localhost:3000/mcp",
      "transport": "streamable-http",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer wf_live_…" }
    }
  }
}
```

For **Claude Code**, register from the shell instead — and see
[Use sk from a coding agent](../authors/coding-agents.md) for the full loop
(briefing hook + knowledge import), which this step does not cover:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http --scope user sk http://localhost:3000/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${SK_API_KEY}"
```

Once connected over HTTP, the client sees your tenant's tools — author and run
workflows through the authoring triad (`author_workflow` to build a grounded
draft, `dry_run_workflow` to test it, `edit_workflow_patch` to refine it, and
`save_workflow_draft` to commit), inspect connectors (`test_connector`,
`list_recipes`), ground answers (`search_knowledge_v2`, `read_knowledge`), and
more. Destructive calls require a confirm first.

**B. stdio (local, conversation-only).** After `sk login`, a client can spawn
the bundled proxy, which reads `~/.sk/config.json` so no key handling is needed:

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "sk-cli": { "command": "sk", "args": ["mcp"] } } }
```

This proxy is deliberately narrow: it exposes only `sk_ping` and
`sk_conversation_create` / `_append` / `_get` / `_list`, for driving the
conversation surface from an IDE plugin. It does **not** carry the tool
catalog above — if you want knowledge lookup, workflow authoring, or connector
tools, use the HTTP path.

Verify the HTTP endpoint by hand:

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:3000/mcp \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer wf_live_…" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"0"}}}'
# → 200 with an mcp-session-id response header
```

---

## Use `sk` from your own machine (instead of `docker exec`)

`docker compose exec engine sk …` is the zero-install path. To run `sk` directly on your
host:

```bash
# 1. Install the CLI (also served by your engine at /install)
curl -fsSL http://localhost:3000/install | bash

# 2. Mint a full admin key — prints a ready-to-paste `sk login` line
docker compose exec engine engine --issue-admin-key --tenant my-org
#   run this on your machine to log the host `sk` in:
#     sk login --engine-url http://localhost:3000 --api-key wf_live_…

# 3. Paste that line, then open the REPL on your machine
sk status
sk            # the same conversational REPL, now host-native
```

Host config lives at `~/.sk/config.json`.

---

## Add a teammate (multi-user)

With the local `subkit` provider, an admin provisions each teammate and the
teammate mints their **own** personal API key from a single-use invite — the
admin never sees that key. Three commands, in order:

```bash
# 1. Admin: create the user (roles: admin | member | enduser, default member)
docker compose exec engine sk users create --email teammate@example.com --role member
# created user
#   id     <USER_ID>
#   email  teammate@example.com
#   role   member

# 2. Admin: issue a single-use invite — the wf_invite_ token is shown ONCE
docker compose exec engine sk users invite <USER_ID>
# invite issued for user <USER_ID>
#   token    wf_invite_…
#   expires  …
# the invited user runs:
#   sk join --invite wf_invite_…
```

```bash
# 3. Teammate (on their own machine, no login required): redeem the token to
#    provision a personal API key into their ~/.sk profile
sk join --invite wf_invite_… --engine-url http://localhost:3000
# sk join: joined — profile 'default' saved to ~/.sk/config.json
#   personal api key prefix: wf_live_…
#   next: sk status
```

Hand the token over securely — it works only once. Admins can review or revoke
un-redeemed invites with `sk invites list` and `sk invites revoke <invite-id>`.

---

## Settings — one surface

Every runtime setting is managed with `sk settings` (the REPL's `/config` opens
the same thing):

```bash
docker compose exec engine sk settings list                       # every leaf + value
docker compose exec engine sk settings get llm.provider
docker compose exec engine sk settings set llm.model '"claude-sonnet-4-6"'   # value is JSON
docker compose exec engine sk settings configure                  # interactive UI
```

A few values are **not** `sk settings` on purpose: `MASTER_KEY`, `DATABASE_URL`,
and `ENGINE_LISTEN_HOST` are process bootstrap bindings; `PORT` and
`OBJECT_STORAGE_*` seed an empty database only. `engine --issue-admin-key`
mints an emergency administrator key (after that, `sk apikeys create`). See
[Operator configuration reference](#operator-configuration-reference) below.

---

## Scripting & CI (non-interactive)

The REPL is for humans; these are for automation. Same engine, same governance.

**Headless authoring** — the conversational loop without a TTY (no slash
commands; the AI completes autonomously up to `--max-turns`):

```bash
docker compose exec engine sk -p "Create a keyless HTTP connector named open-meteo for \
https://api.open-meteo.com, endpoint GET /v1/forecast, then probe it." --output text
docker compose exec engine sk -p "list my workflows" --output json
```

**Declarative workflow** — exact and repeatable; `create` runs
**validate → preview (real dry-run) → save**, so a green result proves the
connector works. Save `weather.json` (use your connector id from
`sk connectors list`):

```json
{
  "name": "Berlin Current Temperature",
  "slug": "berlin-current-temperature",
  "steps": [
    {
      "id": "fetch_weather",
      "kind": "request",
      "method": "GET",
      "path": "/v1/forecast",
      "query": {
        "latitude": "52.52",
        "longitude": "13.41",
        "current": "temperature_2m"
      },
      "on_error": "fail",
      "connector_id": "<CONNECTOR_ID>"
    },
    {
      "id": "extract_temperature",
      "kind": "transform",
      "language": "javascript",
      "on_error": "fail",
      "expression": "const c = input.scope.fetch_weather.data.current; return { city: 'Berlin', time: c.time, temperature_c: c.temperature_2m };"
    }
  ]
}
```

```bash
docker cp weather.json subkit:/tmp/weather.json
docker compose exec engine sk workflows create --file /tmp/weather.json   # validate→preview→save
docker compose exec engine sk workflows run berlin-current-temperature --follow
```

**Key-based connector, fully scripted** — create from a template, attach the
credential without a conversation:

```bash
docker compose exec engine sk connectors create --template stripe --name stripe-prod --skip-checks
docker compose exec engine sk credentials set <CONNECTOR_ID> --mode bearer --token sk_live_…
#   modes: bearer | header | query | basic | aws_sigv4 | none  (probes after, unless --skip-checks)
docker compose exec engine sk credentials list <CONNECTOR_ID>
```

---

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom                                              | Cause / fix                                                                                                                            |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `llm_provider_misconfigured` on an AI command        | Provider key missing/wrong: `sk settings set llm.providers.anthropic.api_key '"sk-ant-…"'` (or re-run `sk init`), then `sk -p "ping"`. |
| `bootstrap token expired`                            | Re-run `sk init` (it auto-detects a fresh token) or re-grep the logs (Step 2).                                                         |
| Connector `probe failed`                             | Wrong base URL / endpoint — tell the REPL the correct values and `/probe`.                                                             |
| `validation failed` on `workflows create`            | Check the JSON against the Scripting section; `connector_id` must be a real id from `sk connectors list`.                              |
| Interactive prompt hangs under `docker compose exec` | Run it from an interactive terminal; Compose allocates a TTY by default.                                                               |

---

## Production deployment

The quickstart above uses the same application image as production with a
separate PostgreSQL container. For production, replace that database service
with managed PostgreSQL and put the engine behind your TLS ingress.

### Deployment Topology

sk compiles to a single stateless binary. PostgreSQL backs configuration,
secrets, metadata, the job queue, scheduler, and pub/sub event bus; a private
S3-compatible service stores binary payloads. No message broker, distributed
queue, or local persistent application volume is required.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Internet(("Internet"))
    Proxy["TLS reverse proxy / LB<br/>(your choice)"]
    Engine["engine container<br/>mikebild/subkit"]
    PG[("PostgreSQL")]
    LLM[("LLM Provider<br/>Anthropic / OpenAI / Google")]
    S3[("Private S3-compatible bucket<br/>files + large results")]

    Internet -- :443 --> Proxy
    Proxy -- :3000 --> Engine
    Engine --> PG
    Engine -. outbound .-> LLM
    Engine -. outbound .-> S3
```

| Concern                        | How sk handles it                                                                     |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Queue / scheduler / events** | pg-boss + outbox in PostgreSQL — nothing extra to run                                 |
| **Standard model**             | one stateless engine service + PostgreSQL + private S3-compatible storage             |
| **High availability**          | run multiple engine containers behind a load balancer (no coordination overhead)      |
| **Production database**        | point at [external PostgreSQL](#external-database); engine auto-migrates on boot      |
| **Release-image rehearsal**    | `docker-compose.yml` runs the released engine image and a separate PostgreSQL service |

### Installation

| Channel              | Detail                                                                                                                                                       |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Binaries**         | macOS (Intel + Apple Silicon), Linux (x64 + ARM64), Windows (x64)                                                                                            |
| **Primary binaries** | `sk` (CLI) and the engine — docs and examples use `sk`                                                                                                       |
| **Install script**   | one-liner for bash and PowerShell                                                                                                                            |
| **Container**        | published image for Kubernetes / cloud-native deployments                                                                                                    |
| **Auto-update**      | binaries check on startup and update in place, gated by a signed `SHA256SUMS` — see [`../admins/credentials-and-keys.md`](../admins/credentials-and-keys.md) |

---

## Operator configuration reference

Every **runtime setting** is managed with `sk settings` (get / set / list / `configure`) — that is the one surface you need. The env vars below are deliberately _not_ `sk settings`, and for a reason worth knowing:

- **`MASTER_KEY` / `DATABASE_URL` / `ENGINE_LISTEN_HOST` are process bootstrap.** They're needed _before_ the engine, its database, or its HTTP API exist. `MASTER_KEY` decrypts product secrets, `DATABASE_URL` locates the canonical revision, and `ENGINE_LISTEN_HOST` selects the bind interface.
- **`PORT` and `OBJECT_STORAGE_*` seed revision 1 only.** Once the database contains runtime state, those bindings never override it.
- **`engine --issue-admin-key` is the operator escape hatch for the _first_ key.** `sk` authenticates with an API key, so it can't mint its own first one; that runs directly against the database on the `engine` binary. Once you have a key, `sk apikeys create` mints more through the API.
- **Legacy config is imported explicitly.** Use `engine --bridge-stateless --legacy-config=…`; production startup ignores `SUBKIT_CONFIG`, config files, and `SK_OVERRIDE_*`.

Everything else lives in immutable PostgreSQL revisions. Full leaf reference:
[`../admins/settings-reference.md`](../admins/settings-reference.md); the
surrounding configuration model is
[`../admins/configuration.md`](../admins/configuration.md).

| Env var                | Default                           | Purpose                                                                                                          |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `MASTER_KEY`           | **required**                      | Product-isolated 64-hex AES-256 key for encrypted secret versions. Losing it makes stored secrets unrecoverable. |
| `DATABASE_URL`         | **required**                      | PostgreSQL connection URL. The image does not contain a database server. `DATABASE_URL_FILE` is also supported.  |
| `ENGINE_LISTEN_HOST`   | `0.0.0.0`                         | Bind interface. The image defaults to all-interfaces so `-p` works; leave it.                                    |
| `PORT`                 | `3000`                            | Revision-1 seed for the server port.                                                                             |
| `OBJECT_STORAGE_*`     | **required on an empty database** | Revision-1 private S3 binding: endpoint, region, bucket, credentials, optional session token, and path style.    |
| `SUBKIT_BOOTSTRAP_KEY` | generated if absent               | Optional fixed one-time onboarding key; invalid after completion.                                                |
| `NODE_ENV`             | `production`                      | —                                                                                                                |

### Bring your own MASTER_KEY

```bash
MASTER_KEY="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" docker compose up -d
```

Store it somewhere safe and pass the **same** value on every run — it must stay constant or previously encrypted credentials become unreadable. Rotation procedure: [`../admins/credentials-and-keys.md`](../admins/credentials-and-keys.md).

### External database

Connect the image to PostgreSQL (managed RDS, a separate container, etc.). The
database is mandatory and the engine auto-migrates on boot:

```bash
docker run -d --name subkit -p 3000:3000 \
  -e DATABASE_URL="postgres://user:pass@db-host:5432/subkit" \
  -e MASTER_KEY="<your-64-hex-key>" \
  -e OBJECT_STORAGE_ENDPOINT="https://objects.example.com" \
  -e OBJECT_STORAGE_REGION="garage" \
  -e OBJECT_STORAGE_BUCKET="private-subkit" \
  -e OBJECT_STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY_ID="<access-key-id>" \
  -e OBJECT_STORAGE_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="<secret-access-key>" \
  -e OBJECT_STORAGE_PATH_STYLE="true" \
  mikebild/subkit:<version>
```

### Persistence & upgrades

The engine is stateless. Back up PostgreSQL and the matching private object
bucket; no engine filesystem or `/data` volume participates in recovery. To
upgrade the Compose deployment, change the pinned `SUBKIT_IMAGE_TAG`, pull, and
recreate the engine. Migrations apply automatically on boot:

```bash
SUBKIT_IMAGE_TAG=<new-version> docker compose pull engine
SUBKIT_IMAGE_TAG=<new-version> docker compose up -d engine
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:3000/health
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:3000/ready
```

### Notes & limits

- **Web-scraping connector**: the image includes the Playwright-matched Chromium build and its operating-system libraries.
- **File scanning**: uploads are not virus-scanned by default — see [`../admins/production-hardening.md`](../admins/production-hardening.md) before accepting untrusted uploads.
- **Horizontal scaling**: run multiple engine containers against the same external PostgreSQL database and private object bucket, behind a load balancer. Settings activate only after every healthy replica ACKs the revision digest.

---

## Cleanup & next steps

```bash
docker compose down            # stop and remove containers; preserve volumes
docker compose down --volumes  # also erase application and database data
```

- [**Using the `sk` REPL**](../authors/repl-tour.md) — the primary interface, in depth.
- [`docs/concepts/connectors.md`](../concepts/connectors.md) — connectors, credentials, OAuth2.
- [`docs/concepts/workflows.md`](../concepts/workflows.md) — steps, versioning, scheduling.
- [`docs/authors/authoring-workflows.md`](../authors/authoring-workflows.md) — conversational authoring, skills, knowledge.
- Operator setup (TLS, external DB, settings): [Production deployment](#production-deployment) below.

<!-- Source: docs/developers/step-kinds-reference.md -->

# Step kinds — field reference

> **Audience:** Contributors and integrators who need the exact field contract of every
> step kind. The concept-level view lives in
> [Workflow execution → Step kinds](../concepts/workflows.md#step-kinds).

A Workflow is composed of Steps. sk ships eight Step kinds; the discriminator field is `kind`, and the schema source of truth is [`apps/engine/src/workflows/types.ts`](../../apps/engine/src/workflows/types.ts) (`StepSchema`). There is no `tool` kind (no docker-based sandbox runner) — this is a data-workflow engine, not a container runtime.

| `kind` | Required fields | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `request` | one of `url` / `connector_id` / `sql`; optional `method`, `headers`, `query`, `body`, `pagination`, `graphql`, `sql`, `s3`, `mcp`, `xml`, `expected_statuses`, `expected_row_count`, `idempotency_key`, `outputs`, `side_effects` | Calls a connector endpoint. Routed through the connector's driver (HTTP, GraphQL, Postgres, S3, MCP) with the tenant's credentials and the governance layer. Each non-HTTP driver is a SUB-BLOCK of `request`, never a step kind of its own, so retry, backoff, `error_policy`, `response_filters` and the versioned output envelope apply identically whichever driver runs. The `mcp` block names one of three operations — `call_tool` (with `tool`), `read_resource` (with `uri`), `get_prompt` (with `prompt`) — against a connector whose driver is `mcp`. Every `call_tool` returns the envelope `{ content, structured_content }`: the typed half is what the remote promised conforms to its declared `outputSchema`, kept separate rather than merged, and `null` when the tool declared none — so a server that later adds an output schema fills the key in instead of re-shaping the output of a saved workflow. `read_resource` and `get_prompt` return their payload verbatim, because the protocol gives neither a typed half. The operation named in the step decides the shape; the reply never does. Connector tests and request steps share the same request execution core, so authoring-time probes and runtime behaviour stay aligned. |
| `transform` | `expression` (for `javascript`); optional `language` (`javascript` — the default and only expression language — or one of the web-scraper extractors `readability` / `html-to-markdown` / `structured-data`), `input_schema`, `output_schema`, `silence_warnings` | Reshapes data between steps. The expression is a sandboxed JavaScript function body with an explicit `return`: upstream step outputs are at `input.scope.<id>.data`, the workflow input at `input.input`, and (inside a loop body) the current item at `input.scope.$item`. JSONata is not a transform language — it survives only in the one-line slots (`loop.over`, `branch.when`, `output_transform`, `data_selector`, `${scope.x.data}` interpolation). The web-scraper extractors carry no `expression` and read the upstream HTML body. No network access, bounded heap and wall-clock per `SANDBOX_MEMORY_LIMIT_BYTES` / `TRANSFORM_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT_MS` (overridable via `sandbox.transform_wall_ms`). |
| `branch` | `when`, `then_steps[]`; optional `else_steps[]` | Deterministic conditional routing. The engine evaluates `when` against scope and dispatches the matching branch — no inference, no fallthrough. |
| `loop` | `body[]`; exactly one of `over` or `data_selector`; optional `fail_fast` | Iterates a collection, executing `body` per item. Inside the body the current item is `$item` (JSONata expressions) / `${item.…}` (request placeholder strings), plus the zero-based `$loop_index`. `fail_fast: true` stops the loop at the first body failure governed by `on_error: "fail"`; the default preserves collect-all behaviour. `item_var` is retired: authoring it is rejected (`validateWorkflowDef`); historical stored versions that declared it keep executing unchanged. `data_selector` is the JS expression form (preferred for new loops, surfaces real exceptions); `over` is the legacy path/JSONata form. |
| `parallel` | `branches[][]` | Executes multiple step sequences concurrently and merges their results. The engine fans out, awaits all branches, then continues. |
| `wait` | `duration_ms` (≤ 24 h) | Deliberate delay for polling, rate-limit management, or human-paced flows. |
| `wait_for_event` | `event_name`, `timeout_ms`; optional `match`, `on_timeout` | Signal-driven HITL pause. The runner inserts a `workflow_waits` checkpoint, polls `workflow_signals` at 1 s cadence, and resumes when a matching signal arrives or `timeout_ms` elapses. The runner does NOT implicitly skip downstream steps on timeout — the workflow author MUST follow the wait with an explicit `branch` step that gates the success vs timeout path on `$.steps.<wait_id>.timed_out`. |
| `call` | one of `workflow_id` or `workflow_slug`; optional `input` | Invokes another workflow. Recursion is capped by `MAX_CALL_DEPTH` (5). |

Every step also accepts the shared base fields `id`, `on_error` (`fail` \| `continue`), `data_selector`, and `timeout_ms`.

## Read/write classification

Request steps carry an optional `side_effects: "read" | "write"` field. When unset, the driver classifies at dispatch time: HTTP `GET`/`HEAD`/`OPTIONS` = read, other methods = write; GraphQL `query` = read, `mutation`/`subscription` = write; SQL SELECT-only = read, anything else = write; S3 GET/HEAD/LIST = read; MCP `read_resource` and `get_prompt` = read, `call_tool` = **write**. A remote MCP tool gets no benefit of the doubt: the specification's `readOnlyHint` is optional and is asserted by the same party whose side effects it describes, so the engine does not read it — an external tool call is a write until someone inside the tenant says otherwise. Set `"read"` explicitly for a POST that is semantically a search, or `"write"` to force-hold a GET that mutates server state. A read override cannot downgrade PUT, PATCH, DELETE, or an S3 mutation; validation rejects new definitions and runtime classification keeps legacy definitions held.

The classification drives dry-run previews: a `dry_run_workflow` preview HOLDS WRITES by default. Read steps execute live against the real upstream; write steps (sends, posts, publishes) are fully resolved — URL, headers, the materialized body — but never dispatched; the held request is recorded as the step artifact. The instruction-grounded preview judge reads the held payloads. In permission mode `auto`, a green judged preview may persist inline; in `ask` or `plan`, it returns `save_required` and the normal human save gate decides. Executing writes for real during a preview requires explicit user confirmation (`execute_writes: true`).

## Wait-for-event timeout pattern

The `wait_for_event` step's `timeout_ms` bounds the per-step wait window. The surrounding `WorkflowDef.timeout_ms` (the workflow envelope) must be ≥ the wait step's bound — the `WorkflowDefSchema` `superRefine` enforces this at save time so a 24 h approval window can't be silently truncated by a 6 h workflow timeout. In practice the envelope should leave headroom for the post-wait merge / abandon transitions; e.g. a 24 h wait inside a 25 h workflow.

Because the runner does not auto-skip downstream steps on timeout, every wait-for-event workflow needs an explicit `branch` step that gates the success vs timeout path. The canonical example is the **`merge-pr-after-approval`** recipe under the GitHub template (`apps/engine/src/connectors/templates.json`): it opens a PR, waits up to 24 h for an external `pr_approved` signal, and routes through a branch step (`when: $boolean($.steps.await_approval.timed_out)`) into either a `merge` request or an `abandon_on_timeout` transform. Cancel-race semantics for human-paused workflows are documented in [`apps/engine/src/conversations/abort.ts`](../../apps/engine/src/conversations/abort.ts) (single-replica caveat, tenant-scoped registry, expected reasons).

## Further reading

- [Workflow execution](../concepts/workflows.md) — the model: lifecycle, triggers, versioning, self-healing.
- [Recipe authoring contract](./recipes.md) — how these step kinds compose into shipped recipes.

<!-- Source: docs/developers/tool-palette.md -->

# Tool palette and dispatch

Every action an LLM can take against sk is a named tool that goes through one registry, one
policy gate, and one audit trail. There are no ad-hoc calls and no surface that quietly
skips a permission check: a write is gated identically whether it arrives over chat or over
MCP.

> **Status:** authoritative. See
> [`apps/engine/src/tools/`](../../apps/engine/src/tools/) for the
> implementation and the subsystem map in `AGENTS.md` ("Architecture And Domain Safety").

## Why this exists

The engine speaks "LLM tool-calling" across two surfaces:

| Surface | Transport | Entry point |
|---|---|---|
| **Chat** | Anthropic-SDK tool calls in a conversation turn | `conversations/tools/sdk-wrap.ts` |
| **MCP** | `tools/list` + `tools/call` over Model Context Protocol | `apps/engine/src/mcp/` |

Before the unified palette, those two paths each owned their own dispatch,
schema, RBAC, audit, and policy. Two failure modes followed:

- **Literal duplication.** `test_connector` existed twice — as a
  `ConversationTool` (`conversations/tools/test-connector.ts`) *and* as an
  MCP-only file (`mcp/tools/test-connector.ts`) — both calling the same
  `probeConnector()` driver and `recordConnectorInvoked()` recorder.
- **Divergent gates.** Chat and MCP each carried their own confirm gate, and
  they disagreed on `tenant_read` escalation: a `probe_connector` POST against
  prod gated correctly on chat and **silently bypassed** on MCP.

One registry, one dispatcher, one policy gate, and one envelope shape close
both gaps. The MCP-side gate is gone; `tools/policy.ts:policyDecide()` is the
only confirm decision in the engine. Per-surface adapters render that single
envelope into MCP transport or chat SDK shape — the only place surface
differences live.

## Concepts

### ToolDescriptor

```ts
interface ToolDescriptor {
  name: string;
  description: string;
  category: "draft_write" | "tenant_read" | "tenant_write";
  inputSchema: unknown; // Zod for conversation tools; JSON Schema for static
  disabled?: { reason: string };
  requires_skill?: string;
}
```

| Field | Role |
|---|---|
| `category` | Drives the policy decision — see *Policy gate (unified)*. |
| `disabled` | Marks a tool `tools/call` rejects with a `not_available_on_surface` envelope pointing at `conversation_start`. |
| `requires_skill` | Gates the tool behind a granted skill. |

**Draft-write tools are HIDDEN from MCP `tools/list`, not badged.** Earlier
they were listed-with-`disabled` as an "honest signal" that the tool exists but
isn't headlessly callable. In practice external clients (e.g. claude.ai) ignore
the `_meta.subkit.disabled` badge, call the tool anyway, get rejected, and churn
instead of authoring — so the catalog `list()` now omits draft-write on MCP
entirely, steering the model to `conversation_start` (the only working authoring
entry point). `resolve()` deliberately still returns the disabled descriptor so
the call-time `not_available_on_surface` backstop stays intact for any client
that guesses the bare name. List and resolve intentionally disagree here, which
is safe because such a call can never execute on this surface.

### Surface

`"chat" | "mcp"` — drives visibility filtering and envelope rendering. No
surface-specific logic in the dispatcher itself; per-surface concerns live in
adapters.

### Chat read-only palette

The `"chat"` surface never sees the full catalog. After the normal
`(surface, mcpMode)` visibility filter, the visible set is intersected with a
fixed name allow-list — `CHAT_READONLY_TOOLS` in
`conversations/tools/authoring-palette.ts`, applied by
`filterByChatReadOnlyPalette()` and resolved per turn in `sdk-wrap.ts`.

The palette is **fail-closed**: an allow-list, not a deny-list. A tool absent
from the set is never dispatched on chat — not if it exists in the registry,
not if the linked user's RBAC would permit it, and not if a granted skill
would surface it in an authoring turn. New tools stay invisible to chat until
explicitly added to the set (guarded by
`conversations/tools/tests/sdk-wrap-chat-surface.test.ts`, which asserts
nothing leaks past it). The set is independent of skill state and tool
category — channel-scoped, not role-scoped.

| Group | Tools |
|---|---|
| Conversational meta | `ask_user_confirm` · `ask_user_choice` · `ask_user_multi` · `ask_user_text` · `ask_user_form` · `cannot_help` · `list_skills` · `load_skill` · `list_attachments` · `preview_attachment` · `get_raw_result` |
| Knowledge + docs (read) | `search_knowledge` · `read_knowledge` · `search_docs` · `list_knowledge_sources` · `get_knowledge_source` |
| Workflows (read) | `list_workflows` · `get_workflow` · `find_workflow` |
| Executions (read) | `list_executions` · `get_execution` · `inspect_execution` · `inspect_execution_step` |
| Connector metadata (read) | `list_connectors` · `get_connector` · `find_connector` |
| Skills (read) | `get_skill` · `find_skill` |
| Schedules (read) | `list_schedules` |
| Run | `run_workflow` |

Deliberately absent: `call_connector`, `probe_connector`, `test_connector`,
the `discover_*` probes, every `draft_write` authoring tool, every
`tenant_write` mutation, and external-MCP tools. Connector access on chat is
metadata-only.

### Catalog grouping on the read tools

`list_workflows` and `find_workflow` return a derived `category` (the catalog
block) and `connectors` (the connector slugs the current version uses) on every
item, and accept both as filters:

| Param | Tools | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `category` | `list_workflows` · `find_workflow` · `list_connectors` · `find_connector` | Restrict to one catalog block |
| `connector` | `list_workflows` · `find_workflow` | Restrict to workflows using that connector (id or slug) |

Workflow categories are derived from the slug corpus — a leading slug segment
shared by at least three workflows forms a block, everything else collects under
`other` — so read a category value off a previous result rather than inventing
one. A connector's category is simply its driver. The `connector` filter counts
both binding forms: a step's `connector_id` **and** a
`${connector.<slug>.base_url}` URL, so a placeholder-only dependant is not
missed. List responses also carry a `categories` array giving the blocks in
render order, which is what `sk` and any dashboard should follow instead of
re-deriving the ordering.

`run_workflow` (with its synthetic `wf_<slug>` peers) is the one action in
the set — running a *saved* workflow. It stays behind
`resolveExecutionToolGate` (default-deny without a bound or explicitly named
saved workflow), per-user RBAC, and the confirm policy, which chat renders as
a native approval card only the requester can confirm. See the *Chat adapter*
section below and the operator page [../operators/chat.md](../operators/chat.md).

### ToolEnvelope (status-discriminated)

```ts
type ToolEnvelope =
  | { status: "ok"; data: unknown; pause?; committed_workflow_id? }
  | { status: "error"; error_code; message; details?; next_best_actions? }
  | { status: "needs_confirm"; confirm: ConfirmEnvelope }
  | { status: "paused"; pause: ToolResultPause }
  | { status: "not_available_on_surface"; reason: string };
```

Replaces the legacy `ok: true | false` discriminated union from
`conversations/tools/index.ts:178`. The status discriminator makes the surface
adapters trivially total — each adapter has exactly one case per status.

### Provider, Registry, Dispatcher

Providers contribute descriptors + executors:

| Provider | Contributes |
|---|---|
| `StaticToolProvider` | MCP-unique handlers: `authenticate`, `list_recipes`, `self_healing.scan`, plus admin-only `subkit_settings` and `subkit_update_setting`. |
| `ConversationToolProvider` | everything in `conversations/tools/index.ts:listTools()`, filtered per `(surface, mcpMode, readOnly)`. |

`buildRegistry(providers)` enforces cross-provider name uniqueness at boot.
`registry.get(name, filter)` resolves an executor; `registry.list(filter)` gives
the visible catalog.

`dispatchTool(deps, invocation)` runs one pipeline for both surfaces:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Call["tool call (chat or MCP)"] --> Resolve{"registry.get(name)"}
    Resolve -->|miss| NotFound["tool_not_found"]
    Resolve -->|hit| Vis{"descriptor.disabled?"}
    Vis -->|yes| NAS["not_available_on_surface<br/>→ conversation_start"]
    Vis -->|no| Confirm{"carries a confirm marker?"}
    Confirm -->|yes| Claim["consumeApproval(confirm_id)<br/>single-use CAS → replayed args"]
    Confirm -->|no| Canon["canonicalize args<br/>(inputSchema.safeParse, once)"]
    Claim --> Rbac
    Canon --> Rbac{"can(permission, resource)"}
    Rbac -->|deny| Denied["policy_denied<br/>audit: POLICY_DENIED"]
    Rbac -->|allow| Policy{"policyDecide(category)"}
    Policy -->|tenant_read · safe input| Proceed["proceed"]
    Policy -->|tenant_write · destructive input| Request["needs_confirm<br/>requestApproval → APPROVAL_REQUESTED"]
    Policy -->|surface mismatch| NAS
    Proceed --> Approve["claimed? recordApprovalApproved<br/>audit: APPROVAL_APPROVED"]
    Approve --> Exec["execute executor"]
    Exec --> Norm["normalize → ToolEnvelope"]
    Norm --> Log["log: tool.dispatch.invoke"]
```

The stages in order: **resolve** → `tool_not_found` on miss · **visibility** →
`not_available_on_surface` on `disabled` · **confirm** → a confirm marker claims
the stored approval and replays its args · **canonicalize** → the tool's own Zod
schema parses the args that will execute, exactly once · **rbac** → `can()` on
those args, before the gate, so an unauthorized caller never opens an approval ·
**policy** → `proceed | needs_confirm | not_available` · **approve** → the claim
that survived rbac + policy writes `APPROVAL_APPROVED` · **execute** the resolved
executor · **normalize** into a `ToolEnvelope` · **log** one `tool.dispatch.invoke`
event per call.

`canonicalize` runs on the first call only. The args stored with the approval were
already canonicalized at grant time, so a replay hands them to the executor
untouched — a schema whose transform is not idempotent cannot corrupt its own
approved payload. It follows that a `ConversationTool` executor **never re-parses
its own input**: the dispatcher is the boundary, and it parses exactly once.

### Policy gate (unified)

`policyDecide()` (`tools/policy.ts`) is a **pure synchronous function** and the
engine's only confirm decision — chat, MCP, and the conversation fast-path all
call it and none re-derives the answer. It has no I/O: the durable half of the
gate lives in `tools/approval.ts`, and audit is emitted by the dispatcher.

```ts
type PolicyDecision =
  | { kind: "proceed" }
  | { kind: "needs_confirm"; envelope: ConfirmEnvelope }
  | { kind: "not_available_on_surface"; reason: string };
```

| Category | Read / write | Default decision |
|---|---|---|
| `tenant_read` | reads tenant state | `proceed` (unless input predicates escalate it) |
| `tenant_write` | mutates tenant state | `needs_confirm` for destructive input |
| `draft_write` | authors a draft | MCP: `not_available_on_surface`; chat: in-loop |

**No `tenant_read` shortcut.** The deleted MCP-side gate returned `proceed` for
every `tenant_read` tool, ignoring `computeModeFromInput` predicates. The unified
gate runs `decideToolMode` for every category — a `tenant_read` tool without a
dynamic predicate still resolves to `no_confirm`, so the common case is unchanged
and `probe_connector` POST against prod now gates on both surfaces.

### Approvals (`tools/approval.ts`)

An approval is a **capability handle, not a re-transmission challenge**.

| Function | Role |
|---|---|
| `requestApproval` | Persists the canonical args (AES-256-GCM, AAD-bound to `tenant_id:approval_id`) and the `APPROVAL_REQUESTED` row in one transaction. |
| `consumeApproval` | Claims the handle with one atomic CAS on `(id, tenant_id, principal_id, tool, surface)` and returns the decrypted args to replay. Every CAS outcome but success writes `APPROVAL_REJECTED`. |
| `recordApprovalApproved` | Writes `APPROVAL_APPROVED` after RBAC and policy pass, immediately before the executor runs. |

The confirmation carries an **id and nothing else**. The client never re-sends the
payload, so there is nothing for the model to swap between preview and approval,
and a ~50 KB body is approvable. A claim is not yet an approval: it burns the
single-use handle, then still has to survive RBAC and the policy gate — a grant
revoked between preview and confirm denies, and the `POLICY_DENIED` row anchors on
the approval's `(resource_type, resource_id)` so the contradiction is one JOIN.
Handles expire after `APPROVAL_TTL_MS` (15 min), measured entirely on Postgres'
clock.

## Adapters

The dispatcher is surface-agnostic; adapters translate the single `ToolEnvelope`
into each surface's wire shape.

### MCP adapter (`mcp/adapter.ts`)

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `listToolsViaRegistry(opts)` | `Tool[]` for `tools/list`. |
| `callToolViaDispatcher(opts)` | `{isError, content[], _meta}` for `tools/call`. |
| `buildMcpStubCtx(opts)` | minimal `ToolContext` so conversation tools run against an MCP caller without a real conversation session. |

Envelope rendering:

| ToolEnvelope.status        | MCP response                                                                                  |
|----------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `ok`                       | `{isError:false, content:[text(JSON.stringify(data))]}`                                       |
| `error`                    | `{isError:true,  content:[text({error_code, message, details, next_best_actions})]}`          |
| `needs_confirm`            | `{isError:false, content:[text(confirm)], _meta:{subkit:{confirm}}}`                          |
| `paused`                   | `{isError:false, content:[text(pause)],   _meta:{subkit:{paused}}}`                           |
| `not_available_on_surface` | `{isError:true,  content:[text({error_code:"not_available_on_surface", reason})], _meta:...}` |

### Chat adapter (`conversations/tools/dispatch-adapter.ts`)

The palette this surface exposes is the fixed
[chat read-only palette](#chat-read-only-palette) above.

- `invokeForSdk(opts)` — single entry point for the chat loop. **Not wired into
  `sdk-wrap.ts` yet** — the chat path stays on its existing inline wrapping
  (which owns rate-limiting, signal handling, event emission, and draft-state
  diff emission). The adapter exists so a future cutover lands in one focused
  change.
- `envelopeToToolResult(envelope)` — back-converts to the legacy `ToolResult`
  shape the conversation loop expects today. The `needs_confirm` case becomes an
  `ask_user_confirm` pause so the elicitation loop picks it up unchanged.

## MCP session and confirmation tools

A handful of MCP tools are not LLM palette items at all — they are the session
orchestration an external client uses to drive an authoring conversation and to
satisfy the write gate. They dispatch through the same RBAC and audit chokepoint,
but they manage *the conversation*, not a tenant resource.

### The conversation cluster

| Tool | Role |
|---|---|
| `conversation_start` | Open a new authoring conversation from a described outcome; returns the `conversation_id`. |
| `conversation_append` | Add the next user message and enqueue the next authoring turn. |
| `conversation_get` | Read-only poll of a conversation's state — completion status, pending elicitation, and the live progress heartbeat (below). |
| `conversation_respond_elicitation` | Resolve a pending elicitation (a form answer, an approval, an OAuth acknowledgement) and enqueue the following turn. |
| `conversation_commit` | Report the persisted commit state of the conversation's workflow — version written, steps present, read from the persisted rows. Read-only; a draft with unpersisted edits returns a NOT COMMITTED error. |

These five are the complete session surface. Authoring turns run in a background
worker (a real turn outlasts the MCP client timeout), so a client `conversation_start`s
or `conversation_append`s, then polls `conversation_get` until the turn reports
`completed`, `failed`, or `input_required`. The [Input Surfaces](./input-surfaces.md#mcp-integration)
page documents the Tasks-capable vs. non-Tasks polling contract in full.

### Worker-stamped heartbeat

A backgrounded turn has no open stream to report progress on, so the worker stamps
its progress into the conversation row as it goes. `conversation_get` returns that
heartbeat so a polling client can render live status instead of a bare spinner:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `phase` | The stage the turn is in (e.g. grounding, drafting, dry-running, critiquing). |
| `elapsed_ms` | Wall-clock elapsed since the turn started. |
| `last_action` | The most recent tool or pipeline step the worker took. |
| `step` | The workflow step currently being authored or tested, when applicable. |

The heartbeat is advisory telemetry for the operator's benefit; the authoritative
terminal signal is still the completion status. A stalled or slow turn is visible
as a growing `elapsed_ms` against an unchanged `last_action`.

### `confirm_tool_call`

**`confirm_tool_call` is a trigger, not a gate.** It cannot approve anything. An
approval is minted UNGRANTED (`granted_at IS NULL`), and the claim CAS demands
`granted_at IS NOT NULL`, which only `grantApproval` sets, and which only a human
channel reaches. So every client may call `confirm_tool_call`, and it succeeds iff a
person already said yes. There is no capability-based refusal, because there is
nothing left for one to protect.

**A human approves out of band, through the approval portal.** The gated call
returns `needs_confirm` carrying a `tool_call_id` (the trigger handle), an
`approval_url` (the human channel), and an `approval.requested` audit row that
persists the encrypted arguments and the `would_write` preview. A person opens the
link, sees exactly what will be written, and grants or declines — one atomic CAS,
recorded as `approval.granted` / `approval.declined`. Afterwards the model relays
`confirm_tool_call({ tool, confirm_id })`, or — if it can set `_meta` — re-issues
with `_meta.sk_confirm: true` + `_meta.sk_confirm_id: <tool_call_id>`. Both are the
same trigger, and both fail with `approval_not_granted` until the human decides.
There is no second door to bolt, because neither door opens by itself.

**A fulfilled native elicitation is a human grant channel.** Conversation workers
persist their confirmation and end the turn; a later `conversation_get` or
`tasks/get` can only resolve it through the active MCP session's
`elicitation/create(mode: form)` request. That delivery is leased, the answer is
stamped `human/in_band_elicitation`, and only then may the harness grant and claim
the held call. A model relay through `conversation_respond_elicitation` is still
refused for approval-bearing rows. Standalone registry/workflow calls retain the
approval-portal flow because they have no persisted conversation task to resume.

**No path re-sends the arguments.** `confirm_tool_call` publishes no `arguments`
property at all, and on the `_meta` path the dispatcher discards whatever the client
re-sent. The engine replays the args it already holds under that `confirm_id` (see
*Approvals* above). The approval is the human's; the model only fires the trigger.
Every path is audited identically.

## Self-diagnosis: `includeStepResults`

`dry_run_workflow` and `run_workflow` accept an optional `includeStepResults` flag.
When set, the response carries the raw per-step inputs and outputs for the run
alongside the normal summary. This is the self-diagnosis lever: an authoring client
(or an operator) that gets an unexpected result can read exactly what each step
received and emitted without a second round-trip, then feed that back into a patch
edit. It is off by default because the raw payloads can be large; turn it on only
when you need step-level forensics.

## Decisions and trade-offs

### Probe + test stay separate (no merge)

| Tool | Operation |
|---|---|
| `test_connector` | driver health check |
| `probe_connector` | caller-specified HTTP on a saved connector |
| `probe_connector_draft` | caller HTTP on a pre-creation envelope |

These are **three semantically distinct operations**. The early plan considered
merging probe+test under one tool with a `mode` arg; the audit found two RBAC
permissions, two audit shapes, and two rate-limit semantics — merging them hides
operational distinctions under one schema. We keep all three names; the MCP-side
duplicate of `test_connector` is the only thing deleted.

### `save_workflow_draft` and `dry_run_workflow` are MCP-hidden

Both are draft-write tools: OMITTED from MCP `tools/list`, and a direct
`tools/call` short-circuits to `not_available_on_surface` with a reason pointing
to `conversation_start`. They are driven by the engine's internal authoring loop
inside a conversation, never by the external client.

| Tool | Why it can't run standalone on MCP |
|---|---|
| `save_workflow_draft` | needs an MCP-side confirm protocol that doesn't exist standalone — the `ask_user_confirm` elicitation is conversation-shaped. |
| `dry_run_workflow` | needs a `def`/`draft_id` input extension — it only reads `ctx.getDraft()`. |

Listing them as callable — even badged disabled — only traps clients that ignore
the badge into calling and churning, so they are hidden outright.

### External-reaching tools are in-palette, not a side channel

A few tools reach *outside* the engine's own state to live upstream surfaces —
`call_connector` (invokes a saved connector), `discover_connector_endpoints`
(fetches and parses a spec), and `fetch_connector_self_description` (live-fetches
a connector's *own* published docs). These are open-world by nature, but they are
still ordinary palette entries: same registry, same `policyDecide()` gate, same
`tool.dispatch.invoke` audit. Egress is guarded and size-capped inside the
executor; nothing about reaching the network earns a bypass.

`fetch_connector_self_description` (`{ connector_id?, kind?: "llms" | "openapi" |
"graphql" | "all" }`) is a `tenant_read` MCP tool — it appears in `tools/list`
and live-fetches the link the connector remembers in its `self_description.links[]`
metadata, transiently, persisting nothing. It is **not** an HTTP route, so it does
**not** appear in the engine OpenAPI spec; the connector's own machine docs
(`llms_txt`, `llms_full`, `openapi`, `graphql`) are described in
[Connectors → Connector Self-Description](../concepts/connectors.md#connector-self-description).

### Remote MCP entries: sk as an MCP client

sk is an MCP *server* to its own clients and an MCP *client* to servers a tenant
connects. The second half lands in this same palette. Every enabled connector
whose driver is `mcp` has its remote surface merged in, so a message naming a
remote tool dispatches in one call rather than a lookup-then-invoke pair.

**Where the servers live.** In `connectors`, like every other integration.
There is no separate MCP registry table, no separate CRUD surface, and no
separate credential store — an external MCP server is created, patched,
enabled, disabled, and deleted through `/v1/connectors` and `sk connectors`.

**Naming.** `mcp_<connector_slug>__<entry>`. The slug half cannot contain `__`
(a DB `CHECK` on `connectors.slug` enforces it), which is what makes the double
underscore an unambiguous split point. `buildMcpToolName` owns the grammar and
**refuses** a pair it cannot address rather than truncating it — a truncated
name still routes, just possibly to a different server. The composed name is
bounded at 64 characters and matches `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$`; no dots.

**Entries are not all remote tools.** Each entry is a `PaletteOperationSpec` —
a name, a schema, and the one remote operation it issues. A remote tool supplies
one each. Where the negotiated capabilities declare resources or prompts, four
engine-minted adapters are added per server: `list_resources`, `read_resource`,
`list_prompts`, `get_prompt`. Adapters appear **only** where the capability was
declared, so the model is never offered an entry whose every call is a protocol
error.

**They are ordinary palette entries.** Same registry, same `policyDecide()`
gate, same durable approval handle, same `tool.dispatch.invoke` audit, same
turn mutex, and an `mcp_external_tool:invoke` RBAC check. The `mcp_` prefix is
what `isDangerousTool` and `getApprovalMode` key on, so every remote entry
confirms before running under `auto` / `ask` / `plan`.

**A server's self-description reaches the model, never the gate.** A remote's
`annotations` (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`) are carried into the entry
description and the audit metadata, and are consulted by no gate whatsoever. A
`tools/call` is a write no matter what the server claims about itself —
`readOnlyHint` is optional, unverified, and asserted by the party whose side
effects it describes. The engine-minted read adapters are the one exception,
and they are reads by the engine's own construction: each is pinned to one
retrieval method and none can reach `tools/call`. Only a tenant-side author can
reclassify a call, with `side_effects: "read"` on a workflow step.

**Results are persisted whole, truncated for the model.** The full remote
payload goes into the tool-call row; the model sees a truncated view, and
`get_raw_result` retrieves the rest.

### Status-discriminated envelope vs. flat `ok` boolean

The legacy `ToolResult` carried `pause` on both `ok:true` and `ok:false`
branches — an awkward shape because "paused but failed" is not a real state.
Status discrimination makes the four valid states explicit and totally
narrowable.

### No HTTP `/v1/tools/:name` surface (yet)

The dispatcher is surface-agnostic, but adding a third per-surface adapter
without a caller violates YAGNI. When an HTTP caller appears, the adapter is a
40-line file.

### Audit lives in the dispatcher

`policyDecide()` is pure. Audit emission (`APPROVAL_REQUESTED`,
`APPROVAL_APPROVED`) happens in the dispatcher around the policy decision. This
keeps the gate testable without DB and centralizes the audit semantics. Per-tool
audits (e.g. `recordConnectorInvoked` inside `test_connector`) continue to fire
from inside the tool's executor.

### Elicitation audit is a tri-state — transport ≠ approval

An elicitation resolve audit row carries up to three independent facts, and they
must not be conflated:

| Fact | Values | Records |
|---|---|---|
| `action` | `APPROVAL_APPROVED` · `APPROVAL_REJECTED` | the *governance decision* |
| `decision_reason` | `user_declined`, `oauth_timeout`, `oauth_elicitation_transport_failed`, … | machine code behind a cancel |
| `elicitation_transport` | `succeeded` · `failed` | whether a `protocol_native` bridge round-trip *delivered* — not whether it was approved |

Crucially, `elicitation_transport: "succeeded"` can coexist with a `cancelled`
resolution: a clean bridge round-trip whose operator declined, or did not
acknowledge an OAuth authorization, succeeded *as transport* but rejected *as a
decision*. An audit query for "successful elicitations" must therefore filter on
`action` / `decision_reason`, not on `elicitation_transport` — equating transport
success with approval double-counts every declined-but-delivered prompt.

A broken transport is *not* a decision at all: when an `ask_user_*` bridge
round-trip fails in transit (or a client auto-cancels the form faster than a
human could render it), the row is **demoted to the portal DB-pause** — it
stays `pending`, the conversation stays `awaiting_input`, and the audit trail
records `ELICITATION_DEMOTED_TO_PORTAL`, never `APPROVAL_REJECTED`. Only the
OAuth OOB flow resolves its approval handle on transport failure
(`oauth_elicitation_transport_failed`), because its state row survives
independently and a retried `authenticate_oauth` resumes the same flow.

### Secret answers never transit the transcript or LLM context

A connector credential the operator supplies never lands in the conversation
transcript, a persisted tool-call row, or the model's replayed context:

- **Over MCP** a secret-shaped form is never sent as `mode: form`. For an unsaved
  bearer, basic, header, query, or AWS SigV4 connector draft, the engine converts
  it to a single-use `mode: url` elicitation. Submission stages the value only for
  the draft probe; a green probe atomically persists the connector and encrypted
  credential. Saved connectors use the corresponding reauthentication URL flow.
  Clients without URL elicitation can still expose the persisted setup action from
  `conversation_get`, but the secret is never accepted through chat text.
- When a secret **is** typed into the sanctioned CLI/web masked form, its answer
  value is projected to `***redacted***` at the single persist chokepoint
  (`resolveElicitation`), and credential subtrees in
  `save_connector_draft` / `update_connector_draft` args are scrubbed before the
  tool-call row is written. The raw value still flows in-memory into the credential
  cache and is stored AES-256-GCM-encrypted; only a by-reference credential lands
  in the draft.

The scrub is field-metadata-driven (it masks exactly the fields the form marked
secret) and targeted (only known credential-bearing tool args) — never a blanket
high-entropy sweep, which would corrupt authored workflow code.

## Layout

```
apps/engine/src/tools/
├── types.ts                    ToolDescriptor, ToolEnvelope, ToolInvocation, etc.
├── registry.ts                 ToolRegistry interface + buildRegistry()
├── policy.ts                   policyDecide() — pure unified policy gate
```
